sources.title: Learn, Earn or Quit: Garry Tan's career framework for choosing jobs in 2022
sources.originalTitle: LEARN, EARN or QUIT | My job/career advice for 2022
sources.summary: Garry Tan argues every job should be judged by whether you are learning, earning, or both, and that you should quit if it is neither. Early in a career, learn first by building real things or winning real customers, then earn, ideally through equity, while avoiding the hedonic treadmill.

principles.text: Judge any job by two tests: are you learning, are you earning? If neither, leave.
principles.quote: are you learning or are you earning if both you're in a great place if it's one or the other that's good too if it's neither it's time to move on you're wasting your life

principles.text: Early in your career, learn first, then earn. Reversing the order risks slow learning and the hedonic treadmill.
principles.quote: learn first then earn that's the best strategy if you try and do it in reverse and you try to earn first you'll probably still learn but maybe slowly

principles.text: Hustlers break in by doing the work unasked: build the improvement for a product you like, or send founders customers.
principles.quote: if you see a product website or service that you like and you have some improvements you can suggest you gotta build it or design it or write it yourself and then cold email them

principles.text: Don't wait for the perfect problem. Start building something real; you only learn creating by doing.
principles.quote: it just has to be a real problem that your software can actually solve

principles.text: A great thing you made beats a credential and puts you in the top 10 percent without a pedigree.
principles.quote: when you create something impressive that users love it's better than a credential

principles.text: Equity is the highest form of earning, and founders or early employees can learn while they earn.
principles.quote: to make the most amount of money you need to create true wealth by owning the stock of a company that became worth a lot of money

sources.title: How to find a billion-dollar startup idea: avoid mimesis, use your unique experience, notice gaps
sources.originalTitle: Billion dollar startup ideas
sources.summary: Garry Tan argues most founders copy whatever is already successful (photo sharing, travel plans, local events) because desire is mimetic. Real breakout ideas come from unusual personal experience (Flexport, Patreon), start as toys, and are found by working on hard problems while noting gaps and anomalies.

principles.text: Don't copy the ideas that are already hot; desire is mimetic and crowds produce infinite competition.
principles.quote: Everyone's making the same photo-sharing, podcasting, travel plans, local event apps. Probably because desire is mimetic. We want what other people want.

principles.text: Great startup ideas look like toys at the start, so lack of obvious fame is not a signal against an idea.
principles.quote: the most famous startups were not famous at the moment when they were started.

principles.text: Your unique, different experiences are the raw material for innovative connections and a winning idea.
principles.quote: What makes you new, different and unique in the world will be the exact thing that makes you succeed.

principles.text: Look for founders and ideas rooted in deep, intimate knowledge of a domain, like Ryan Petersen's supply chain experience behind Flexport.
principles.quote: My favorite pitch meetings are with founders who teach you something about the world you didn't know before.

principles.text: You don't need to be novel, but if there's competition you must be clearly better, faster or cheaper.
principles.quote: if there's competition, you have to be better, faster, cheaper in order to stand a chance. Competition is not your friend.

principles.text: The first version can be imperfect; disruptive tech often undershoots user needs before improving rapidly.
principles.quote: it's also okay if the first version of your startup is not quite perfect.

sources.title: How venture works: what Garry Tan looks for in VCs and founders at Initialized
sources.originalTitle: You can be a VC (I’m hiring): How venture works & what it takes to fund billion dollar startups
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how a VC fund exists to return money to limited partners, why brand and early access matter, and what makes a good investor. He stresses technical builders, contrarian belief, and being fair, direct and honest, then announces Initialized is hiring a principal and a partner.

principles.text: Back technical, product and design-oriented founders; the ones who can build it usually do.
principles.quote: at initialized we have a strong preference for technical product and design-oriented founders because those are the builders who have actually changed the world the ones who can build it usually do.

principles.text: Founder drive and persistence are powerful signals; a builder who can make you believe can make everyone believe.
principles.quote: if you have a builder who can make you believe then they can make everyone believe and that's how you can build something truly great

principles.text: Avoid paint-by-numbers, buzzword-combo startup ideas; look for independent first-principles thinkers.
principles.quote: we're looking for people who are independent thinkers who think from first principles and if you're that kind of person you're gonna see paint by numbers right away

principles.text: Test for contrarian insight by asking what someone believes that nobody else believes.
principles.quote: the best way to figure out if someone sitting across from you has secret knowledge at all is to ask them what do you believe that nobody else believes

principles.text: Being fair, direct and honest wins in venture's long iterative game; bad actors suffer adverse selection.
principles.quote: the best founders can choose anyone and they will choose those who are most trustworthy first being a bad actor is adverse selection in an iterative infinite game like venture capital

principles.text: When a startup struggles, investors should find the root cause rather than squeeze or micromanage founders.
principles.quote: instead of making founders feel like employees the right thing to do is help identify the root cause

sources.title: Co-founder conflict: how too little or too much conflict kills startups, and how to fix it
sources.originalTitle: Co-Founder Conflict & Why I Quit my Startup | How to Fix a Dying Company | Founder’s Journey: Ep.2
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how avoiding conflict with his Posterous co-founder led him to quit in 2010, and how to spot and fix both too little and too much co-founder conflict. Fixes include resolving disagreements on the spot, assigning one owner per area, listening with steel-manning, and getting coaches and trusted advisors involved early.

principles.text: Don't perform a good co-founder relationship; actually build one. Avoiding conflict to look harmonious backfires.
principles.quote: don't make it look like a good startup or a good co-founder relationship spend time actually making it a good startup and actually a good co-founder relationship

principles.text: When you disagree with a co-founder, stay in the room until it's resolved, even if it means cancelling your weekend for a retreat.
principles.quote: if you don't agree on something don't leave the room until you have a resolution if an hour is not enough cancel your weekend go on a hike even go camping get out of dodge have a retreat

principles.text: Don't sacrifice what you know is right for harmony; give more feedback and make sure you're heard.
principles.quote: you can't sacrifice what you know to be right in order to get that harmony early you've got to fight don't swallow your words if you have a point make sure you are heard

principles.text: Constant fighting usually means unclear roles. List every business area and assign exactly one accountable owner to each.
principles.quote: make a list of all the areas needed for your business then figure out who's best at each part and assign one person to it

principles.text: The owner gathers feedback, then makes the call; everyone agrees to disagree and commit, so you stop refighting decisions and move fast.
principles.quote: the owner makes the call and when the call is made everyone agrees to disagree and commit that way you're not fighting the same battles over and over

principles.text: Hire an executive coach early and bring in trusted investors, advisors and founder friends; don't cheap out when your company is on the line.
principles.quote: third-party help when you're at an intractable state can literally save your startup

sources.title: My failure as a manager: finding your true self to lead integrated teams
sources.originalTitle: My failure as a manager: How to find your true self to make and manage the best teams
sources.summary: Garry Tan shares a 360 review revealing he relied on his team to say no for him because he was conflict-avoidant. Using neuroscience and Keegan's stages of adult development, he explains how noticing internal conflict, then expressing a clear preference, makes you a better leader and builds stronger teams.

principles.text: Use 360 reviews to learn how your team really experiences you; they surface blind spots you can't see yourself.
principles.quote: a 360 review is an absolutely powerful tool for you to know how you're doing and what you could be doing better

principles.text: Leaders must be clear and decisive; relying on others to say no for you is a management failure.
principles.quote: relying on the team to say things that i needed to say myself that's always going to be worse than doing it yourself

principles.text: Modeling other people's motivations makes you a better designer, VC and manager, but you must not lose your own viewpoint.
principles.quote: one of the things that allows me to do a good job as a designer vc or manager is to be able to construct models of behavior of other people based on their experience not just mine

principles.text: Hire a strong team and set values so they can carry you when you're weak, but don't make that a permanent substitute for your own voice.
principles.quote: i'd built a team and set up values that they could work towards even if in the moment i couldn't express that preference myself

principles.text: Notice internal conflict through physiological signals, pause, and give a voice to each part of you to find what you truly want.
principles.quote: if i can give a voice to the different parts of me then i can also notice what i truly want and then i can express a preference when before i would have been unable to

principles.text: Aim for Keegan stage four: a self defined by values you authored yourself, not by others' expectations.
principles.quote: stage four is pretty awesome that's the stage where the person's sense of self is determined by a set of values that they have authored for themselves

sources.title: Design for Startups: product, interaction and visual design for founders
sources.originalTitle: Design for Startups by Garry Tan (Part 1)
sources.summary: Garry Tan walks founders through design as a self-taught practitioner: empathy-driven product design (personas, PRDs, P0-P3 priorities), interaction design (command language, remove or chunk actions, steal proven patterns) and visual design (contrast, closeness, grid). He closes with usability testing and customer support as the feedback loop.

principles.text: Design is how it works, not just how it looks; form should follow function.
principles.quote: design is how it looks it truly is not merely how it looks it is actually also how it works

principles.text: Don't chase novelty in design; novelty is the opposite of functionality. Steal proven patterns.
principles.quote: as designers you probably shouldn't be spending too much time trying to be extremely novel because novelty is the opposite of functionality

principles.text: Start from empathy and a crisp problem statement; with no real problem, design is just art.
principles.quote: if there's no problem then there's no solution it ends up being designed for its own sake and you know design for its own sake isn't design its art

principles.text: Write personas and a prioritized spec (P0-P3) so you know what to cut; scope, quality and time are the three levers.
principles.quote: one of the most dangerous things in product development period is that if you don't have these priorities you don't know what to cut

principles.text: Use direct command language and an obvious call to action; startups can't afford the passive voice big companies get away with.
principles.quote: everything that you write needs to be direct it has to be a direct personal voice and you need the call to action be incredibly obvious

principles.text: Treat customer support as product feedback: fixing the long-tail bugs one user reports creates evangelists, and a hundred people who love you beats a thousand who like you.
principles.quote: you don't have to just throw that email in the garbage you can say oh my god that's a bug oh I'm gonna fix it and then once you do that you have an evangelist for life

sources.title: Garry Tan's unconventional founder advice: be a super-knife, stay small, get therapy early
sources.originalTitle: Unconventional Advice for Founders [Entire Talk] - Garry Tan (Y Combinator)
sources.summary: Garry Tan, at Stanford ETL, shares lessons from his own mistakes (including turning down Palantir) and 20 years in startups and YC. He argues founders should be multi-skilled generalists, act small and hands-on with early users, deal with childhood baggage early, and work on weird problems they uniquely understand.

principles.text: Don't box yourself into one narrow role; be a generalist who can do many things.
principles.quote: you are not a tiny washer in a machine you should be everything you should not Define yourself just because the machine wants you to be an interchangeable part in the machine

principles.text: Act small even when small: do unscalable things and talk to users directly as the CEO.
principles.quote: the whole Advantage is that you're a real human being we are so starved for real authentic connection that if you can just go talk to people and say hey I'm the CEO what do you need like that is the most powerful thing

principles.text: Reply to every customer email within minutes and fix bugs on the spot.
principles.quote: we would aim to reply to every single email within 10 minutes of receiving it and if there was a bug we'd fix it on the spot

principles.text: A single human reply lifts return rates; even devtools are effectively consumer go-to-market.
principles.quote: if someone posted and did not get a reply only 16% of people would come back to that Forum but if you got even one reply 26 person percent would come back

principles.text: Startups run on a loop of co-founders, product, customers and capital; when one stalls, push another and come back.
principles.quote: if you can't get any more of any one of these things go to some of something else go get that and then come back to those other things

principles.text: Ignore media hype and pick weird problems you uniquely know; the best ideas often seem like bad ones.
principles.quote: ignore all of that and then focus on you know what do I uniquely know and what do I believe in and even if it's really weird maybe I should pull on that thread

sources.title: Garry Tan: Own your intelligence with personal AGI, a markdown brain and skill files
sources.originalTitle: Garry Tan: Own Your Intelligence
sources.summary: Garry argues AGI is arriving diffused as a personal agent running on your own context, not as a single event. He lays out the stack (rented model + owned context + harness), a five-step plan to build a library and skill files, and argues skill files must be owned by you, not your employer.

principles.text: Personal AGI = frontier model (rented) + your context (owned) + a harness; the leverage is in context, not weights.
principles.quote: a frontier model which is rented and a commodity and getting cheaper by the quarter plus your context which is owned by you and unique

principles.text: Treat AI as a workforce, not autocomplete; same model yields 2x or 100x depending on context and timing.
principles.quote: the fastest growing founders we fund are not treating AI as autocomplete. They are treating it as a workforce.

principles.text: Start a brain as one folder of markdown files and compound daily; don't build the warehouse first.
principles.quote: Nobody builds the warehouse first. First, you build one shelf.

principles.text: Fat skills, thin harness: a skill is a page of English a smart intern could follow; markdown is code.
principles.quote: If a smart intern could follow it, an agent can run it.

principles.text: Split work between latent space (judgment, taste) and deterministic code (SQL, arithmetic, scripts).
principles.quote: The fix is having the model compute the way humans compute. the latent and the deterministic markdown files calling databases and scripts.

principles.text: Never do one-off work: skillify every task so learning compounds and you never ask twice.
principles.quote: If you have to ask for something twice, you failed.

sources.title: Every company needs a Brain: wiring work as markdown skills, resolvers and a library
sources.originalTitle: Every company should have a Brain — Garry Tan, Y Combinator
sources.summary: Garry Tan argues AI leverage comes from how you wire the work, not the model: skill files are employees, resolver tables are org charts, and a company brain is a library plus librarian. He covers latent vs deterministic compute, context engineering, brain hygiene, and "skillify it" so nothing is done twice.

principles.text: AI leverage comes from how you wire the work, not from the model; 2X and 100X users run the same Claude.
principles.quote: The 2X people and the 100X people are using the exact same Claude. Same weights, same context window, same API. So, the leverage is not in the weights. It's in how you wire the work.

principles.text: Map agent tooling to an org: skills are employees, resolvers are org charts, evals are performance reviews.
principles.quote: A skill file is an employee. It has one capability, one job, written down clearly enough that someone can execute it.

principles.text: Treat AI as a managed workforce, not autocomplete.
principles.quote: The fastest growing founders we fund are not treating AI as auto-complete. They're treating it as a workforce.

principles.text: Put judgment in latent space (the LLM) and exact computation in deterministic code; most AI bugs come from mixing them up.
principles.quote: All of the bugs, all of the AI engineering that we run into that's a problem, it's usually because something is happening in one side of the equation that should be in the other.

principles.text: Never do one-off work: when the output is good, skillify it so you never ask twice.
principles.quote: Because if you have to ask for something twice, you failed.

principles.text: A company brain only compounds with hygiene: provenance, contradiction checks and a librarian who prunes.
principles.quote: Retrieval is easy. Being worth retrieving from is the product.

sources.title: How Garry Tan builds an AI-native software factory with skills, resolvers and evals
sources.originalTitle: Stanford CS153 Frontier Systems | The AI Native Company: How One Founder Becomes a 1000x Engineer
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how coding agents let one founder do the work of hundreds, and the primitives he uses: skills, resolvers, skillify, tests and a memory brain. He stresses pairing deterministic code with latent-space agents, and judging results by whether customers actually pay.

principles.text: Stop avoiding big scope: with coding agents one person can attempt work that used to need hundreds.
principles.quote: my response to that, based on my experience with uh coding agents and what's happening right now, is actually let's boil the ocean.

principles.text: Agent failures usually come from mixing deterministic work and latent-space work; put each in the right layer.
principles.quote: you need to make the latent space work with the deterministic space.

principles.text: Use a resolver instead of a bloated instruction file: load instructions only when a task needs them.
principles.quote: anytime you have to write to the change log, load change log.md.

principles.text: Once an agent task works, skillify it, but writing the skill and code is only a small part; tests and evals make it reliable.
principles.quote: Writing the skill and writing the code is only two out of the 10 steps.

principles.text: Avoid shipping AI slop by driving test coverage to 80-90% with an engineering review step.
principles.quote: to get to 80-90% test coverage so that I am not shipping slop.

principles.text: Judge output by real-world results: does it work for customers and are they paying, not lines of code.
principles.quote: Does it work for your customers? Are people actually paying? That's actually the true metric.

sources.title: Critiquing AI startup websites: clarity, one CTA, and showing a feat of strength
sources.originalTitle: Critiquing AI Startup Websites with YC President Garry Tan
sources.summary: Garry Tan and YC designers critique AI startup homepages (Rosebud, MagicFlow, Reality Defender, Pump, Voiceflow). Core lessons: make it instantly clear what you do and who it's for, drive one opinionated call to action, demo the product early, and use real customer language and social proof.

principles.text: Don't be clever if clever means confusing. A homepage must say what it is and whether it's for me.
principles.quote: you don't want to be clever if clever equals confusing and that's like the first thing that people are trying to understand when they hit a website is what is this and number two being is it for me

principles.text: Be opinionated: pick one primary action, make it the high-contrast button, demote everything else to links.
principles.quote: if you really want people to try the beta make that the call to action and then make learn more instead of a button that's equal weight just make it a link and you know one of the most important things to use is contrast

principles.text: Tie the homepage to your main KPI and push secondary products to secondary pages to get users to the aha moment fast.
principles.quote: I would recommend for Rosebud to figure out what their main kpi is and what outcome they want from people that hit their website

principles.text: For AI products, show a feat of strength: a demo of magic output people have never seen before.
principles.quote: there's some sort of feet of strength that you can show it's like they skip down to the lower tiered things like the most important thing who is it who's it for

principles.text: Generic workflow tools win by focusing on specific, common use cases rather than abstract capability.
principles.quote: nobody's like man I really need workflow software instead there's a specific problem that they're looking to solve and so usually what works kind of to your point earlier is to actually focus on very specific use cases

principles.text: Write the homepage for your ICP and use the exact words existing users use to describe your product.
principles.quote: go talk to your existing users ask them how would you describe my product and then take the exact phrase that they say and just put that up at the top of your site

sources.title: Garry Tan: New rules for founders in the agent era (a16z)
sources.originalTitle: Garry Tan: New Rules for Founders
sources.summary: Garry Tan argues founders should trust first-hand knowledge over what's hot, stay earnest, and turn every business process into a markdown skill file that agents run on loops. He explains why agents erase management bureaucracy, why token-maxing lets you live in 2028, and why a startup can reorganize in ways a Microsoft cannot.

principles.text: Don't chase what's hot. Work on what you uniquely know and are interested in, and trust your direct experience.
principles.quote: the right question is like what are you interested in? What do you know uniquely?

principles.text: Earnestness takes courage: believe your own first-hand experience over crowd opinion or blog posts.
principles.quote: if you know something, it sort of if someone just like comes and contradicts you or even if like a blog post or like someone on Twitter uh contradicts you, you're like, "Well, I I don't agree with that because I believe my own direct experience."

principles.text: Real knowledge comes from going down to the first-party experiment or customer, not from published maps. Great things start as cult-like contrarian beliefs.
principles.quote: everything that's awesome in my life is kind of a cult. That starts with some sort of truth or belief that flies in the face of an orthodoxy

principles.text: Treat every business process as a markdown skill file: do it once perfectly with the agent, fix errors as bugs, then run it on a cron.
principles.quote: a markdown file is an employee. And it's an employee that will do the job perfectly every single time and it'll do it like as many times as you want.

principles.text: Building agentic systems is finding bottlenecks and instructing the agent to write software or a skill that removes each one. Add provenance and conflict sweeps as data grows.
principles.quote: you're seeing where the bottlenecks are and then you know almost every single time it's like how do I just instruct the agent to create a piece of software or a markdown file that blows away that roadblock

principles.text: Founders should token-max with open agent harnesses, giving themselves permission to spend heavily so they effectively live in 2028 today.
principles.quote: you have to give yourself permission to token max in that way.

sources.title: Garry Tan on YC's structure, resilience and community: Out of Office walk through SF
sources.originalTitle: Garry Tan is Out Of Office
sources.summary: Garry Tan walks through San Francisco with Michael McNano and explains why YC dropped its continuity fund to focus on one core business, why rejection is part of the founder test, and why venture should be bigger and less clubby. He also covers how he got into local politics and why community building matters.

principles.text: Being rejected is a normal first step; founders face constant rejection, so treat it as a resilience test.
principles.quote: the first step to getting into YC is getting rejected from YC.

principles.text: Founders get rejected at every turn (users, investors, hires, commenters), so build tolerance early.
principles.quote: you're going to be rejected in countless ways as a founder at every turn at every turn of the journey.

principles.text: Take pro rata to keep owning decacorns, since most returns come from a few huge outliers and dilution kills them.
principles.quote: just taking the paradas means you never miss the decacorns and you know how the power law works

principles.text: Stay a lifelong partner to portfolio companies: no formal end to support after the program.
principles.quote: Make us earn it. Come back. Like do office hours with us.

principles.text: Treat YC like a two-sided marketplace where investors are scarce supply and founders are near-limitless demand.
principles.quote: the limiting reagent for Airbnb is actually hosts

principles.text: Early-stage investors should avoid herd syndicates and show up before a company is obvious.
principles.quote: Show up, do early stage, you know, fun people before it's obvious.

sources.title: Garry Tan on YC, building without playing business, and AI-era distribution and startups
sources.originalTitle: Y Combinator CEO Shares How They Turn Wild Ideas Into Real Companies
sources.summary: Garry Tan (YC CEO) explains why YC's simple process works, why founders must set their own frame and talk to real customers, and why creators win distribution. He argues LLMs with good evals let small teams replace rote knowledge work and build huge businesses.

principles.text: Don't let media or competitors define your game; you'll end up playing the wrong one.
principles.quote: when you're not careful, you sort of allow media or other people to sort of frame your reality and then you just play the wrong game.

principles.text: Focus on your own users and profitability, not the game investors or press push you into.
principles.quote: just play your own game. Like make up your own mind.

principles.text: Build your worldview from first-source customer data, not from narratives told to you.
principles.quote: it's important to build your worldview on how the world works directly from customers and their customer data.

principles.text: Businesses must act like creators, otherwise they pay the big ad networks for attention.
principles.quote: if you're running a business today, you kind of have to be a creator because if you're not a creator you got to buy eyeballs somehow

principles.text: AI startup play: find firms spending heavily on rote knowledge work and replace it with LLMs plus workflow and evals.
principles.quote: go and find real people who like are running businesses and they're spending hundreds of thousands of dollars a year on giant teams of people doing like rote, repeating knowledge work.

principles.text: Ideas alone aren't enough; you must act, talk to users and build.
principles.quote: you actually have to go with your hands and go talk to users and you know, sit and build a thing.

sources.title: Garry Tan on YC: make something people want, founder mode, and founder psychology
sources.originalTitle: Garry Tan on the Past, Present, and Future of YC
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how YC runs as a managed network-effects marketplace, why founders should be in the Bay Area, and how self-awareness shapes startups. He also covers co-founder conflict, fundraising as a starting gun, craft in building, and his prompt-iteration workflow with AI.

principles.text: Make something people want: get real paying, retaining customers early, and fundraising becomes easy.
principles.quote: the number one thing that a startup founder can do going into YC is like make really really valuable things and get real customers that you know pay and retain and then fundraising is easy because everyone can see it.

principles.text: Fundraising is the starting gun, not the finish line; treat raised money like debt to return at a big multiple.
principles.quote: I was like, "No, no, no. That's not the finish line. That's the starting gun, guys."

principles.text: Great co-founders fight constantly but preserve the relationship; suppressing disagreement backfires.
principles.quote: Great co-founders fight absolutely all the time and about everything, but mainly because they care so much and they do it in a way that like preserves the relationship.

principles.text: A startup takes on its founder's patterns, so inner work improves hiring, firing and conflict handling.
principles.quote: how you do anything you know how you do anything is how you do everything right

principles.text: Location matters: staying in the Bay Area makes a billion-dollar outcome about 2.5x more likely.
principles.quote: It's two and a half times more likely if people choose to stay in the Bay Area that their company ends up being worth a billion dollars.

principles.text: Evolve your prompts: feed inputs and outputs to an LLM, then ask for the next version of the prompt each iteration.
principles.quote: you'd be like give me the next version of the prompt

sources.title: Garry Tan on YC in the age of AI: agency, taste, and prompting as a hiring signal
sources.originalTitle: Y Combinator in the Age of AI | Ep. 43
sources.outlet: Uncapped with Jack Altman and Y Combinator
sources.summary: Garry Tan, with other YC partners, explains how Claude Code and Codex change what founders can build and how YC evaluates them. He argues for judging builders by how they work, moving decisively, and treating AI as a reason to attempt more rather than staff less.

principles.text: Judge builders by how they prompt coding agents; it reveals systems thinking and craft better than a resume.
principles.quote: You can tell a lot about whether someone can build just from like how they prompt the agents and it's like do they know systems

principles.text: The best proof someone can make something people want is that they already did it.
principles.quote: the only way you can really tell if they can make something people want is like they did it already

principles.text: Agency and taste are the universal founder traits: see a real problem, believe you can solve it, then build and obsess over details.
principles.quote: the most important thing is you know agency and taste. Like agency is I see this person and they have this problem and I believe I can solve it using technology

principles.text: Craft shows in the parts nobody looks at; how you do anything is how you do everything.
principles.quote: How you do anything is how you do everything. Uh my favorite Steve Jobs quote.

principles.text: With AI coding tools, decide by trying both options instead of debating architecture for weeks; speed of decisions is the edge.
principles.quote: Like we don't have to do that now. Like we could just try both. Like go into plan mode and then just do it.

principles.text: Throwing away two years' worth of work is cheap now, and it isn't wasted because you learn and get better with the tools.
principles.quote: you could do two years of work, realize that like actually nobody wants this or there's too much competition and you throw it out and then do it again. And the thing is like that's not throwaway.

sources.title: Running YC like a founder: lean vs fat startups, listening to customers, and AI-era moats
sources.originalTitle: Running Y Combinator Like a Founder | Garry Tan | Ep. 7
sources.summary: Garry Tan talks to Jack Altman about running YC with zero-based accounting and founder energy. He covers how to advise founders, what makes a great founder, when to raise big versus stay lean, and how AI changes team size but not moats.

principles.text: Raise big only if elite investors back you; otherwise start lean, because lean is how you earn the right to go fat.
principles.quote: how would you even get to the point where you could be a fat startup? Well, you got to do it lean.

principles.text: The best founders are the best listeners; pulling requirements from customers early turns into customers pulling product later, which is product market fit.
principles.quote: basically that yanking turns into like they're pushing like and that's product market fit.

principles.text: Advise as a soft advisor, not a boss. Spiky, even wrong, advice beats median advice founders can get from any podcast.
principles.quote: what's really valuable is to have people around who have seen enough and are intuitive enough about like ideas and technology and teams that they can give you even spiky advice

principles.text: AI changes how big a team you need, not the moats. Switching costs, proprietary data, brand and network effects still decide winners.
principles.quote: the moes are all the same, right? Like switching cost, data that like, you know, you have access to that nobody else has.

principles.text: Early on, most of the value of an advisor or investor is helping you avoid the many ways startups die.
principles.quote: there's like a billion ways to die.

principles.text: Build a shelling point for talented builders and the capital, customers and knowledge follow. Culture is everything, so be willing to prune.
principles.quote: The world needs shelling points for um for builders for talented people and then their capital exists, their customers exist

sources.title: Garry Tan on how YC evaluates startups: product-market fit, co-founders, fundraising, culture
sources.originalTitle: How YC's Garry Tan Evaluates Startups | Episode 3 of the Investor + Operator Podcast
sources.summary: Garry Tan draws on Palantir, Posterous and YC to explain why founders miss product-market fit, why answering "both" is a strategic mistake, and how to read customer feedback. He also covers co-founder conflict, founder-led culture, fundraising in a tough market and why the startup ceiling keeps rising.

principles.text: Pick one path and say no to the rest; answering "both" lets competitors win each space.
principles.quote: because we chose something in between we sort of did both poorly and then we allowed our competitors to basically win in their respective spaces

principles.text: Find a narrow, underserved segment and build a much better wedge there instead of a vague broad product.
principles.quote: she started spending a lot more time with a certain segment of people so she discovered skilled nursing facilities and convalescent homes

principles.text: User feedback is worthless until money or behavior changes; people are polite and will lie to you.
principles.quote: until they're paying for something or changing a behavior that they would only do out of self-interest they're lying to you

principles.text: In startups there is no B+; aim for the A+ because anything less fails.
principles.quote: there's no you know a b is an F in startups pure like basically it's either an A plus or an f

principles.text: Great founders explain complex breakthroughs in very few words, since they must close customers, hires and money.
principles.quote: really really great Founders are able to communicate in very very few words these incredibly complex ideas

principles.text: In a hard fundraising market, aim for profitability or cash-flow break-even instead of relying on the next round.
principles.quote: the safest thing is try to get profitable

sources.title: Garry Tan on why AI-era startups are scaling to $10M+ ARR in months, and how YC supports them
sources.originalTitle: YC’s no-fluff playbook for scaling past $10M ARR (with Garry Tan)
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how Casetext turned a limited SEO legal product into a billion-dollar outcome by chopping LLM tasks into small, evaluable steps, why narrow vertical AI beats general models, and why YC batches now grow 10-20% a week. He also shares his prompt-iteration workflow for writing video scripts and how he restructured YC around the core batch and lifelong partner support.

principles.text: Scope narrowly into an underserved vertical and build exactly what those users need; general models can't yet do the work.
principles.quote: if you like scope what you're doing and make the thing that is perfect for that set of people um there you can't just take chat GPT and have it do this type of work yet.

principles.text: Target the labor spend, not the software spend: AI products can capture the people-cost wallet that dwarfs the software budget.
principles.quote: for every $100 they bring in in revenue, they spend about a dollar on software like Service Titan, but they spend5 or $6 on actual people picking up the phone and doing scheduling

principles.text: AI makes buyers say yes fast because a demo shows direct bottom-line savings, shortening sales cycles and accelerating revenue growth.
principles.quote: I see a demo, it's really impressive. Uh, I could see how that would hit my bottom line or basically create a better product or service immediately. Um, and then yeah, I need it right now. When can you start?

principles.text: Make LLMs reliable by chopping work into small human-sized steps, with test inputs and evals for each task.
principles.quote: you should actually have tests for a bunch of different inputs and outputs and you should have evals that actually um give you a sense and certainty about specific tasks.

principles.text: Don't judge a small market too early: the data and user understanding you gather can become a moat when technology shifts.
principles.quote: all of which turned into a tremendous moat for them literally right at the correct moment as technology itself shifted

principles.text: Use AI as a co-writer by iterating the prompt: label each output, refine, then have the model output an improved prompt each session.
principles.quote: given uh what we did in this session to improve the prompt, output the next version of the prompt. And so now I've done this about 20 or 30 times.

sources.title: The 7 Most Powerful Moats for AI Startups: speed first, then Helmer's seven powers applied to AI
sources.originalTitle: The 7 Most Powerful Moats For AI Startups
sources.summary: Garry Tan and the Light Cone hosts apply Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers (process power, cornered resources, switching costs, counter-positioning, brand, network economies, scale economies) to AI startups. Garry's core message is to find a painful problem and move fast first, since moats only matter once you have something worth defending.

principles.text: Find a real person with a real problem and solve it first; moats come later.
principles.quote: this is sort of why we generally tell people to go find a person with a real problem and then go solve that problem first.

principles.text: Moats are for scaling a working business; don't pick or drop ideas based on forecast moats, speed is the first moat.
principles.quote: all the things that we're about to cover, aside from speed, are sort of one to a billion, one to 10 billion, one to a hundred billion, one to a trillion-dollar sort of problems.

principles.text: Start with a specific person whose pain is severe and existential, not a nice-to-have.
principles.quote: You should start with do I have a specific person who has some sort of pain point and it's pretty painful.

principles.text: Forward-deployed engineering builds a cornered resource: real customer data and workflows nobody else has.
principles.quote: they're going out and getting a cornered resource in the form of real data and real workflows. Literally sitting with a customer who normally would never get access to good software.

principles.text: Superior engineering is the most profound modern process power; use code gen to scale it.
principles.quote: One way to look at it is way better engineering is actually that's like the most profound form of process power.

principles.text: AI vertical SaaS can capture far more wallet share by charging for the work done rather than software seats.
principles.quote: because you're not like 1% of wallet share, you can get to 10.

sources.title: Garry Tan on getting addicted to Claude Code: tests, speed and fewer excuses
sources.originalTitle: We're All Addicted To Claude Code
sources.summary: A Light Cone conversation with Kelvin French Owen on coding agents. Garry describes returning to building after years in manager mode, why test coverage unlocked his speed, and how agents raise the bar for shipping software that works for users.

principles.text: Agents with CLI access to your real environment can debug deep issues and write the regression test, so the bug never recurs.
principles.quote: this thing can debug nested delayed jobs like five levels in and figure out what the bug was and then write a test for it and it never happens again. This is insane.

principles.text: Invest in test coverage early. With strong tests, agent-driven development speeds up and needs little manual checking.
principles.quote: I was like, "All right, today's refactor day. I'm going to do get to 100% test coverage." And then I just sped up like crazy.

principles.text: Coding agents let one builder do the work of a small team, which makes returning from manager mode to building worthwhile.
principles.quote: I can do five people's worth of work in like a single day. It's like rocket boosters.

principles.text: Anyone can now make something, but building what people actually want is still the hard part, even for well-resourced teams.
principles.quote: anyone can make something but then the something people want is very hard

principles.text: With agents, there are far fewer excuses for software that doesn't quite work for a user, including less common stacks.
principles.quote: there are far fewer excuses for software that doesn't quite work for a user you know now than ever actually.

sources.title: Tokenmaxxing: how Garry Tan rebuilt as a solo builder with AI agents, G Stack and G Brain
sources.originalTitle: Tokenmaxxing: How Top Builders Use AI To Do The Work Of 400 Engineers
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how he went back to coding while running YC, using Claude Code, Conductor and Open Claw to ship at roughly 400x his old output. He covers boiling the ocean with tokens, thin harness plus fat markdown skills, high test coverage, and why people should own their personal AI.

principles.text: Token max: spend more compute to make work complete, cross-referenced and 20-source deep instead of settling for one source.
principles.quote: if there is incremental work that makes something more complete, more awesome, more uh, you know, in the case of um, this type of writing, like, we want it to be more representative of reality.

principles.text: Boil the ocean: with agents you no longer have to settle for the scope a human would have budgeted.
principles.quote: particularly when building a Gentex software now, you don't have to settle for um what we did when we were humans writing the code.

principles.text: Treat token spend like San Francisco rent: it is more expensive not to spend it, so push hard on the best models.
principles.quote: Token maxing is going to be one of those things for founders that we sort of have to teach them where it's not immediately obvious that you shouldn't

principles.text: Put judgment and instructions in markdown, and deterministic actions in code; most agent failures come from using code for things that need judgment.
principles.quote: all of the difficulty in in agentic engineering today is when people try to do things that should be in markdown in code, and it fails because code is brittle

principles.text: Reach 80-90% test coverage on AI-written code; untested agent output shipped to users is slop.
principles.quote: get to 80 to 90% tests. Like, if it's not tested and you're just throwing users in there, like, it's slop.

principles.text: Keep the human in the loop to supply agency and taste; use agents for the work you don't want to do, including automated QA with a real browser.
principles.quote: I never want to be entirely out of the loop. I just want the machine to do the stuff that I don't want to do.

sources.title: Six skills for startup success: what founders should build before starting
sources.originalTitle: Six skills for startup success
sources.summary: Garry Tan lists six skills that raise a founder's odds: engineering, product, design, sales and marketing, finance, and management and leadership. Go deep in one or two, stay broad in the rest so you can hire and work with experts, and fill the gaps with a team. Skills make startup risk more calculated, not deterministic.

principles.text: Be deep in one or two core skills and broad enough in the rest to judge and work with experts.
principles.quote: Be deep in one or two of these areas but broad enough to be dangerous in the rest. You actually need this to be able to tell who's actually good in those positions and to be able to work with those best people in those expertise areas.

principles.text: More skills attract better cofounders and employees, since talent avoids projects that look likely to fail without them.
principles.quote: The more of these skills you have, the more you will attract high quality people to come work with you, whether it's cofounders or employees.

principles.text: Technology is the ultimate moat; non-technical founders should learn to build a good-but-imperfect version to stand out.
principles.quote: If you understand the craft and you can build a good but not perfect version of what you ultimately want to build, you can get the ball rolling.

principles.text: Product is a continuous process of finding and refining product-market fit; learn it by shipping and talking to users.
principles.quote: Build something and release it, release it to users and see if they stick with it.

principles.text: Interaction design is the core of design and ties directly to product; taste matters for every business now.
principles.quote: Interaction design is probably the meat of design when I think about it.

principles.text: Finance is not critical at the start but becomes essential from zero to one, to know whether you are growing or dying.
principles.quote: Finance and budgeting allows you to make sense of the decisions you have to make in a business.

sources.title: Default alive: how Gobble turned $1M/mo burn into profit by cutting marketing and trusting cohorts
sources.originalTitle: Sell? Die? No. Grow profitably: why default alive matters
sources.summary: A conversation with Gobble founder Ooshma Garg, where Garry (a board member) frames what to do when a flailing competitor's IPO kills your fundraising: test whether you're already profitable. Covers proprietary IP for retention, cohort retention as the key health metric, and why founders should try profitability before selling or shutting down.

principles.text: Early on, startups are judged by popularity (voting machine); later, by what cash the business throws off (weighing machine).
principles.quote: The game is a, it's a popularity contest early. It's basically a voting machine early, and then later, it becomes a weighing machine.

principles.text: When you can't raise, try profitability before selling, shutting down, or recapping; it restores your leverage.
principles.quote: Sell? Die? No. Get profitable.

principles.text: Cohort retention reveals the true health of a business; the best brands' curves flatten to an asymptote.
principles.quote: I think cohort retention is one of the most important tools for every founder because it really tells you the health of the business, period, as a brand, as a going concern.

principles.text: Digital ad channels have depth limits: the first customers are targeted and sticky, but marginal customers get worse, especially with heavy capital.
principles.quote: in the search for more and more marginal customers, you're actually getting customers that are worse.

principles.text: Founders have a growth knob: burn cash to grow faster, or grow slower and sustainably, even profitably.
principles.quote: There are lots of places where the founder has this growth knob, they can choose, do we grow faster and burn a lot more money or do we grow slower but much more sustainably?

principles.text: Always try going profitable; Garry regrets never charging at Posterous despite massive usage.
principles.quote: So always remember, you can go profitable, or at least you can try and it's a very important tool for the tool belt and we should have tried, we never did.

sources.title: Changing the world without losing yourself: five lessons from Semmelweis
sources.originalTitle: Changing the world can make you insane, but it doesn't have to: 5 tips
sources.summary: Using Ignaz Semmelweis, who cut maternal deaths with handwashing but died in an asylum, Garry lays out five lessons for founders pushing new ideas against resistance. The core point: a breakthrough is only half the work; communicating it, persistently and professionally, is the other half.

principles.text: Speak for yourself; data and other people won't carry your message for you.
principles.quote: Don't expect others to speak for you. Certainly the data can't speak for itself. In fact, without you, the data is mute.

principles.text: Practice writing and social media so you can communicate with strangers when it matters.
principles.quote: If you're watching this, you should practice writing and social media. Get into the habit of being able to communicate with strangers on the internet.

principles.text: Don't ragequit; feel the emotion but let the rational part of you make hard decisions.
principles.quote: You do have to make a decision, but when you do, feel the emotions, but be sure it's the rational part of you doing it.

principles.text: The establishment is often wrong; keep saying what you know is right, backed by data and conviction.
principles.quote: the establishment is often absolutely wrong. It's an act of courage to continue to say what you know to be right.

principles.text: Don't stoop to your critics' level; how you argue matters.
principles.quote: no matter how wrong your haters are, don't stoop to their level. When they go low, we go high.

principles.text: A breakthrough only has impact if you spread and communicate it effectively.
principles.quote: The breakthrough is only half of the work. The other half is spreading it to the rest of the world.

sources.title: Should you work on that startup idea? Ask "Why me, why now" and find a moat
sources.originalTitle: Should you work on that startup idea? Ask: why me, why now
sources.summary: Garry Tan argues that pointing at a good idea isn't enough; founders must stress-test who they build for, whether it's feasible, and what unfair advantage they hold. He uses Standard Cognition and Posterous to show that a technology or insight no one else has can be the moat that justifies a startup existing.

principles.text: A right-direction idea isn't enough; you must build the spaceship, not just point at the moon.
principles.quote: You can't just point at the moon, you've got to build the goddamn spaceship.

principles.text: Before building, define who you build for, what problem they have, and whether your solution is feasible, affordable and better than alternatives.
principles.quote: Who am I building for? Who's my audience? What problem do they have?

principles.text: Ask why now and what you have that nobody else has; the answer is your moat and what makes the product protectable.
principles.quote: Why now? What do I have that nobody else has? Is it technology? Is it something that would prevent other people from just copying it?

principles.text: Moats take many forms: pure technology, lighthouse customer relationships, better go-to-market, or content.
principles.quote: The best moat of all is often actually real pure technology.

principles.text: A lighthouse customer can unlock a whole industry; Envoy started by landing Airbnb among its first 10 clients.
principles.quote: Envoy, the sign in, check in service that you've probably already used in Silicon Valley, they got started by selling Airbnb in their first 10 clients.

principles.text: Weak answers aren't just a reason to quit; they show what to work on as a founder, and engineers can build tech to fill the gap.
principles.quote: this set of questions helps you think about the questions you need to answer. This focuses you on the things that you need to work on as a founder.

sources.title: Timebox your way to product market fit: limit tries per hypothesis
sources.originalTitle: Timebox your way to startup product market fit
sources.summary: Garry Tan argues founders fail by not trying enough distinct hypotheses, so they should explicitly timebox each product-market hypothesis (a set of people plus a problem) and move on. He breaks failure into acquisition problems and not-a-real-problem, and lists levers for retention and pilot expansion.

principles.text: You have a finite number of tries; timebox each one so you can try more things and maximize your odds of success.
principles.quote: you have a finite number of tries. But if you timebox your tries, you'll get to try a lot more things. And that will maximize your chance of success.

principles.text: A product-market hypothesis is a specific set of reachable people plus a problem to solve for them.
principles.quote: A set of **people** that you can reach, and

principles.text: Diagnose failure in order: first can you get people to know and use it, then is it a real problem.
principles.quote: A, it's a real problem, but you **can't get people to know about it and use it**, or, B, it's **not a real problem**. In that order!

principles.text: For acquisition, try many channels instead of repeating one or two; there are no silver bullets, only lead ones.
principles.quote: The most common failure point when working on customer acquisition is getting stuck on one or two things, and trying those, over and over and over again, doing more of what doesn't work.

principles.text: Pilots that don't expand signal a product that doesn't stick; you need expansion and net retention to raise a Series A.
principles.quote: You need expansion. You need net retention. And if you can't, this isn't something people want.

principles.text: Set the timebox so it is neither too short nor too long: too short abandons something that could work, too long burns runway.
principles.quote: **Too short,** and you may have given up on something that could have worked. **Too long,** and you've wasted your time. You'll never get that time back.

sources.title: Selling your startup: Garry Tan and Andrew Lee on M&A types, timing and process
sources.originalTitle: Andrew and Garry's guide to selling your startup
sources.summary: Garry and Andrew Lee lay out the three kinds of acquisition (strategic, revenue, talent), when to consider selling, and how to run an M&A process. Key lessons: companies are bought not sold, build a BATNA, go through the product owner instead of corp dev, and never treat M&A like a VC fundraise.

principles.text: Startups are bought, not sold: a bigger company buys when it has something to protect or a new line it wants to own.
principles.quote: the old adage, I think, rings true that companies are bought, they are not sold.

principles.text: Before product-market fit, stay focused on product; with no PMF you only have an acqui-hire to offer.
principles.quote: if you don't have product market fit yet, you don't have anything to sell.

principles.text: Think about M&A as risk management when you are not default alive and may run out of runway before the next raise.
principles.quote: if you're looking down the road and you think you're going to run out of gas before you get to the next gas station, or the gas station might be closed for you, that's when you need to think about M&A

principles.text: Selling along the way is legitimate; it lets you take care of employees, investors and yourselves.
principles.quote: It's okay to sell your business along the way, actually.

principles.text: Don't run an M&A process like a VC fundraise: corp dev wants to pay less, while VCs get rabid when more bidders appear.
principles.quote: for M&A, it's almost always people treating their M&A process like another fundraising process.

principles.text: Always keep a BATNA (raising money, growing revenue, cutting costs, competing offers), because corp dev's job is to push the price down.
principles.quote: Deals fall through, Always maintain some sort of BATNA. [Corp dev's] entire job is to bring the price of the deal down.

sources.title: Last minute advice for YC applicants: six tips from Garry Tan
sources.originalTitle: Last minute advice for YC applicants
sources.summary: Garry Tan's 2014 advice to YC applicants covers who should apply, how to pick a problem, team composition, writing clearly, getting feedback and not waiting for permission. The core lessons apply to any early startup: solve a real problem or do it right, pair a builder with a hustler, and write in plain English.

principles.text: Pick a hair-on-fire problem nobody has solved, or solve an existing problem so much better that it is done right.
principles.quote: They either solve a hair on fire problem that has never been solved before OR they solve a problem that has other solutions, but they do it so much better that they are "done right."

principles.text: Technology has no value on its own. It only matters when it solves people's problems.
principles.quote: Great hackers get caught up in technology, but technology doesn't create value in and of itself. Technology is only useful for solving people's problems.

principles.text: If you are new, explain what you are. If you are not new, explain how you are different.
principles.quote: If you're new, focus on explaining what you are. If you're not new, focus on explaining how you're different. If you're neither of these types, you're doing it wrong.

principles.text: A strong founding team needs both a builder and a hustler. Builders alone can't reach users and hustlers alone can't make product.
principles.quote: I've seen teams of hustlers fail because they can't create any product on their own. I've seen teams of pure builders (amazing designer / engineers) that fail because they can't put the product in the hands of users.

principles.text: Unclear writing signals unclear thinking. Write everything down, then edit mercilessly in plain English, not corporate speak.
principles.quote: If a founder can't express their ideas clearly to others, then the simplest and likeliest explanation is actually that the idea is not particularly clear to them either.

principles.text: Don't wait for permission. Keep building the startup whether or not an accelerator accepts you.
principles.quote: You've got to keep working on the startup no matter what. Realize that you don't need anyone to give you a permission slip to create your own startup.

sources.title: What to do when someone steals your idea: execution beats ideas
sources.originalTitle: What to do when someone steals your idea
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains why good startup ideas are rare and arise from technology, regulation, or macroeconomic shifts, so copycats are inevitable. Ideas only multiply execution; the response is to share loudly, own the problem space, and ship faster than copycats, who can only copy an older version of you.

principles.text: Working startup ideas are rare and unlock via technology, regulation, or macroeconomic shifts, so answer 'why now'.
principles.quote: Good ideas that will actually work are very, very rare, and they come about for just a few reasons. One, technological, two, regulatory, or three, some sort of macroeconomic force that's happening.

principles.text: Because 'why now' forces are shared, others will find your idea too; the idea is just a multiplier on execution.
principles.quote: the idea is only a multiplier on execution. The ideas are out there, everyone can sort of pursue them.

principles.text: Win by execution: build what people need and be chosen over all alternatives.
principles.quote: What's your product like? Is it actually what people need? And do people choose you over all possible alternatives?

principles.text: Don't clam up when facing competition; lean in and be the most associated with the problem space.
principles.quote: You actually have to be so deeply associated with that problem space, and being the best solution for that problem, that you win.

principles.text: A great idea alone isn't enough; success takes manual, relentless work to push it to customers.
principles.quote: a great idea on its own will not be enough. In order to actually take advantage of it, you're going to have to jam it down their throats.

principles.text: Outrun copycats by shipping and going to market faster, so they only copy an older version of you.
principles.quote: even the people who are trying to copy you can only copy the version of you from six or nine months ago.

sources.title: Spotify as a case study in making something people want
sources.originalTitle: Spotify as a simple case study in making something people want
sources.summary: Garry Tan uses the New Yorker's Spotify profile to show the anatomy of making something people want: a precisely defined broken problem, a measurable product bar (200 ms), proprietary tech that only needs to buy a 6-month head start, and a painful schlep that becomes the moat.

principles.text: Start with a simple problem statement: know exactly what is broken. Era-defining startups begin this way.
principles.quote: They started with a simple problem statement. All of the great era-defining startups seem to start that way. What was broken? They knew exactly what was broken.

principles.text: Define a concrete, measurable success bar for the product so you know what winning looks like.
principles.quote: They knew how to measure success. Clearly if you could make a streaming service act as if it were on your local hard drive, you could win.

principles.text: Your technical advantage doesn't need to last forever; it only needs to keep copycats a step behind while you pull ahead.
principles.quote: You don't need a technological advantage that lasts forever (though of course that'd be preferable) — just one that will last enough such that your competitors can only copy your innovation from 6 months ago.

principles.text: Doing something that hadn't been done before is a real edge, even though software can be cloned.
principles.quote: Novel tech is not an infinite defense, but it was enough of one for Spotify to get off the ground.

principles.text: The schlep is the moat: hard, grinding work founders would avoid if they knew it upfront creates protectable long-term value.
principles.quote: If founders knew how much work these things would be, often they wouldn't do it. But they do, and that's protectable long term enterprise value.

principles.text: Beat the incumbent behavior (piracy) by building a better product, because people just want a great experience.
principles.quote: What if you can make a better product than piracy?

sources.title: Garry Tan on the 4 habits of auteurs, via Hideo Kojima's Death Stranding
sources.originalTitle: The 4 habits of auteurs (Hideo Kojima, Death Stranding)
sources.summary: Garry Tan analyzes how Hideo Kojima made Death Stranding to extract four habits of great creators: a real mission, making your own decisions instead of following surveys, knowing what to outsource versus do yourself (while collaborating well), and showmanship. He applies these lessons to founders and indie makers.

principles.text: Have a mission: decide what effect you want to have on the world and orient the whole project around it.
principles.quote: First, mission. Have one! Think about what you want to do in the world, what effect do you want to have? And orient your whole project around it

principles.text: Make your own decisions; don't outsource creative direction to surveys or popularity.
principles.quote: Second, make your own decisions. Don't rely on surveys, don't rely on what will be popular.

principles.text: As companies grow they get risk-averse; quantitative thinking feels safer but can't produce truly original work.
principles.quote: When things get big, they get safe. And it often feels safer to outsource your decision making to a survey to quantitative thinking.

principles.text: Delegate most things but keep a few critical ones yourself; know what to outsource, what your team does, and what you must do.
principles.quote: Both great founders and true great auteurs know what they can outsource, know what they can give to their own team, and they have an intuitive sense for what they need to do themselves. It's not everything, it's just a few things.

principles.text: Great creators collaborate with a 'yes, and' mindset, incorporating others' ideas to build something bigger than one person could.
principles.quote: You need to be able to listen, you need to be able to say yes, you need to be able to incorporate other people's ideas, and only then can you collaboratively create something greater than what you could create individually.

principles.text: Showmanship sets the tone and expectations so team, partners and recruits treat the work as something special.
principles.quote: For an auteur it's about being different, and setting expectations so that your team, and everyone around you really treats this as something that could be great, something special.

sources.title: Deprogramming corporatism: why big-company habits kill founders and early hires
sources.originalTitle: Deprogramming corporatism
sources.summary: Garry Tan explains how big-corporate culture (busywork without results, cover-your-ass politics, buzzword-following) trains people in habits that fail in startups. The fix is relentless focus on concrete results, building product and talking to customers, and a founder culture reinforced by the people around you.

principles.text: In a startup you can't just look busy; you must actually make a product people want, because there is no air cover.
principles.quote: There’s no air cover for startups. You don’t have backup troops. It’s just you versus the world. So naturally, if your product or service sucks, then you die.

principles.text: Be wary of hiring big-company directors and managers; they often fail fast in startups, to everyone's surprise.
principles.quote: often they’ll try to grow the team by hiring experienced directors and managers from corporations that are well known and successful. Many of them fail pretty quickly, and it’s always a surprise to everyone, especially the experienced hire.

principles.text: Founders and CEOs must keep the team focused on what matters, not on covering themselves or taking credit.
principles.quote: Startups can sometimes develop a cover-your-ass culture too, but that’s the job of the founders and CEO to keep people focused on things that actually matter.

principles.text: Don't follow buzzwords or trends; you have to be right about the future and make life better for specific paying customers.
principles.quote: Startups can’t survive blindly following buzzwords or whatever trend is hot because you actually have to know what’s coming in the future and be right.

principles.text: Work on things you know are right that most people don't yet know; ask what valuable company nobody is building.
principles.quote: It turns out you have to work on things that a) you know are right, and b) most people don’t know yet.

principles.text: The antidote to corporate habits is results: build product, talk to customers, and think in concrete numbers.
principles.quote: We spend a lot of time trying to get founders to focus on action and results — build product, talk to customers, that’s it. Think in terms of concrete numbers

sources.title: GStack: how Garry Tan ships like a team of twenty with Claude Code
sources.originalTitle: GStack (README by Garry Tan)
sources.summary: Garry Tan's README for gstack, his open source "software factory" that turns Claude Code into a virtual engineering team of role-based slash commands. It shows how one builder runs 10-15 parallel sprints with a think, plan, build, review, test, ship process, and why testing, visual design iteration and QA make AI-driven shipping safe.

principles.text: Give AI agents structured roles and a sprint process; structure is what makes parallelism work.
principles.quote: Without a process, ten agents is ten sources of chaos. With a process — think, plan, build, review, test, ship — each agent knows exactly what to do and when to stop.

principles.text: Manage parallel AI agents like a CEO: check in on key decisions and let the rest run.
principles.quote: You manage them the way a CEO manages a team: check in on the decisions that matter, let the rest run.

principles.text: Measure productivity by shipped output normalized for AI inflation, not raw line counts or who typed it.
principles.quote: The point isn't who typed it, it's what shipped.

principles.text: Give agents eyes: a QA step that opens a real browser, fixes bugs, and writes regression tests unlocked far more parallel workers.
principles.quote: `/qa` was a massive unlock. It let me go from 6 to 12 parallel workers.

principles.text: Aim for full test coverage; tests make AI-assisted coding safe instead of reckless.
principles.quote: 100% test coverage is the goal — tests make vibe coding safe instead of yolo coding.

principles.text: Explore design visually by generating several variants and iterating on feedback, rather than describing a vision in words.
principles.quote: No more describing your vision in words and hoping the AI gets it. You see options, pick the good ones, and iterate visually.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues every job should be judged by whether you are learning, earning, or both, and that you should quit if it is neither. Early in a career, learn first by building real things or winning real customers, then earn, ideally through equity, while avoiding the hedonic treadmill.

chunks.heading: Garry's learn / earn / quit framework
chunks.text:
- Garry's test: "are you learning or are you earning?" Both means a great place. One of the two is still fine. Neither means "it's time to move on, you're wasting your life."
- Learn first, then earn. He calls it (via his friend Steven Sinofsky) "the protein before the carbs."
- Earning first usually still teaches you something, but slowly, and it can cost a lot and trap you on a spending treadmill.
- If you are in neither, plot your exit.

chunks.heading: How to start learning: pick maker or hustler
chunks.text:
- Most people early in their careers should focus on learning first.
- Two paths: maker (design, product, engineering) or hustler (management, sales, marketing).
- Step one is learning about yourself: what you enjoy and what puts you in a state of flow.
- Step two is acquiring the skill. If you love it, the 10,000 hours won't feel like work.
- Garry cites Bill Gates: the people who reach 10,000 hours are those who chose, and were chosen, many times. About 90% drop out at each early stage (50 hours, then another 50) because they dislike it or aren't good.

chunks.heading: Breaking in as a hustler
chunks.text:
- Marketing: "helping other people communicate their problem and how their solution is the best."
- Find a product, website or service you like, suggest improvements, then build, design or write the improvement yourself.
- Cold email the founder with it, or just send it.
- Sales: go get customers without being asked and send them to a founder. "They'll always take your email, they'll always remember you."

chunks.heading: Breaking in as a builder
chunks.text:
- Build it yourself instead of relying on others. Find a real problem your software can solve and ship a first version.
- Don't wait for the perfect problem; it only has to be real and solvable.
- Example: some of the best founders he has met started with gradebook software because they had teachers nearby who were frustrated with their gradebooks. Many later built billion-dollar companies in other areas, but they learned to create there.
- "Creating you can only learn by doing." Make something, then iterate until users love it.
- A product users love beats a credential. A beautiful app, website or elegant GitHub repo puts you in the top 10% with no credentials, even without Stanford.
- His own example: at 14 he got a job cold calling the Yellow Pages internet section, pointing to an award-winning website he made for his junior high underground newspaper. He then cold emailed his way into his first coding job.

chunks.heading: Earning: equity is the highest form
chunks.text:
- The best way to earn is equity: own stock in a company that becomes valuable. A founder starts with 100% of something worth nothing, then makes it worth something.
- Cash can be large too. He notes Google's revenue of over $166B across about 135,000 employees is over $1.2M per employee.
- Founder math: owning 10-30% of an exit worth tens or hundreds of millions to billions can mean becoming a centimillionaire to billionaire.
- Early employees might hold 25 basis points (0.25%) up to 2% or more. Joining early means less equity but a company not yet at its peak value, and it can be an amazing deal if growth is fast.
- Founders and early employees can learn while they earn.

chunks.heading: Warning: the hedonic treadmill and meaningless jobs
chunks.text:
- Many people trade happiness for financial stability. He says that is not necessarily bad, but warns of the cycle: earn, spend on a bigger house, car or nicer things, spend more, repeat. Buying things you don't really want doesn't deliver the satisfaction you're after.
- Advice for would-be founders: if you are young and thrifty, don't inflate your lifestyle. Save that money so you can invest your time in building your own startup or "wealth engine."
- Some high-paying jobs feel meaningless, and the more you're paid, the more meaningless the job can become. He argues "you only get one life, it's too short to waste" on unfulfilling work, even if comfortable.
- If you don't learn and don't love the job, leave once you've earned enough to take the leap.

chunks.heading: Garry's own learn-and-earn history, and when to quit a bad startup
chunks.text:
- Palantir: learned to run teams and build product from scratch while earning equity in what became a $40B company.
- Y Combinator: learned to invest and work with startups at the earliest stage, while earning valuable carry.
- Now: he learns daily from founders as founder and managing partner of his own VC firm. He runs YouTube for fun and donates the proceeds to nonprofits like Code2040, but learns from viewers' comments and DMs.
- Bad startup example: a junior-year enterprise software internship from the Stanford career fair. The company raised money but never closed customers. He made marketing material, mock-ups and prototypes for sales pitches, they never closed a sale all summer, and the startup died. He neither earned much nor learned much.
- His rule: if you aren't learning, can't earn equity or a good salary, and it isn't fun or meaningful, "you gotta quit."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues most founders copy whatever is already successful (photo sharing, travel plans, local events) because desire is mimetic. Real breakout ideas come from unusual personal experience (Flexport, Patreon), start as toys, and are found by working on hard problems while noting gaps and anomalies.

chunks.heading: Why good startup ideas look bad at first
chunks.text:
- Garry says most founders copy the same ideas: "photo-sharing, podcasting, travel plans, local event apps." He says "desire is mimetic. We want what other people want."
- Founders copy whatever has already succeeded, because that is the obvious thing to follow.
- Garry says that is the wrong approach. The most famous startups were not famous when they started.
- He quotes Chris Dixon: great disruptive ideas are hard to spot because "when they start they're toys." Examples he gives:
  - The personal computer ("why would anyone want a computer on every desk?").
  - Bitcoin ("your magical internet beans are a joke").
  - Social networking (people asked how Facebook could ever make money).
- Garry's warning: hundreds of thousands of people now chase the same ideas, and as Peter Thiel says, "infinite competition is for losers."

chunks.heading: Your unique experience is the source of the idea
chunks.text:
- Garry endorses Steve Jobs's point about innovation. You need to zoom out and connect experiences, and you can't have "the same bag of experiences as everyone else" or you will make the same connections.
- His advice: get different experiences, embrace being weird, and know that "what makes you new, different and unique in the world will be the exact thing that makes you succeed." He says this is why diversity matters.
- Find a problem that needs solving from inside your own experience, rather than copying the founders below.
