chunks.heading: Flexport: a founder who knew a hidden market intimately
chunks.text:
- Garry was an early investor in Flexport (through Y Combinator and his fund Initialized). It is now worth more than $3.2 billion.
- His take on meeting Ryan Petersen: he knew immediately that Ryan had "stumbled onto a huge market."
- Garry's favorite pitch meetings are "with founders who teach you something about the world you didn't know before." Global logistics was one of those, and Ryan knew it intimately.
- Ryan's path:
  - One of the first Amazon third-party sellers, roughly 10 to 15 years before the video, paying $40 a month.
  - Imported motorbikes and electric scooters from China.
  - Lived in China for two years running the supply chain.
  - Never treated it as a startup. In Ryan's words, it was "a couple of guys trying to earn a living."
- The idea came from personal experience of the supply chain.

chunks.heading: Patreon: seeing a broken problem early as a creator
chunks.text:
- Garry met Jack Conte and Sam Yam very early, when they were just starting Patreon. Patreon is now worth more than $1.2 billion.
- Jack started the band Pomplamoose with his wife and posted music videos on YouTube from 2008, in the first wave of creators using the platform.
- He saw that monetization for creators was "totally broken" and that there had to be a better way for people reaching millions online to make a living.
- Garry's takeaway: they saw the problem very early because they lived it, and that funded "a new generation of creator."
- His caveat: "These are just breadcrumbs. History doesn't repeat, but it rhymes." Don't do what they did; find what is unique to you.

chunks.heading: Pitfalls: novelty and imperfect first versions
chunks.text:
- You don't have to be novel. Flexport and Patreon were not the first attempts at their ideas.
- If there is competition, you must be better, faster and cheaper to stand a chance. "Competition is not your friend. It's fierce and it will make your startup fail."
- The first version doesn't need to be perfect. Garry cites Chris Dixon on disruptive tech being dismissed as a toy because it undershoots user needs while still developing.
- Example: the first telephone carried voice only a mile or two. Western Union passed on acquiring it because it couldn't see the use for businesses and railroads. They failed to anticipate how fast the technology and infrastructure would improve.
- The same mistake, he says, was made by mainframe makers about the PC and by telecoms about Skype.

chunks.heading: How to find a good idea: Paul Graham's process
chunks.text:
- Garry points to Paul Graham's 2012 essay on startup ideas. The advice he highlights:
  - Work on hard problems, driven mainly by curiosity.
  - Keep a "second self watching over your shoulder, taking notes of gaps and anomalies."
  - Give yourself time. You can control how fast you become a prepared mind, but not when the stimuli that spark ideas arrive.
- The cautionary example: if Bill Gates and Paul Allen had forced themselves to come up with an idea in one month, they might have picked a month before the Altair even appeared.
- They saw the Altair in a magazine in Harvard Square, wrote to the company, and offered to do a BASIC for it. Altair BASIC became a hit and the company became Microsoft.

chunks.heading: Garry's closing advice
chunks.text:
- Don't build another "photo-sharing-travel-plans local events" startup.
- Find something new, follow your interests, and note gaps, anomalies and things you genuinely believe the world needs.
- Keep improving your builder skills: engineering, product management, leadership, consistency, conscientiousness and communication.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how a VC fund exists to return money to limited partners, why brand and early access matter, and what makes a good investor. He stresses technical builders, contrarian belief, and being fair, direct and honest, then announces Initialized is hiring a principal and a partner.

chunks.heading: How a VC fund works: returns, limited partners and why the fund's results matter
chunks.text:
- Garry says a VC firm exists to generate returns for investors. The money he invests is not his; it comes from "limited partners": endowments, nonprofits, retirement plans and sovereign wealth funds that professionally manage most of the world's money.
- He invests in the best possible founders because the goal is to return far more to those limited partners than they put in.
- He cites Sequoia (started in 1972 with an $8 million fund, now funded companies representing more than $3.3 trillion in value) and Y Combinator (about $400 billion of wealth created, founded 2005, where he worked and got his start).
- Initialized, which he started in 2012 with a first fund of $7 million, is now involved in over $100 billion of market cap in under nine years. It returned hundreds of millions of dollars to its first investors on Coinbase's IPO day.
- Initialized was the first investor in almost a dozen startups now worth over $1 billion, including Instacart, Flexport, Patreon, Rows, TruePill, Standard Cognition, Cruise Automation, Opendoor and Blend.
- Coinbase: he paid 15 cents a share about nine years before the IPO; shares topped out at $420 on IPO day. The point he draws: "we were first, way before it was obvious."

chunks.heading: Why VC is winner-take-all, and why the brand is not the point
chunks.text:
- Garry says that who funds a startup matters a lot, much like a degree from Harvard, Stanford or Oxford. A startup backed by a top VC firm can hire smarter people, raise more money from better next-stage investors, and build a better product that wins.
- He is explicit that this is how it works, not that it is good: VC is winner-take-all, so founders (and people choosing a VC career) should pick wisely. Getting the right investor early can be pivotal.
- His caution: being the best-known brand is "the sizzle", but "the steak is in the returns."
- Cynicism does not work in VC. Firms fund ideas while they are still not obvious and often seem crazy to the public, so you have to believe in building the future.

chunks.heading: Favor technical, product and design-oriented builders
chunks.text:
- Initialized has a strong preference for technical, product and design-oriented founders, because "the ones who can build it usually do." YC likewise prides itself on partners with deep product or technical backgrounds.
- He contrasts today with the late-1990s bubble (hit-and-run, sales-led companies with weak products, "forget details, just do deals") and calls the swing toward realness a good thing: it is less about money or bluster and more about founders who deliver.
- Instacart story: the YC application deadline had passed two months earlier, and Apoorva Mehta emailed YC alumni for introductions. Garry replied that a late application was "nearly impossible," which Apoorva read as "possible." Apoorva then ordered a six-pack of beer through Instacart to Garry at YC headquarters; the driver texted when delivered, and Garry called half an hour later and invited him to meet the partners the next day.
- Garry says that as an engineer and designer, once he used the app he knew YC had to fund it. It did not matter that dozens of startups (like Webvan) had tried and failed; what mattered was that this founder had built something truly great. Instacart is now worth tens of billions.
- The lesson he takes: drive and never giving up are recognizable, and "it all boils down to belief." A builder who can make you believe can make everyone believe.

chunks.heading: Be contrarian and right: avoid paint-by-numbers ideas
chunks.text:
- Garry says many giant startup outcomes are both contrarian and right. In a cynical world, the person with deeper real belief is who he looks for.
- He draws on Peter Thiel: to be contrarian "is to actually think about things," to have well-defined beliefs and think for yourself.
- Paint-by-numbers ideas are like bad Hollywood pitches (a college football star joins elite hackers to catch the shark that killed his friend). The startup version strings together buzzwords such as sharing, mobile and social. Thiel's line he repeats: "the something of somewhere is really mostly just the nothing of nowhere."
- Hollywood-style ideas sometimes work, but founders pursue them at a far higher rate and they produce much more failure.
- Garry cites René Girard's mimetic theory (our desires come from other people) as the basis for why people crowd into the same ideas.
- His test for secret knowledge: ask "What do you believe that nobody else believes?" He looks for independent, first-principles thinkers who can see paint-by-numbers immediately; the crowd (get-rich-quick people, scammers, do-nothings) does not see value where he does.

chunks.heading: Be a benevolent investor: fair, direct and honest
chunks.text:
- Garry says what matters most is being fair, direct and honest. He admits the firm is not perfect, but intends to build a venture firm that wins "without playing the games that are commonplace" in venture and business culture.
- His argument: greed is not good. The best founders can choose any investor and will choose the most trustworthy, so being a bad actor is adverse selection. In an iterated, infinite game (venture structures last 10 to 14 years, and increasingly longer, to get from idea to IPO) you may win a deal but lose in the long run.
- He quotes Bill Walsh ("the score takes care of itself"): focus on the process and quality of execution, and winning follows. His version: "do right and you'll win."
- Funds can afford to behave well when returns are strong. He cites Jason Lemkin: with a 1x net fund a write-off is high drama; in a 2x net fund every write-off hurts; in a 4x-plus net fund write-offs don't matter. Initialized is that third kind, with five core funds and $770 million in committed assets.
- The failure pattern he describes when investors squeeze founders in trouble: (1) the team misses revenue targets for a quarter, (2) the investor starts micromanaging, (3) the founder spends more time on board reports than fixing the problem, and the startup never recovers. "Squeezing harder on a handful of sand will force more grains out."
- His alternative: help find the root cause (executive roles and responsibilities, business model, go-to-market, or product). "You can only help if you first do no harm." He believes this is why Initialized will win.

chunks.heading: Hiring at Initialized: roles and who fits
chunks.text:
- Garry announced Initialized was hiring through an open search, which most VC firms don't do. He says diversity of experience and background improves decisions.
- Principal: no investing experience required. Could be a founder or executive who can help startups go from zero to one. The role mainly helps founders and also teaches how to make investments.
- Partner: better for people with investing experience and a successful track record, such as an angel investor or a partner or principal at another firm.
- No required school, and no need to have worked at Google or Facebook; he cares about what you have done and can do.
- These are fairly senior roles because founders need experienced help: "everybody wants to tell you how to do it but they never did it" (Jay-Z).
- His view on capital: people say too much money chases too few good ideas and teams, but he thinks there is an infinite number of problems to solve and of smart, good people to solve them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how avoiding conflict with his Posterous co-founder led him to quit in 2010, and how to spot and fix both too little and too much co-founder conflict. Fixes include resolving disagreements on the spot, assigning one owner per area, listening with steel-manning, and getting coaches and trusted advisors involved early.

chunks.heading: Why Garry left Posterous: the cost of avoiding conflict
chunks.text:
- Posterous grew 10x yearly and became a top-200 site in about two years. By the end of 2010 growth had flatlined, and the co-founders (friends since college) could not get along.
- Garry resigned from his last startup at the end of 2010. In the weeks before, he couldn't sleep or eat and his heart rate felt pegged at 120. He says the physical symptoms were his non-verbal brain "going on strike" against a story he told himself.
- He calls co-founder disputes "the number one early startup killer." In hindsight he says the rift was "entirely preventable."
- His warning: "You can't count on good times forever... winter is coming." Good growth hides problems underneath.

chunks.heading: What went wrong: too little conflict
chunks.text:
- Garry and his co-founder stopped spending time together because they were avoiding conflict. When the business needed them most, they hadn't resolved issues for so long that the relationship failed too.
- He mistook the appearance of a good co-founder relationship for a real one. His advice: "Don't make it look like a good startup or a good co-founder relationship. Spend time actually making it a good startup."
- He blames himself. On product, personnel and strategy he "buckled" and "self-abandoned," sacrificing what he knew was right to the idea that good co-founders don't fight. Resentment grew.
- Tells that you're in this state:
  - You haven't spent time with your co-founder outside work.
  - You keep interactions to a minimum.
- His first executive coach, Cameron Yarbrough of Torch, taught him to watch for the "four horsemen" from psychologist John Gottman: defensiveness, criticism, contempt, stonewalling. Gottman uses them to predict marital failure with high accuracy, and Garry says the same holds for co-founders.

chunks.heading: Fixing too little conflict
chunks.text:
- If you disagree, don't leave the room until you have a resolution. If an hour isn't enough, cancel the weekend, go on a hike or camping trip, and hold a retreat on the spot. "Those other things can wait."
- He says some of the best billion-dollar company founders he knows did exactly this.
- Give more feedback. "Err on the side of giving more feedback," and communicate exactly what you feel, in the right way.
- He has always valued harmony, but learned (sometimes the hard way) that you can't sacrifice what you know is right to get it. "Don't swallow your words. If you have a point, make sure you are heard."

chunks.heading: Symptoms of too much conflict
chunks.text:
- Decisions are hard to make, and every proposal gets viewed through "how will the different factions view this."
- Horse trading ("I can have this if you can have that"), long acrimonious meetings, and paralysis over small decisions.
- Uncertainty about which venue should even decide an issue.
- Settled decisions get re-litigated, with old arguments renewed and past outcomes used as justification for new conflicts.
- Being able to identify factions at all is a clear warning sign. Worst is blending unrelated decisions because different groups want different things.
- Usual root cause: roles aren't well defined, so people don't know who is in charge of what.

chunks.heading: Fix: one owner per area (the Heroku approach)
chunks.text:
- Make a list of every area the business needs, decide who is best at each, and assign exactly one person.
- Garry recalls the Heroku founders doing this at Y Combinator: they listed every task the company did and found exactly one owner, a founder or executive "whose ass was on the line to deliver that thing."
- Why it works:
  - It's clear who to talk to, and because it's written down everyone can see it. The owner collects feedback before deciding.
  - You move fast. The owner makes the call, and everyone agrees to "disagree and commit."
  - You stop re-fighting the same battles and stop waiting weeks, months or years for decisions.

chunks.heading: Listening: steel man, don't straw man
chunks.text:
- If conflicts are fundamental, start listening. The loudest person shouldn't automatically win; that's conflict avoidance of a different stripe, giving no space to competing ideas.
- Listen first and let the other side know you hear them. Repeat back the strongest version of their argument (a steel man).
- He cites a Stripe PM Shreyas Doshi thread on why listening is hard: fear of being wrong, desire for validation, lack of curiosity, urge to impress, feeling of superiority.
- Garry admits he is "terrible at this." He is often so busy composing what to say that he fails to be present, especially when the content cuts against his convictions. He says those are the most important moments to listen.

chunks.heading: Get outside help early
chunks.text:
- Talk it through with other founders, friends, coaches, or whoever you trust. Getting out of your own head helps.
- Hire an exec coach: "I can't recommend it enough for founders," especially when company-killing conflict is on the line. He suggests bringing them in early, individually or as a group, like a marriage counselor.
- He recommends Torch (torch.io), the coach marketplace founded by his first exec coach Cameron Yarbrough, which he helped fund and start.
- Cost: don't cheap out. "Making the wrong decisions will cost you your company and your vested equity." Pick coaches appropriate to your company's stage.
- Involve your board, investors, advisors and closest founder friends. "You can't do this alone." Don't broadcast the problem, but keep trusted people close despite the embarrassment; they offer new perspective.
- He notes that pretty much every founder he has talked to has some form of this problem, and he offers DMs on Instagram to help people find support.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan shares a 360 review revealing he relied on his team to say no for him because he was conflict-avoidant. Using neuroscience and Keegan's stages of adult development, he explains how noticing internal conflict, then expressing a clear preference, makes you a better leader and builds stronger teams.

chunks.heading: Garry's 360 review: the "relies on others to say no" feedback
chunks.text:
- Garry did a 360 degree review in April 2020. His exec coach interviewed the people he worked with most, one on one, then anonymized the feedback.
- A 360 is "an absolutely powerful tool for you to know how you're doing and what you could be doing better."
- The feedback that landed: "Gary relies on other people to say no for him. He feels things but does not articulate them until later. People can't immediately understand what he thinks or feels about a situation."
- He calls this a manager's red flag. He wasn't doing his job and wasn't being clear when he needed to be.
- Root cause: he was conflict avoidant and could not say no or even express a preference in the moment.
- A year-later 360 showed he had solved it: he no longer asks others to fight his battles, and the team is happy.

chunks.heading: Why Garry ends up debating both sides: modeling other people
chunks.text:
- Garry often argues both sides of a decision. One side is his own viewpoint, shaped by experience (a go/no-go on a product, how much to pay for something).
- The other side is detailed mental models of what others want: customers, users, investors, co-workers. Their motivations and needs differ from his.
- He sees this as a strength. Building models of other people's behavior from their experience, not just his own, is a big part of what makes him good as a designer, VC and manager.
- The failure mode is when the internal argument isn't resolved. He then makes a poor leadership decision or leans on others to "interpret the tea leaves and say yes or no for me."
- His diagnosis: "I am not integrated enough." Other people's wants were so vivid to him that he sometimes lost his own perspective.

chunks.heading: The "many minds" idea from neuroscience
chunks.text:
- Garry draws on Michael Gazzaniga's split-brain research, shown in Adam Curtis's documentary "Can't Get You Out of My Head."
- In a patient whose brain hemispheres were surgically disconnected to stop epilepsy, a second force kept taking control (for example, one hand picking clothes she didn't want).
- The argument: the human brain holds multiple selves, each taking control at different moments. The conscious verbal self makes up stories to rationalize what the others did.
- Garry's summary: "many minds decide and then our verbal centers rationalize." The unified self may be an illusion.
- His point for leaders: if you can't integrate the minds inside yourself, you can't integrate a team. Start at the individual level, then do it for the team.

chunks.heading: Kegan's five stages of adult development
chunks.text:
- Garry uses Harvard researcher Robert Kegan's ladder as a map for how to grow:
  - Stage 1: impulse and reflex (infancy, early childhood).
  - Stage 2: sense of self ruled by one's own needs and wishes; others matter only if they support those.
  - Stage 3: self is socially determined, based on real or imagined expectations of others. Garry places this around our twenties.
  - Stage 4: self is determined by values you have authored yourself. Rarely achieved, and only in adulthood.
  - Stage 5: self is no longer bound to any one aspect of yourself or your history; you focus on the flow of life. Garry says it "sounds like nirvana."
- Moving past stage 3 requires asking whether you can transcend your own bodily needs and your desire for money, sex, fame and material goods.
- Garry's self-diagnosis: he was stuck in stage 3, a socially constructed self, which is why he couldn't state a preference.

chunks.heading: How hiring covered the gap
chunks.text:
- Knowing deep down he'd struggle with saying no, Garry hired well and set up values the team could work toward even when he couldn't voice a preference himself.
- He credits the strength of that team for getting him through a very hard time.
- His caveat: "relying on the team to say things that I needed to say myself, that's always going to be worse than doing it yourself."

chunks.heading: Garry's method: notice the conflict, then inflect into it
chunks.text:
- Through coaching and therapy, he learned to notice when internal conflicts are happening.
- His signal is physiological: faster breath and heart rate, a hot face.
- At that moment he pauses and takes stock of the many minds. Giving a voice to each part lets him see what he actually wants, so he can express a preference when before he couldn't.
- He cites Ray Dalio on meditation as a key to success: slowing things down so you can act calmly in chaos, "just like a ninja in a street fight."
- Chaos and conflict are a given. Separating what you truly want from your modeling of others is how you reach Kegan stage 4, "a life that is truly authored by you."
- Payoff for teams: leaders who are integrated and aware at the individual level can integrate their team into "a powerful resolute super organism" that builds products bigger than any one person. "Knowing is half the battle."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan walks founders through design as a self-taught practitioner: empathy-driven product design (personas, PRDs, P0-P3 priorities), interaction design (command language, remove or chunk actions, steal proven patterns) and visual design (contrast, closeness, grid). He closes with usability testing and customer support as the feedback loop.

chunks.heading: Product design starts with empathy, not novelty
chunks.text:
- Garry defines design as "creating things for users that work well and delight them." He rejects the idea that design is only how something looks; it is also how it works.
- He puts function before form. His examples of form over function include Apple's notched-iPhone marketing image ("I'm not here for the notch, I'm here for the content"), a romantic restaurant where you can't read the menu, and a beautiful door that needs a "PULL" sign because nobody can tell how to open it.
- He argues novelty is the opposite of functionality: "there's very little totally new under the sun," and founders shouldn't spend much time being extremely novel.
- He treats empathy as the thing founders must spend the most time on. He recalls Paul Graham pushing the Posterous team to ask what users are thinking, feeling, and why they showed up. He also recommends Dale Carnegie's "How to Win Friends and Influence People" as required reading, because you must become genuinely interested in other people's point of view.
- His mental model: building a product is throwing the best possible party. No line, someone friendly greets you at the door, takes your coat, and shows you where your friends are.
- Design with no clear problem is art, not design. His example is a lineup of absurd inventions, each solving the inventor's own interest rather than a user's problem: "now you have two problems."
- He recommends Dieter Rams' principle that good design is "as little design as possible" and Don Norman's "The Design of Everyday Things."

chunks.heading: The three layers of design for startups, and who should do them
chunks.text:
- Garry splits startup design into three layers:
  - **Product design:** what is the problem and who is it for.
  - **Interaction design:** how users accomplish their goals (flows, wireframes).
  - **Visual design:** the last mile, pixel-level composition or HTML/CSS.
- The ideal is a co-founder who can do all three (and code, and handle business), a "unicorn." If you find one, make them a co-founder, but only after you've known them for a while.
- The process is roughly a waterfall: requirements, then interaction design, then visual design, then engineering, with conversation throughout.
- He stresses that at the early stage the founder owns all of it and shouldn't box themselves into one role. Design sits alongside product management, engineering, and customer support.
- He says he is self-taught: trained as an engineer, never went to design school, employee number 10 at Palantir, then Posterous (funded by YC in 2008), then 10 batches advising YC founders as a designer in residence.

chunks.heading: Writing a PRD with personas, using Posterous as the example
chunks.text:
- Start with a problem statement. Posterous's 2008 YC application framed it as: blogging platforms were stale, the iPhone was new, and email was a universal way to get content online.
- Use personas to make users specific people. Posterous had three:
  - **David the dad:** comfortable with technology, owns the newest iPhone.
  - **Grace the grandma:** ASUS netbook, Hotmail, doesn't really understand how it works.
  - **A social-network-native persona:** with her own distinct needs, in the early social media era.
- He says to give personas backstory where useful: technology comfort, browser, email client, device. Personas also create productive tension (David versus Grace).
- This matters for B2B too. Even in industries like construction or freight, you'll have an executive decision maker and a line-level worker with very different motivations and capabilities.
- Group requirements into coherent features an engineer can pick up. Posterous's list:
  - Post by email with plain text.
  - Post by email without an account.
  - Photo attachments, multiple attachments into a web gallery, video.
  - Anti-spoofing security.
- "Post by email without an account" was intentional. There was no signup flow on the homepage; you emailed post@posterous.com and got a reply with your new URL. It opened the product to non-technical users and cemented a new behavior.
- The security feature mattered because Michael Arrington reviewed the launch on TechCrunch and immediately had technical friends try to spoof his Posterous email address. The team had already prevented it.
- The step before all of this is user research. He says founders should do it themselves, not outsource it, as a basic part of customer development. Talking to people you want to build for can even reveal which problem to solve.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing with P0-P3 and the scope/quality/time trade-off
chunks.text:
- Garry assigns every feature a priority:
  - **P0:** the core; if you don't do it, why are you here.
  - **P1:** wouldn't ship without it.
  - **P2/P3:** nice to have; the devil in the details often lives here.
- Also note which persona wants each feature (for example, photo attachments served David and Irene as power users; no-account posting served the less technical users).
- Put the work in a bug database and link it to the PRD, wireframes, and visual comps. He says every team should use one, and it becomes more important as the team grows.
- A sprint should be short, two to three weeks, "the shorter the better." Without priorities, "you don't know what to cut," and a two-week sprint becomes a month, then three.
- You always have three levers: scope, quality, and time. Cut scope from the bottom of the priority list; otherwise time slips or you ship bugs to production.
- P3 items still help engineers architect for later (for example, knowing video is coming means they don't build the media classes for photos only).
- He says many bad product decisions you see in a settings panel come from teams skipping this prioritization and shipping.
- He claims doing this basic step already puts you ahead of many peers.

chunks.heading: Interaction design: command language, fewer steps, and stealing patterns
chunks.text:
- People treat computers like people. Garry cites his Stanford research with the late professor Cliff Nass: politeness gets politeness back, and mirroring effects show up without avatars or anthropomorphism. He mentions BJ Fogg and Byron Reeves as part of that work.
- So interaction design is about commands, and it includes writing. Users read copy in their own voice and tend to do what they're told.
- A common founder mistake is passive, disembodied, third-person copy. Big companies like Microsoft get away with word-salad product names because they have scale and a sales force; startups can't afford that.
- Use direct, personal command language, high contrast, and an obvious call to action. Be opinionated about what the next user action should be, so someone landing on a page or app just knows what to do.
- Two ways to get people to act:
  - **Remove actions.** Paul Graham asked why the 2008 signup page had a confirm-password field. Just let people use "forgot password." Removing it can raise signup conversion by as much as 50 percent. "Cognitive load is an incredibly real issue."
  - **Chop up an action** into steps, such as a wizard (his example is the Windows 95 style, and tax-like B2B configuration flows).
- Don't be novel at this stage. "Steal what works": pull-to-refresh, swipe left to right (Mailbox, sold to Dropbox), and other established patterns. He says you can get very far on design patterns alone and points to pattern galleries on the web.
- Watch for mixing modalities, such as swipe-style pagination dots on a desktop site with a touchpad.
- Deliverables are wireframes or prototypes (OmniGraffle or similar): text, calls to action, and screen-to-screen flow, with no color or finished fonts yet.

chunks.heading: Visual design: contrast, closeness, grids, and removing ornament
chunks.text:
- Garry's rule: "when you're forced to be simple, you actually have to solve the real problem." Avoid ornament and ask whether anything (text, lines, borders, even colons on form labels) could be removed without losing meaning.
- He cites Edward Tufte's "chart junk": charts with no axes, odd gradients, and decorative backgrounds.
- Visual design is not self-expression; it is about what information you're trying to get across.
- His three principles:
  - **Contrast.** Use bold, color, and size to mark what is more and less important. "If everything is bold, nothing is bold."
  - **The squint test.** Squint at a page; your eye should land on the highest-contrast element, and you should make out the basic shapes without reading.
  - **Closeness.** Group related things. His example is a login form that seems detached from account creation.
- Contrast plus closeness gives visual hierarchy, and a grid supports it. He credits Twitter's Bootstrap for putting a flexible grid into everyone's hands.
- Users scan for the highest-contrast items (headings exist for this reason) to decide whether the page matches their goal, then dive deeper.
- For layout, his sequence is: use padding and margin and a proper grid first, a line if needed, and a box last. Boxes draw a lot of attention (good around a call to action), but overuse makes everything compete. Whitespace helps focus attention.
- He credits the minimal techniques to Swiss design and the folks behind Helvetica.

chunks.heading: Feedback: usability testing and customer support
chunks.text:
- Design isn't done at creation. His airport analogy: the sign designer knows where everything is, but a first-time visitor gets lost. Feedback exists to solve that.
- **Usability testing.** Start once you have wireframes, before writing code. Print them out, sit with people who have never seen them, ask open-ended questions ("What are we looking at? What would you click next?"), and prompt lightly with the user's goal. This is far cheaper than fixing bugs in code later.
- **Customer support** is "way under-appreciated." Most teams treat the support line like a shredder.
  - Specs and designs cover the 80 percent case, but there are thousands of once-in-a-blue-moon cases, and added up they make a broken product. "The devil truly is in these long-tail bugs."
  - Big companies keep designers and engineers away from support and treat users as cattle. A founder's advantage is being human and fixing the bug.
  - Fixing it creates an evangelist for life. Quoting Paul Buchheit: don't make something a thousand people kind of like; make something a hundred people absolutely love. Support is how you get there.
  - He says the designer, who thinks through the user, is the best person on the team to advocate for users.
- Product development is a perpetual cycle: research, product design, interaction design, visual design, build, usability testing, support, repeat. You don't need a person for each step, but you need to spend time on each.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan, at Stanford ETL, shares lessons from his own mistakes (including turning down Palantir) and 20 years in startups and YC. He argues founders should be multi-skilled generalists, act small and hands-on with early users, deal with childhood baggage early, and work on weird problems they uniquely understand.

chunks.heading: Mental health and the founder's inner state
chunks.text:
- Garry says unexamined childhood trauma shows up in how founders manage conflict. His parents were immigrants, his father struggled with alcoholism and holding a job, and money was tight.
- At his first company he avoided conflict until he blew up at people. A direct report told his co-founder Garry was "the worst manager he'd ever had" and had never been so disrespected.
- He took the online Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) test and scored very high. He recommends it, and says a high score is okay and you don't have to pretend to be normal.
- He credits years of therapy and coaching with letting him approach conflict in a healthy way, and calls himself a work in progress.
- His failure mode: Posterous didn't work out partly because he hadn't dealt with this early enough, and by the time he was making hard calls on teams it was "a little bit too late."
- Startups take on the personality of their founders, so unexamined demons end up in the company.
- His advice is to get therapy early. It sounds expensive, but people spend 10x to 1000x more on things that won't fill the hole when all they needed was to talk to someone.

chunks.heading: The $200M+ mistake: turning down Palantir
chunks.text:
- In 2004 Garry was a level 59 PM at Microsoft making $74,000 a year. Peter Thiel took him to dinner and wrote a check for $74,000 in cash so he could quit at zero risk and join friends starting Palantir.
- Garry said no because "I might get promoted to level 60 next year." Palantir had offered about 1% of the company. He later joined as employee number 10 and designed the logo. He estimates the missed stake at roughly $350M to $500M, and calls it his "$200 million mistake."
- Lesson 1, media is stale: anything you read in the press is a third-hand account of what happened six months ago. He judged Palantir by what he could read (selling enterprise software to three-letter agencies wasn't in the news) and got it exactly wrong.
- Lesson 2, great ideas sound dumb: the iPod was dismissed as "all that hype for an MP3 player." In 2003 he skipped Google because nobody on campus thought it would make a dollar.
- Two Venn diagrams matter. One is people who can build technology and people who understand hairy problems nobody else can solve. The other is ideas that are actually good but look like bad ideas. At YC this shows up as founder-market fit. He points to Thiel's *Zero to One* for the second.
- Lesson 3, he spent his money: he took on a nice apartment and a new car on top of student debt, trying to fill "a hole in my heart." He says he should have husbanded every dollar as months of freedom to create equity.

chunks.heading: How to think about big companies and jobs
chunks.text:
- Work is a transaction. Microsoft made about $650,000 in profit per employee while paying him $74,000. Unless you own the place, you get a fraction of the value you create.
- It isn't valueless: you get money and stability, and above all you can learn something there. He says to leave big tech before it makes you soft.
- At Microsoft he owned a tiny checkbox in a dialog box (Windows Mobile ActiveSync, which users called "Microsoft ActiveStink"), and he wasn't having fun.
- He rage-quit a job roughly every couple of years once he was six or seven years in. In hindsight each time he had learned what he wanted to learn. He doesn't recommend burning bridges, but says "learning or earning" is what matters.
- He would have done web software in 2003 rather than Windows Mobile.
- Don't sell your time. He spent four years as a consultant and started at 14 by cold-calling the Yellow Pages for an internet design agency job, using the money to help his parents buy their first home.
- His advice to his younger self at 18 or 22 is to make products instead. Time is the most precious finite asset, while software or hardware can "keep making money" while you sleep.

chunks.heading: How Posterous started and the Katamari model
chunks.text:
- Garry had just rage-quit Palantir and was working at a friend's startup as a designer while taking $200 cash photography jobs off Craigslist. He attended one of the first YC Startup Schools at Dinkelspiel Auditorium, sitting on the floor with a big Canon lens.
- Event photography was missing, so he put his photos on the blog platform he was building on the side with his friend Sachin Agarwal. He posted it to Hacker News, and Paul Graham and Jessica Livingston then interviewed them for YC.
- TechCrunch's Michael Arrington left them on top of the homepage all weekend, which brought 10,000 signups, then 20,000. They grew it into a top-200 website and sold it to Twitter.
- He says it started by figuring out what skills and equipment he had and how to turn them into something useful for others, not by asking anyone to be a mentor.
- Katamari Damacy is his metaphor for a startup. You roll a ball that sticks to things smaller than it, and if you try to grab something too big you bounce off and shrink.
- You are picking up three things: co-founders and people, a product that solves a problem and brings customers, and capital that lets you hire and buy more customers. This becomes a virtuous cycle.
- It works as a loop. Push on whichever of the three you can move, switch focus when you stall, and come back. A great co-founder helps you win customers, which helps you raise money, which helps you hire.

chunks.heading: Be a Swiss Army knife and act small
chunks.text:
- Don't let the market turn you into an interchangeable part, such as a "junior back-end Redis engineer." Be a "super knife" who does many things.
- He bought a Wenger Giant Knife on eBay for $4,700. A commodity Wenger pocket knife costs about $3, so versatility is worth over 1,000x.
- Non-technical people who ask how to start should learn to code. This isn't to become the coder but because it improves hiring, customer conversations and speed.
- Don't try to look big. Don't mimic Microsoft's homepage language. The advantage of a new startup is being a real human at a time when people crave authentic connection.
- Treat startups less like building a car and more like throwing a great party: greet people, take their coat, introduce them to friends. Great design and breadth matter for that.
- Most companies treat their support inbox as "a suggestion box that goes straight to the shredder."

chunks.heading: Fanatical customer support and being a real person
chunks.text:
- At Posterous, once the team was seven or eight people, they split the days of the week and each person owned the inbox all day. The aim was to reply to every email within 10 minutes and fix bugs on the spot.
- Being hands-on and authentic ("I'm the CEO, what do you need?") is an unscalable thing he considers very powerful. Customers will tell you what they want if you listen.
- He cites an early study of Usenet. When a post got no reply, only 16% of posters came back to the forum. With even one reply, 26% came back.
- That 10-point retention difference compounds into the difference between a flatlining startup and a working one.
- It applies to B2B and dev tools too. There are only about 30 million developers, so developer tools are effectively "a consumer go-to-market" with 30 million consumers instead of a billion.

chunks.heading: Choosing problems, timing, and mission
chunks.text:
- To find good problems, do something weird. Ignore Time, TechCrunch and what's hot on Twitter, and focus on "what do I uniquely know and what do I believe in."
- His examples are Kyle Vogt at Cruise, who loved self-driving cars at MIT when nobody thought it was a commercial business, and Brian Armstrong reading the Satoshi Nakamoto white paper.
- On school versus startups, school is fun and one of the best places to meet co-founders. His bar for quitting is to know who you are, be good at things, have found co-founders, and have an idea you think you uniquely can solve.
- He was a late bloomer and didn't start a company straight out of college. He needed Microsoft, a startup stint and learning to manage people first. He says some of the best YC founders aren't fresh out of college, and you should follow your own path.
- He rejects the "speedrun society" path of making as much money as possible and then saving the world (he mocks "save the shrimp" and virtue signaling). He recommends Randy Komisar's *The Monk and the Riddle* and says you don't have to live on the deferred life plan.
- He disagrees with the finance adage of "too much money chasing too few good ideas." He says there are far too many unsolved problems, and builders should be accelerationists working on human abundance.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry argues AGI is arriving diffused as a personal agent running on your own context, not as a single event. He lays out the stack (rented model + owned context + harness), a five-step plan to build a library and skill files, and argues skill files must be owned by you, not your employer.

chunks.heading: Personal AGI is general intelligence for one person, not a god in a data center
chunks.text:
Garry rejects the "AGI as a singular event" framing. He argues AGI is arriving diffused, as "your agent running on your context doing your work," which he calls personal AGI. He separates it from rented products:
- A $20/month chatbot, better autocomplete, or a calendar-only assistant is "a subscription you rent." It resets when you close the tab, knows what everyone knows, and gets "a lobotomy on someone else's schedule" when the company pivots.
- Personal AGI is an agent on your infrastructure, reading memory you own, running procedures you wrote, and compounding.
- Corporate AI improves only when the company ships. Personal AGI improves every day because it knows more of your life. One is "a product you consume," the other "an asset you build."
- He believes intelligence of this kind should be "owned by you, not rented."

chunks.heading: The equation for the next decade: rented model + owned context + harness
chunks.text:
Garry's formula: a frontier model (rented, a commodity, cheaper every quarter) plus your context (owned, unique) plus a harness that wires them together (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Claude Code, or Codex). The result is an agent that acts like "a very fast version of you."
- "Model quality is rented but your brain is owned."
- 2x people and 100x people use the same Claude, with the same weights, context window and API. The leverage is in what context you give it, how relevant it is, and whether it arrives at the right step.
- Paul Graham's "make something people want" and "do things that don't scale" still govern. Agents are how one founder now does unscalable things at scale.

chunks.heading: Personal output multipliers and portfolio evidence
chunks.text:
- In 2013, as a YC partner building Bookface at night, Garry shipped about 14 useful lines of code a day. Today he runs YC full-time, with a 5:00 kid pickup, and estimates about 400x his 2013 output.
- Under a pathological verbosity penalty (assume bloated code, half scaffolding, self-flattery) it is still "8x at the absolute floor" and roughly 10x that in the middle of the range.
- He says the multiplier applies to design, product management, growth and every knowledge-work area, not just code.
- In YC's Winter 25 batch, a quarter of companies had code bases that were 95% AI generated. They use agents for everything, and the batch is on track to be one of the fastest growing and most profitable in YC history. He admits he cannot prove causation.
- Revenue per person: Emergent (Summer 24) went from public launch to nine figures of revenue in eight months and was 15 people at $15M annualized. Retail (Winter 24) hit $60M annualized with about 40 people.
- His claim: the fastest growing founders "are not treating AI as autocomplete. They are treating it as a workforce."

chunks.heading: GBrain: the library plus the librarian
chunks.text:
Humans hold about seven things in working memory, and every checklist, org chart and standup is a prosthetic for that limit. An agent holds about a million tokens (roughly 1,000 pages). The real question is what decides which three books are open on the desk.
- Garry's personal OpenClaw has a Karpathy-style knowledge wiki of about 220,000 markdown pages: 25 years of his life, including email, meetings, notes, photos, drafts and mistakes, compiled and curated mostly by agents.
- Example: when a founder emails about a crisis, the agent has already pulled every prior conversation with that founder and three portfolio companies that hit the same wall, with what worked.
- A typical day: overnight inbox processing (not sorting), triage using context on who the sender is and what they are really asking, a morning briefing, pre-meeting prep docs, and finished research.
- GBrain is free and open source, with a hosted version at gbrain.io. Coding framework GStack has 123,000 GitHub stars, in the top 100 open source projects in GitHub history.
- It started as "a folder," a few markdown files about companies and people. "Nobody builds the warehouse first. First, you build one shelf."

chunks.heading: Fat skills, thin harness: markdown is code
chunks.text:
Skill files are pages of English. His example: when a Circle Back meeting recording lands, transcribe with speaker labels, extract commitments, owners and deadlines, cross-check named people against the library, file summary and transcript, and flag (don't override) contradictions.
- Test: "If a smart intern could follow it, an agent can run it." He says "Markdown is actually code... The compiler is a language model."
- A skill file is an employee; a resolver is an org chart. You can run "an organization of one plus your agents" before incorporating.
- At YC, media, events and finance staff who never open a terminal build skill files and scheduled jobs. One finance person compiled about 100 Excel workbooks into a single app with an internal agent.
- Latent vs deterministic: judgment and taste belong in latent space (steered by markdown); arithmetic, SQL and scheduling belong in deterministic code. Seating five people is latent; building custom schedules for 6,000 conference attendees needs markdown files calling code and a SQL database. "The model fails where we fail."
- Compendium skill example: five days before the talk, his agent bought three Spinoza biographies (about 1,500 pages), then produced a dated chronology, points of biographer disagreement, verbatim quotes with chapter citations, and the 10 most tellable moments ranked with delivery notes.

chunks.heading: Five steps to start, and the 90-day curve
chunks.text:
1. Tonight: pick a harness and run an agent on your own machine. Ferrari is OpenClaw/Hermes with GBrain; "the Honda is really good, too" (Codex, Claude Code). "The concepts are the point."
2. This weekend: start a library as one folder of markdown. Export notes and email, write one page per project and person (what you build together, what they care about, what you owe them, what they said last time). Unindexed inbox history is "your moat just lying there."
3. Write your first skill file for the task you hate most each week. Explain it in plain English, let it get it wrong, correct every exception.
4. Make it a recurring job (for example every morning at 7, or every Friday). Waking to finished work shifts "the day stops being the unit of work."
5. Never do one-off work. After each task, ask the agent to "skillify" it (a skill in GBrain). "If you have to ask for something twice, you failed."

Expected curve: week 1 is a toy; week 4 the flywheel catches; week 12 the library "answers before you finish asking," with a dozen skills and a tool others want to borrow, "which in this room is called a startup." Most quit in week two. He warns that a brain nobody curates is "a garbage dump with great search," so use provenance on every fact, contradiction checks, and a librarian whose job is pruning.

chunks.heading: Own your skills, or your job becomes a skill file
chunks.text:
- Fictional Maya teaches her agents 40 skills over two years. If the files live in her repo, they go with her and she compounds. If they live in the company's repo, she leaves with nothing: "She didn't have a career. She had an extraction."
- His doctrine: "skill files are yours. Own your skills because if you don't, your job becomes a skill file." Keep brain and skills in a repo you control from day one, before any platform or acquirer has an opinion.
- Any comfortable arrangement where your judgment compounds in someone else's repo is "a thousand gilders a year." He ties this to starting a startup. "Entire startups these days will be markdown files."
- Software no longer needs to be precious: build a tool for an audience of one in a weekend. Scratch your own itch because "scratching itches is nearly free"; tools others beg for may be companies.

chunks.heading: Answers to three objections, and why he open sources everything
chunks.text:
- Models will make harnesses obsolete: as models improve, the differentiator moves to context. "The weights are everyone's. The library is yours." Each release is "a free upgrade to a workforce I already own."
- Is it just RAG: "Postgres is just B-trees." Retrieval is the primitive; the product is what gets written down, enriched and linked, hot vs cold memory, and arbitrating conflicting facts. "Being worth retrieving from is the product."
- Privacy: his brain runs on his own infra, repo and keys. The default is a life already scattered across 10 clouds. "Custody is the security model."
- Open sourcing: he can because YC means he need not monetize infrastructure, but his belief is that "tools of the powerful should be given away." Private leverage creates "a priesthood"; giving it away creates "a renaissance."
- Expect backlash: "First, they quote tweet you, then they clone you." He notes loud critics of agent-written code are shipping agents too.
- Example: a friend built an 80,000-markdown-file brain for his son's rare epilepsy. "Nobody is coming to build yours for you."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues AI leverage comes from how you wire the work, not the model: skill files are employees, resolver tables are org charts, and a company brain is a library plus librarian. He covers latent vs deterministic compute, context engineering, brain hygiene, and "skillify it" so nothing is done twice.

chunks.heading: How Garry builds an AI-native company: skill files as employees, a company brain, and "400X" leverage
chunks.text: **Source:** "Every company should have a Brain", AI Engineer, 2026-07-25 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eBUyTS7SzV4)

chunks.heading: The 400X claim: the leverage is in how you wire the work, not the model
chunks.text:
- In 2013, as a YC partner building YC's internal social network, Garry could write about 14 usable logical lines of code a day. Median output in the literature of that era was roughly 15, with some people at 50.
- Today he runs YC full-time, works fewer hours (he has a 5:00 p.m. kid pick-up), and estimates his output at about 400X.
- He stress-tests it himself: assume the agent writes bloated code, assume half is scaffolding, assume he is flattering himself. It is still "8X at the floor and 80X in the middle."
- His key point: "It's not the model." The 2X people and the 100X people use the exact same Claude, with the same weights, context window and API. "The leverage is not in the weights. It's in how you wire the work."
- Evidence from YC: in the Winter 2025 batch, a quarter of companies had code bases that were 95% AI-generated. That batch became the fastest-growing, most profitable in YC history. 94 companies have crossed $100M in revenue from a seed check in YC history.
- He says he can't prove AI-generated code caused the growth. Still, the fastest-growing founders "are not treating AI as auto-complete. They're treating it as a workforce."

chunks.heading: Wiring the work: every agent concept maps to an organization
chunks.text:
Garry's core framing is that what we've learned building with agents maps one-to-one onto an organization.

- **A skill file is an employee.** One capability, one job, written clearly enough that someone can execute it.
- **A resolver table is an org chart.** Example: "whenever you need to alter a test, load tests.md." It is what many people build when Claude Code complains their CLAUDE.md context is too big. A task comes in and the resolver decides who handles it.
- **Filing rules are internal process.** They cover whether the resolver is actually working and in compliance.
- **Trigger evals are performance reviews.** Example: a test that checks whether, when you need to alter a test file, tests.md actually gets loaded.
- All of this is markdown files, "and maybe there's some TypeScript in there, too." Organizations that once took a thousand people are now markdown. "We've been building organizations this whole time, but we didn't have a management layer, but now that's what we have."
- Working with Claude Code or Codex is not writing software. "You're hiring, training, and managing a workforce made of markdown."

chunks.heading: What AI-native companies look like (YC examples)
chunks.text:
- AI-native companies encode sales, support, ops and finance as skills, which are written procedures their agents execute. They hire engineers to maintain those skills and to do the work the skills can't do yet.
- Garry's example: it will even file your taxes if you have a skill file for it.
- **Emergence** (AI app builder, Summer 2024): public launch to nine figures of ARR in eight months. It was only 15 people when it crossed $15M ARR.
- **Retail** (Winter 2024): $60M with about 40 people.
- He says that revenue per head "did not exist before. Not in software, not in oil, not in railroads, never." These companies are not freaks of nature, just "the first companies built natively on the new physics."
- His bar for a YC batch: every founder doing "a former person's entire year worth of work in a single day." If you aren't, "your competitor is, and they will eat your lunch politely and thank you for it."

chunks.heading: Beyond engineers: YC's own transformation
chunks.text:
- The leverage is not only for engineers. At YC, media people, event staff and the finance team are building skill files and cron jobs, many of whom had never opened a terminal.
- One finance team member collapsed about a hundred Excel workbooks into a single app, built with YC's internal OpenClaw and company brain. "She's not a programmer. She's a manager of agents now and everyone at YC now is."
- This is why YC runs at its scale with a staff that "would look like a rounding error at any other comparable firm." The goal is not 400X engineers but "one company that operates at the level of 400X everyone else."

chunks.heading: Latent space vs. deterministic space
chunks.text:
Garry says most AI engineering bugs come from computation happening on the wrong side of this split.

- **Latent space (the LLM):** taste, judgment, understanding what a human means by something vague, non-deterministic calls. You steer it with markdown.
- **Deterministic space (code):** what engineers know, such as TypeScript or Elixir/Erlang that agents write.
- **Worked example:** Startup School with 6,000 people. One experiment is to seat 800 at a time so the people on each side of you are the right people to meet. The seat arrangement, a multi-dimensional array of 800 seats, "must not live in the context window." The LLM does the human part of judging who fits; the placement is computed deterministically.
- The human version would be printing 800 pages in a big room for a month. Now it can take about 10 minutes and "a couple hundred dollars worth of tokens," something he says was impossible about six months ago.

chunks.heading: Working memory and the company brain
chunks.text:
- Humans hold about seven things at once (Miller's "seven plus or minus two"). Every checklist, org chart and filing cabinet is a prosthetic for that limit, and almost every company is still organized around "the seven-digit brain."
- An agent holds about a million tokens, roughly a thousand pages. He explained it to his 10-year-old as three Harry Potter books open at once, able to find a needle in any and synthesize across all three in seconds.
- But "your company is not three books. Your company is a library": every email, meeting, decision and its reasoning, customer conversation and postmortem. The question is "who decides which three books are open on that desk." That is context engineering.
- A company brain is "the library plus the librarian."
- On "this is just RAG": retrieval is the primitive, the way Postgres is "just B-trees." The hard parts are what gets written into the knowledge wiki, how it is enriched and linked, what is promoted to hot memory versus filed as cold reference, and who arbitrates when two facts disagree. "Retrieval is easy. Being worth retrieving from is the product."

chunks.heading: Garry's own brain (GBrain) and how it behaves
chunks.text:
- He builds it in the open as **GBrain**. It is MIT open source, free, and works with any harness, though it "loves" the open client Hermes agent. He describes it as "effectively Postgres for agents": a retrieval layer that decides which three books to load for any task.
- His personal brain is about 220,000 pages, written mostly by his agents from his email, meetings, 20 years of notes and his lived experience.
- Example: when a founder emails him about a crisis, before he finishes reading, the agent has already pulled every prior conversation with that founder, three portfolio companies that hit the same wall, and what worked for them. "That's the difference between an assistant and a colleague."
- He is not trying to make money from it: "the layer should be open the way Linux is open." He hopes someone builds the defining company in this space and says he'd like to fund them at YC.
- He says you don't need his tools: "Open Claw is the Ferrari... but Codex is a really good Honda. It will do 90% of this." The concepts matter, not his repos.

chunks.heading: Brain failure modes and the "skillify it" discipline
chunks.text:
- **Failure modes:** a brain nobody curates "becomes a garbage dump with great search." Retrieval surfaces stale facts with total confidence. A bad skill file encodes a bad process forever.
- **The fix is memory plus hygiene:**
  - provenance on every fact
  - contradiction checks when new information collides with old
  - a librarian (human plus agent) whose job is pruning
- Treat the brain like production infrastructure and it compounds. Treat it like a dumping ground and you get "a very confident agent that is wrong in ways nobody can trace."
- **His signature rule: never do one-off work.** When you're happy with an agent's output, "skillify it," turning what you just did into a reusable skill. He has a blog post on X on this (search "skillify it") and a skill file you can load into your own harness.
- "If you have to ask for something twice, you failed." An organization that captures what it learns gets smarter every day; one that doesn't "wakes up every morning with amnesia, no matter how good the model is."
- "Model quality is rented, but if you build your brain, you own that brain."

chunks.heading: What to build now
chunks.text:
- **Build an AI-native company, not a company that just uses AI:** a thin team, skill files for everything, the founder still in the code, and a company brain plus personal AI from day one. The library compounds from week one.
- **Greenfield he'd pursue at 25:** "every company on this earth is about to need a brain": the memory layer so you never re-ask what you knew, personal AI that actually knows you, and the librarian that picks the three books.
- **Mindset:** he calls fear about jobs "a failure of imagination" and says "Abundance is not a policy paper, it is shipped software."
- **Example he cites:** a friend whose son has a rare form of epilepsy built a repo of 80,000 markdown files, a company brain for one boy. It pushed him to the edge of what humanity knows about his son's condition, with "no lab, no grant, no permission."
- Closing line: "We can boil the ocean now." Go write the test, ship the skill, and build the brain that makes every company after yours easier to build.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how coding agents let one founder do the work of hundreds, and the primitives he uses: skills, resolvers, skillify, tests and a memory brain. He stresses pairing deterministic code with latent-space agents, and judging results by whether customers actually pay.

chunks.heading: Garry's G-Stack: coding agents as a software factory
chunks.text:
- Garry says he wasn't coding in December 2025, then used Claude Code to write around a million lines of code. He did it in part by recreating a startup he had built twice before in about 5 days.
- He cites Steve Yegge's claim that people using AI coding agents are 10x to 100x more productive, and that engineers at Anthropic are about 1,000x as productive as Googlers were in 2005.
- G-Stack hit 87,000 GitHub stars and G-Brain 13,000, for more than 100,000 total. About 15,000 people use G-Stack daily, with hundreds of thousands of skill invocations.
- His shift in framing: in 2025 AI was a "copilot"; in 2026 it is a "software factory". The factory's job is to fight slop and hallucinations by default.
- Production quality: `plan-eng-review` is the skill he runs about 20 times a day to reach 80-90% test coverage, so he ships code he relies on rather than demo code.
- On lines of code: LOC alone can be a garbage metric. The real tests are whether it works for him, whether it works for customers, and whether people pay. Nothing in the harness tells the model to write more lines; the pressure is toward dense, concise code.
- His personal arc: Posterous (YC 2008) took about $4M, 10 people and 2 years, and sold to Twitter for $20M. He says one person on a $200/month Claude Code Max plan can now build the same software in about 5 days.

chunks.heading: Persona skills and "boil the ocean"
chunks.text:
- He found it useful to pull specific personas out of the model's latent space as skills.
- `/office-hours` distills YC office hours. He fed in 3-4 months of transcripts across thousands of conversations, then cut it down about 90%. It asks what the problem is, who the customer is, how you know, and what you are building.
- `plan-ceo-review` asks for the 10x version of the product, the "platonic ideal". Garry's PM background at Palantir and Microsoft shaped this: find the perfect form of the thing, then lay a straight roadmap from where you are to it.
- He rejects the old "don't boil the ocean" reflex: "let's boil the ocean." One person at a terminal can do the work of roughly 500 to 1,000 people, so inherited expectations of what a founder or small team can do are "a thousand X wrong."
- Models haven't caught up. Claude Code will estimate 3 weeks for a plan, and after approval it is done in about an hour.

chunks.heading: Skills, resolvers, and the deterministic vs latent split
chunks.text:
- His agentic systems broke when deterministic work (belongs in code) was put in markdown skills, or when judgment work (belongs in the LLM) was put in code.
- Example: seating 8 dinner guests works in latent space with ChatGPT. An 800-person dinner or 6,000-person Startup School does not, because the model hallucinates at that scale. That calls for latent and deterministic parts working together.
- A skill is a runbook: steps any human or agent can follow, possibly with branching, and it can call code.
- OpenClaw and Hermes Agent now let non-technical, process-oriented knowledge work be automated. He mentions Twilio for phone calls and Gemini Live for booking or buying, and says you no longer have to wait for Google to ship the phone-booking demo.
- Code example: OpenClaw kept assuming he was in Greenwich, UK. He wrote a TypeScript `context-now.mjs` with tests and built it in, so time and upcoming items come from code, not the latent space.
- Resolver: Claude Code warns when `CLAUDE.md` is huge (for example 40,000 tokens). The fix is a resolver, a master directory that says "when you write to the change log, load `change-log.md`." Instructions load only when needed. He calls it the core of a really great agent.
- Example: signature checks route to an executive-assistant skill that looks up the brain repo for how to do it, a specific "skill pack".

chunks.heading: Skillify: turning a one-off into a tested skill
chunks.text:
- Workflow: get the agent to do a task exactly right once (his example: "save this article"), then tell it `skillify`. He uses it about 20 times a day.
- He says writing the skill and the code is only 2 of roughly 10 steps. The rest:
  - Unit tests for the code.
  - LLM evals for the skill file.
  - An integration test.
  - A resolver trigger in `agents.md`, and a test of it.
  - An LLM-as-judge eval that the trigger is broad enough to fire.
  - `check resolvable`, to keep skills DRY and avoid several skills doing the same thing.
  - An end-to-end smoke test.
  - A schema for where it lives in the memory repo.
- He compares this to the 10-20% of people in finance orgs who do compliance: agentic systems are messy and human-like, so they need the checking.
- Org mapping he draws: skill = an employee with a capability; resolver = the org chart; filing rules = internal process; check resolvable = audit and compliance; trigger eval = performance reviews.
- Planned: a cross-modal eval where Opus, GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek-V4 rate inputs and outputs and feed ratings back to the sub-agent to iterate toward something about 10x better. He quotes a YC founder: Claude Code is "my ADHD CEO" and Codex is "my nearly non-verbal 200 IQ CTO."

chunks.heading: G-Brain: memory for agents
chunks.text:
- G-Brain is a three-layer memory system built on Karpathy's knowledge-wiki idea. A plain wiki fell over because it only used grep.
- He added vector search, RRF fusion, backlinks and a typed knowledge graph (graph database).
- Next: an epistemology layer to tell hunches, beliefs held by specific people, and world knowledge apart, so it can spot early contrarian beliefs (his example: someone at Stanford believes X before anyone else, then proves it).
- Before v1 (hoped within weeks) he wants a fully dynamic ontology, since the current schema is built for him. A researcher, journalist or politician would each need a different schema.
- His stance: he is building for himself and open-sourcing it so everyone can. "I am not a guru. I am just an entertainer" (Alan Watts).
- His exhortation: the lecture is useless unless students open their own Hermes or Claude, load G-Brain, try the roughly 40 skills, skillify their own work and release it. Founders should "meta prompt one another."

chunks.heading: The AI-native company: a closed loop
chunks.text:
- The AI-native version embeds an agent (Hermes or OpenClaw) in all decision-making. It needs read access to every artifact the company produces: codebase, Discord, recorded meetings.
- Garry says founders still working at "copilot level from last year" won't make it; the new role is the "AI founder", someone living at the edge of the tools.

chunks.heading: Taste, evals, and wedges for new startups
chunks.text:
- Shipping code goes to zero cost; what doesn't is taste.
- Startup wedge: pick a painful workflow, go deep with customers, and act as the forward-deployed engineer. Go "undercover": founders of Happy Robot (logistics) and Salient (loan servicing) didn't come from those industries and learned by shadowing or taking jobs.
- Example companies: Salient (voice agents for loan servicing, closed top US banks), Happy Robot (freight agents, Series B, 10x revenue in a year), Reducto (document processing, which improves RAG and memory).
- White space: Anthropic's industry-usage chart shows about 50% penetration in software but wide gaps in back office, finance, data, academics, cybersecurity and customer service. Garry calls it room for hundreds of AI unicorns.
- Growth benchmark: PG's bar was 10% week over week, hit by roughly the top 1% historically. Garry cites the latest YC batches, where on average companies roughly 3x within 3 months. His framing: "first pitch of the first inning."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan and YC designers critique AI startup homepages (Rosebud, MagicFlow, Reality Defender, Pump, Voiceflow). Core lessons: make it instantly clear what you do and who it's for, drive one opinionated call to action, demo the product early, and use real customer language and social proof.

chunks.heading: Landing page first impression: say who it is for and what it does
chunks.text:
- Garry says a startup's first job on its homepage is to answer two things fast: "what is this" and "is it for me".
- He calls this a hierarchy, like Maslow's: if a visitor can't tell who the product is for, nothing lower on the page helps.
- He warns against clever taglines: "You don't want to be clever if clever equals confusing."
- On Rosebud ("AI generated game assets", "game development", "GPT to game"), he is distracted by three concepts at once. He notes founders often like taglines they find clever because they know the product, which makes it harder for new visitors.
- On Reality Defender, he is halfway down the page and still can't tell what the product does. He says most visitors won't try that hard.
- He wants a visitor to look at the page and think "that's for me", which means writing the page for one specific customer (the ICP), not "anyone who might need our technology". In his words, being too general is "a little bit problematic".

chunks.heading: Use your customers' own words for the headline
chunks.text:
- Garry's tactic for a vague homepage: talk to existing users and ask "how would you describe my product?"
- Then take the exact phrase they use and put it at the top of the site.
- His reasoning: the phrase that resonates with existing users is likely to resonate with similar potential customers.

chunks.heading: One opinionated call to action, with contrast
chunks.text:
- Garry recommends deciding the main KPI and the outcome you want from people who hit the site. He guesses it is not "explore all of these products and pick the one you like".
- He uses Rosebud as the example. It shows four or more products (asset generator, game dev platform, skyboxes, talking heads), and he suggests focusing on the primary one (likely game assets) and moving the others to secondary pages.
- Be opinionated with the buttons: make "try beta" the main button and turn "learn more" into a plain link instead of an equal-weight button.
- "One of the most important things to use is contrast" to tell the user what to do.
- Rosebud's "try beta" matters because it signals the product isn't vaporware.

chunks.heading: Show the product and a feat of strength
chunks.text:
- For AI products, Garry wants an animation or video showing the product, ideally "a feat of strength": type a few things and see magic output you couldn't produce before.
- He says these demos are why people are so excited about the technology right now.
- Get visitors to the aha moment as quickly as possible, directly inside the product.
- Don't make people click to try the product. Rosebud could put a few clickable example ideas or a fly-out on the home page. Garry's logic: "every time you make people do extra clicks you have risk of drop off".
- He likes a "how it works" section early on because it raises understanding quickly, comparing it to doing a demo in a YC interview.
- Specific, concrete claims work well (for example, "30 percent cheaper and 25 percent faster"), though he notes visitors will wonder how you know. A footnote isn't required.

chunks.heading: Generic products: lead with specific use cases
chunks.text:
- On MagicFlow (AI workflow builder), Garry draws on YC's experience with generic workflow companies.
- His point: nobody wakes up thinking "I really need workflow software". People have a specific problem to solve.
- What works is focusing on the most common specific use cases to get people into the product. Then they discover they can do more.
- He likes naming familiar tools (Hugging Face, Stability AI, ChatGPT, Replicate) because visitors recognize their own stack and feel the product is for them.
- He likes claims that look like they came from many user conversations, such as faster and cheaper, because they answer "why not just build it myself".

chunks.heading: Don't put a wall in front of the demo
chunks.text:
- On MagicFlow, the "drag and drop" demo shows a hand cursor but clicking drops you into a login wall. Garry says it doesn't build trust.
- His fix: "do your first one free", with no account required up front. Prompt for signup only when the visitor wants to save or use the result, because by then they're invested.
- If you must gate, give context about why signing up helps, and don't pretend a mock is a live try-it.
- His framing: "you're always fighting the urge for the back button or to go look at Hacker News."
- His main feedback on MagicFlow: the good material is small and buried on the side, and "you want to hit people over the head with it" or visitors scroll past.

chunks.heading: Spacing, motion and polish as trust signals
chunks.text:
- On Reality Defender, Garry says uneven spacing (too much between header lines, too little between logos and body) and wrong header line height break the "enterprise trust" feeling for him.
- Most people won't consciously notice, but some will. He says good spacing contributes to a feeling of quality, and small fit-and-finish flaws "ruin the illusion".
- On Pump (cloud cost savings), the bright colors and constant movement overwhelm. Garry's advice: "less is more".
- Use animation sparingly, to draw the eye to the one thing you want people to notice next.
- He contrasts this with Voiceflow, which has motion that intrigues rather than overwhelms.

chunks.heading: Differentiation, social proof and what a good page looks like
chunks.text:
- As a YC partner, Garry asks of Pump: dozens of products cut cloud costs, so why this one? He says visitors will be asking the same.
- Pump's real differentiator seems to be group buying (companies pooling for better AWS pricing), but it is buried. He says to hit people over the head with whatever is different.
- Make the savings concrete up front. For Pump, the aha is showing how much a visitor would save, making it a "no-brainer".
- Put FAQs within easy reach, with the most important question first, so a skeptical visitor gets answers in about two clicks.
- Social proof helps: a recognizable customer logo, ideally with a case study from the number one customer. He wants a known customer who saved X percent.
- Reality Defender earns trust through government and enterprise logos and a broadcaster case study, but it still lacks data to make him enter his info.
- Voiceflow is his positive example (very good as a design review): a clear call to action, a hero interaction that explains the product before reading, calm scroll, many recognizable customer logos, and real quotes from named people at those companies. He says it feels trustworthy and he "would totally use this".
- He suggests studying older, iterated products like Voiceflow. They have spent years refining, so "you get to take their learnings for free".
- Why-now framing: for many AI startups, "why now" is the key question, and a new category sometimes has to be described from scratch.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues founders should trust first-hand knowledge over what's hot, stay earnest, and turn every business process into a markdown skill file that agents run on loops. He explains why agents erase management bureaucracy, why token-maxing lets you live in 2028, and why a startup can reorganize in ways a Microsoft cannot.

chunks.heading: Ambition, earnestness and the "don't be a lemming" lesson
chunks.text:
- Garry's central regret: he chased "what was hot" instead of what he knew. Around 2003 he left web programming right as Web 2.0 and social took off, and chose Windows Mobile because "the next hot thing will be mobile."
- He frames the right question as "what are you interested in? What do you know uniquely?", not "what's hot, what should I work on?"
- He defines earnestness as courage: trust your own direct experience even when a blog post, a tweet, or a smart investor contradicts it. Hence his "don't lar" meme at Startup School.
- He tells his own mistakes publicly and plans to keep doing so: "I'm a little bit doomed to be the first principal storyteller of all the mistakes that I made."
- He calls himself a late bloomer, and says introspecting on mistakes and choosing differently next time is the hope: "I can make mistakes and then I can introspect."

chunks.heading: The Palantir miss and how to read the map vs the territory
chunks.text:
