- Frat brothers Joe Lonsdale and Stephen Cohen, then interns at Peter Thiel's hedge fund, got Garry flown to dinner with Thiel. Thiel offered a $70K check, which matched his Microsoft pay.
- Garry declined because he "might get promoted to level 60 this year." He now estimates this as a $2-4 billion mistake.
- The pattern he names: he was "working backwards from the map instead of looking down at the territory." Joe and Stephen were among the smartest people he knew, and the universe was telling him to join them.
- The thesis he took from Palantir: the best computer scientists in Palo Alto were building things that DC and three-letter agencies had no access to. "The future is already here. It's not evenly distributed."
- First-principles knowledge works like science: go down into the experiment and talk to first-party people, and you get secret knowledge.
- His takeaway: "Everything that's awesome in my life is kind of a cult." It starts with a truth that flies in the face of orthodoxy. A lone person with a belief is a crazy person; the second person who joins (the Derek Sivers dancing-guy talk) turns it into a party.
- Chris Dixon's test for interesting ideas: can you find the edge? The best ones start as weird toys, and the people behind them were fringe outsiders (Homebrew Computer Club "was not where you were getting laid").

chunks.heading: What YC figured out and why community matters
chunks.text:
- He credits Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Trevor Blackwell and Robert Morris with seeing that many very smart people lacked access to Silicon Valley, which used to require the right school, the right contacts, and cracking a social scene ("sceners").
- YC's answer was a website, 12 questions (later a one-minute video), and builders on the other end giving a fair shake.
- Today YC has 16 equal partners, all of whom went through YC. About 7,000 people attended Startup School in San Francisco, most for the first time. He calls it "Birthright but for tech."
- Core value he cites: a community where you can be real. At a TechCrunch-style event everyone says "killing it." Founders need someone to call on the day the best customer leaves, the best engineer quits, or a co-founder loses hope.
- Co-founders: everything else equal, having them is net very good, but vibe and agentic coding are shifting this. "Any given person could be 400 of that person from nine months ago."

chunks.heading: Founder ambition in the agent era (what founders should do now)
chunks.text:
- The game changed. "Don't chase your success or my success." Founders should be more ambitious than ever.
- SaaS warning: a pure per-seat SaaS product may not exist in 5-10 years. It is fine as a wedge, but in 2026 it must lead to a moat around data, network effects, or something else. Two years ago a 10-20x forward revenue multiple on SaaS was "iron law."
- Code is no longer precious. The new scarce things are agency and taste, and he thinks both are practiced, not innate: "that's how you get better."
- Just use the tools: build trivial things on every model to learn, like arranging a zen rock garden. The output matters less than the practice. He notes few people show their work.
- Origin of gstack: after Boris Cherny's appearance on the Light Cone podcast and friends going back to coding, he started messing around. He turned YC office-hours rhetoric into a markdown file for raising founder ambition, told Claude to "reduce the strength and intensity of this prompt by 90%," then open sourced it. He jokes "we can't give away the crown jewels for free."
- He says to apply to YC only if you are a top-10% Claude Code user, judged by how thoughtful you are about users, product and design.

chunks.heading: Agent loops, skills and token-maxing
chunks.text:
- Interesting loops are business loops, where output changes how the business operates.
- Token-max on purpose. Frontier labs constrain cost and compute in their apps, so to go all the way he uses Hermes agent or OpenClaw and loads 800K to 1M tokens per request. At full strength it costs roughly $50-100K a year, but "you basically get to live in 2028." He says founders and CEOs should give themselves permission to do this.
- GBrain: he extracted the agentic RAG part of his Garry's List newsroom repo (garryslist.org, "an agentic newsroom"), including after-the-fact graph generation, and it beat other open-source memory systems. Its purpose is to let the agent know which million tokens to keep in its head for a task.
- The skill loop:
  - Do a task by hand with the agent, iterating until it is right.
  - Have it "skillify" the task into a markdown file plus code plus tests.
  - Put it on a cron.
  - Any later failure is just a bug fix that is then fixed forever.
- "A markdown file is an employee." It does the job the same way every time. He applies this to sales, marketing, support, everything.
- gstack for engineering followed the same loop: QA via a browser tool, a PM skill, an eng manager skill enforcing unit and end-to-end coverage, until all that was left was black-box testing. The work becomes finding bottlenecks and instructing the agent to build software or a markdown file that removes each one.
- Claim: companies can now go from zero to $15M ARR in about four months with two or three people and a few hundred skill files.
- Failure modes at scale: with many markdown files, provenance and conflict management matter. When two facts conflict, provenance tells you which is newer and wins. A cron job should sweep for accuracy.
- Experience helps: 35-45-year-old founders who have "been around the block" (he cites Peter Steinberger) are a megatrend, because they know what to build and now have 400x leverage.

chunks.heading: Running a company through agents (the Brex example)
chunks.text:
- Pedro of Brex got Garry into OpenClaw. Brex built and open sourced "Crab Trap," an agent that watches all of OpenClaw's network traffic. That squares the safety issue for a heavily regulated fintech.
- Pedro's agent reads meeting transcripts from direct reports two levels down, including meetings he is not in. It surfaces what is broken, such as a compliance team issue, and he can walk in with the answer.
- Garry's thesis: a classic reason businesses fail is that they get too big to fit in one head. Humans hold about "seven plus or minus two" things; a person plus an agent can effectively hold "three Harry Potter books." The world, including government, is built around human limits and is not ready for agents.
- His expectation: products and services should be 100-1000x better, not just cheaper.
- Org design: the mid-level coordination layer (what PMs did) should be agents, with execs setting direction and individuals deciding execution. He recounts his Windows Mobile days, when he and a PM mentor had to go to the Windows team "with a baseball bat" because bugs were ignored. A cron-run markdown file tracking blockers and dependencies could have replaced that.
- Large orgs like Microsoft can't reorganize this way. "A startup can. And every startup must."
- Toyota production system analogy: let the worker on the line change the line, since they have the most context. He ties this to an agent-facing bug endpoint from Claw Visor (a YC company) where agents file bugs and get a live reply: filed, fix coming next week, here's a workaround. He says AI erases the "API line" (Venkatesh Rao's concept).
- He cautions that the white pill is slowness: companies, government and society move slower than you think, so he expects about 20 years for society to fully absorb AI. Big incumbents have real moats.

chunks.heading: Where computing and consumer AI go next
chunks.text:
- The next computer will likely be voice-first with deep memory and context: "watched over by machines of love and grace," a benevolent assistant that knows your hopes, fears and desires. The path runs through computer use, memory, diarization and ingestion.
- Prediction: 2027 will be "the harness wars," a "war for a billion consumers" and a return of the browser wars, once today's frontier-level compute costs about $50-100 in two or three years. Cost is the current constraint.
- He notes he was too early in thinking it was all about to happen right after converting to OpenClaw.
- Consumer AI is underbuilt and zero marginal-cost distribution should unlock new consumer products as model costs fall.

chunks.heading: Civic engagement and San Francisco
chunks.text:
- Garry says the case for hope is that US rule of law holds and people in government are mostly earnest. Jury duty in San Francisco showed him an orderly process, and tech is roughly 10-20% of the city, so "we actually have a say."
- What made it personal: a DA ignoring heinous crimes against Asian elders and a school board hostile to Asian-American kids taking algebra in middle school. He benefited from algebra in public middle school in Fremont and says it led to calculus by senior year and Stanford engineering.
- He ties it to a pattern: the same ideologues oppose data centers and housing, and "words have meaning, supply and demand exists, incentives exist."
- His diagnosis: when builders don't speak up and don't hold media accountable, things get deranged. He cites local TV not covering anti-Asian crime. Communities organized, including at farmers markets, to push back.
- His stance: "put your body on it" (Mario Savio), accepting reputational cost as a covenant with fellow citizens.
- Garry's List (garryslist.org) aims to export the San Francisco playbook to LA, New York, Minneapolis, Seattle and other blue cities.
- His advice: act local. Care about housing, crime, treatment and recovery in your own city. "If we fix local, state and national will fix itself."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan walks through San Francisco with Michael McNano and explains why YC dropped its continuity fund to focus on one core business, why rejection is part of the founder test, and why venture should be bigger and less clubby. He also covers how he got into local politics and why community building matters.

chunks.heading: Garry's Cultural Politics: Why He Fights for San Francisco
chunks.text:
- Garry says Bay Area tech and local government are tied together. He grew up in Fremont, and SF is "a little bit of a one industry town."
- When critics say "get out techies," he calls it "actually a call to, you know, let's destroy the city."
- He points to Oakland as the warning: it lost its sports teams and is "one of the most dangerous places in the country now."
- His stance: "I'm not going to Austin. I'm not like leaving the city. There's no place to run to. So we just said we're not going to leave. We're going to stand and fight."

chunks.heading: How He Got Into Local SF Politics
chunks.text:
- The trigger was a COVID-era Clubhouse room where then-DA Chesa Boudin said crime was down while Garry saw Asian-American elders being attacked. Asian-Americans are about 35-40% of SF.
- He cites Hanako Abe's death (New Year's Eve 2020, a repeat offender arrested about 30 times) as the moment accountability "seemed like there was going to be no accountability."
- Nancy Tung, who ran against Boudin, offered Clubhouse listeners a walk through SF politics. Garry took it, and she became "a really big mentor."
- He learned the city by following people deep in the weeds on Twitter/X: nonprofit operators like Stop Crime SF and people who read city budgets. He argues that if you search actively rather than trust the feed, "it's all available to see." Then he met them in person, "like an internet meetup."
- The second issue was education. He says SF eighth graders found it hard to take algebra. His own path (food-insecure at times, public school, calculus, Stanford, computer engineering) came from a good public education, so he refuses to bring thousands of families to SF to start companies while their kids can't get algebra.
- He frames the failures as over-equity driven by "pathological empathy" that destroys safety and education.

chunks.heading: Why Small Local Money Works
chunks.text:
- Garry says people pour millions into national races while "very small amounts of money" in local politics move things much more.
- He gave "a couple hundred grand" total and says that is "a relatively small in the global sense amount of money" for the effect.
- He credits a shift in the Overton window: he started saying things people feared would get them fired (e.g. that violence against elders needs accountability), nothing happened to him, and others privately agreed.
- Results he cites:
  - Boudin recalled; Brooke Jenkins is now DA.
  - Three school board members recalled; algebra "coming back a little bit too slowly."
  - A moderate, pro-business, pro-public-safety Board of Supervisors, "for the moment."
  - Nancy Tung now heads the SF Democratic Party.
- His 10-year goal: "San Francisco Democrat" should mean something different. "You can be in tech, you can be prosperity, you can create abundance, but then also you can make it work for everyone in your community."
- He backs paying taxes if the money buys safety and schools, and wants to build housing ("rent should not be $10,000 a month for a one-bedroom").
- He does not want office: being an elected official "seems terrible"; he is "pretty focused on money and media," with politics maybe 10-20 years out.

chunks.heading: Building Community as a Strategy
chunks.text:
- Garry bought a converted 1902 church (former Church of Christ, Scientist) in the Mission as an "event house." He found it through Redfin, got roughly $1.5M off after it sat about 2 years with no offers, and uses it as a salon.
- It seats about 50 for dinner and holds about 150. Guests have included Pat Gelsinger, Peter Thiel, London Breed and Scott Wiener.
- His reasoning: after COVID, "a lot of my job is just bringing people together."
- Uses: political events, YC events, founder dinners. He personally funds about 50 companies a year, and YC partners also invest.
- On the internet vs. in person: "when you sit down for a drink with someone and you get to know someone, it just hits different." He wants tech to get involved in local community: neighbors, churches, Chinatown businesses and activists.
- He belongs to the Lion's Den karaoke bar in Chinatown (membership placard reads "Twitter Menace") and says politicians, local business people and activists mix there.

chunks.heading: Handling Backlash and Public-Figure Noise
chunks.text:
- Sauna incident: founders at a dinner asked to jump in his sauna and took a selfie; it spun into rumors. He suspects many accusers were rejected from YC repeatedly: "something breaks in people's brains." His rule now: "no haters in the sauna and no selfies," and no deal talk there.
- Tupac karaoke incident: he says he sang "Hit 'Em Up" at a dads' karaoke night, politics had him fired up, he changed a lyric, and people "didn't get the joke." He apologized the next morning, said "that's just not me," and noted the climate of political violence.
- Rule he now follows: delete Twitter from his phone after a couple of drinks. He expects phones to eventually block this for us ("Do not rage tweet").

chunks.heading: Handling Rejection at YC
chunks.text:
- Garry says YC rejects 99.3% of applicants. Rejection emails go out and he gets angry tweets and emails.
- Average accepted founder in the latest batch applied at least twice, and more of them were rejected multiple times than accepted on the first try.
- He treats it as a resilience test: "the first step to getting into YC is getting rejected from YC." Founders will face rejection from users, investors, hires, Hacker News and reviewers: "everyone's going to hate you."
- Some founders have "never failed in their entire lives" and then "get punched in the face with users."
- Joke he floated: make accepted founders hang from a fixed bar for 60 seconds, then a mental-toughness seminar if they can't. He says startups are "almost no better exercise or test of endurance."
- On errors: YC is human and misses both ways, rejecting winners and admitting weaker teams. Unicorn rate is "only 6 to 12%."

chunks.heading: YC Strategy: One Team, No Growth Fund
chunks.text:
- Garry's path: designer in residence and partner at YC, left to found Initialized with Harj Taggar and Alexis Ohanian (he credits Harj as hiring him at YC), then returned as YC CEO after Paul Graham and Jessica Livingston tracked him down. Brett Gibson now runs Initialized.
- He says about 90% of Initialized's wins came from YC and credits the YC ecosystem for its successes (e.g. Rippling, Flock Safety).
- The old YC Continuity growth fund is gone. His reasoning: with about 7-9% ownership in each company, taking pro rata means YC never misses the decacorns, and the power law means most return is in decacorns (Stripe, DoorDash, Coinbase, Airbnb), not just unicorns.
- Airbnb example: YC invested about $12-15K for 7%, returned $2B at IPO, and would have returned about $7B with pro rata for a couple hundred million more.
- A good YC return is "8x." The old structure couldn't do pro rata because it hadn't raised the money.
- Now: one team of 15 equal general partners, one partner per company for life ("people should think about YC as the defining equal partnership in all of venture"). Eliminating the separate team removes the extra relationships and structural friction.
- Message to founders: YC owns about 7% of you, so "make us earn it. Come back. Do office hours with us." He gives founders his cell number.
- YC also wants to be a friend to other investors: "We're out of competing with you. We just want to take our pro rata."

chunks.heading: The Future of YC and Venture
chunks.text:
- Garry's model for YC is Airbnb-style: a two-sided marketplace where demand (the batch) is huge and supply (great early-stage investors, the "superhosts") is the limiting reagent.
- He wants YC to grow because "venture can and should be 10 times bigger." Batch size grew mostly because acceptance went from about 2-2.5% to about 7%, and AI made starting easier.
- Outcome scale: when he started Initialized fund one, Dropbox at about $4B (2011) looked like the ceiling; he now says $50B and $100B are on the table. He wants YC to create many future Elon Musks (and "$1.5 trillion" outcomes).
- On capital: "it's not clear to me capital is going to be a bludgeon anymore." More value will go to "discernment, taste, ability to help."
- Advice to VCs: do early stage and "show up," fund people "before it's obvious," and club together less. He criticizes the 2018-style playbook of one firm leading and friends following as a lock-in.
- He doesn't want seven trillion-dollar companies: "we should have thousands of companies worth billions to tens of billions of dollars," and says AI makes that moment possible.
- He told Michael he likes that Michael is a consumer founder turned investor and builds an audience, calling that the smartest use of his background.

chunks.heading: Faith, Meaning and the AI Moment
chunks.text:
- Garry is a converted Christian who grew up atheist (dad Buddhist, mom Christian) and had a rough childhood. The turning point in his mid-20s was a Rumi poem about the wise man and the snake: God lets us struggle with evil and difficulty so we grow.
- He church-hopped in his 20s (Korean church faith healing, Pentecostal tongues). His route to faith was worship music more than intellect.
- He sits on the board of Acts 17, the nonprofit that brought Peter Thiel and Pat Gelsinger on stage; founders include Michelle Stevens (wife of Anduril's Trae Stevens). Aim: give people a chance to be "seeking" without being told this is the only way.
- He attends Epic Church in SF with his family; his kids like Sunday school. He says Epic roughly doubled attendance in a year.
- His explanation for tech's religious turn: people look for meaning at "the dawn of AGI," with "existential angst" after COVID. Bay Area faith is mostly non-denominational and Jesus-focused rather than "hellfire and brimstone."
- He likes Trae Stevens' idea of "good quests": work on things that "link us to our fellow man" and solve real problems rather than "help people click on ads."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan (YC CEO) explains why YC's simple process works, why founders must set their own frame and talk to real customers, and why creators win distribution. He argues LLMs with good evals let small teams replace rote knowledge work and build huge businesses.

chunks.heading: How Garry builds on distribution, AI leverage and YC's simple selection process
chunks.text: **Note on source:** The transcript attributes the speaker only as the YC CEO, and the speaker is addressed as Garry throughout.

chunks.heading: YC's simple, fast selection process and the numbers behind it
chunks.text:
Garry describes YC as "kind of a miracle" that is earnest and simple: make something people want, apply, and YC tries to find the things that could be really big.

- The terms are the same for everyone: about 7% equity plus a bunch of money, and a room full of the top 1% of people building.
- The application is a one-page online form. The interview is 10 minutes, then a thumbs up or down.
- He argues this simple process picks winners at a higher rate than investors with elaborate processes. Banks pitch "differentiated process" and "smartest people in the room," but YC runs the simpler process and wins.
- YC has 14 equal group partners (himself included). They hand-read applications, and the 10-minute interview is with a human, not an AI.
- Garry says roughly 5-10% of companies in a batch become $1B+ companies. The numbers he cites on that:
  - Airbnb: under $20,000 invested became about $2B at IPO.
  - He estimates a few billion dollars of value created per batch.
  - He puts it at roughly $20M of carry per employee per year, and close to $100M per employee per year in value created overall.
- He says a YC white paper is coming. It looked at investors who put money into at least 3 YC companies per batch from 2018 to 2020. The top decile returned 16x, the top quartile 8x, the median 5x and the bottom quartile 3.3x. For comparison, he says a top-quartile VC fund in a given year is typically about 3x.

chunks.heading: What early winners look like and the "capital as a service" idea
chunks.text:
- Garry says extreme winners look very similar to average founders early on. Brian Armstrong of Coinbase was a solo software engineer working on anti-fraud at Airbnb who had never started a company, never done a product launch and never raised money.
- His profile of who YC funds: "highly technical people who are just like sort of smart and earnest."
- He says the point of YC's early work with founders is the basics, such as launching and raising.
- Capital as a service, which he credits to Chamath's idea, is plausible to him. A founder connects Stripe, a bank account and QuickBooks, an LLM ranks whether the business is real and does the due diligence, and anyone who clears the bar gets money.
- He says the hard part is getting really smart people to work on a thing like that.

chunks.heading: Why founders must build their own audience and distribution
chunks.text:
- Garry argues that if you run a business today you kind of have to be a creator. Otherwise you must buy eyeballs, and Google and Meta hold the monopoly on them.
- Their second-price auction mechanism extracts every incremental dollar of gross margin. If you and a competitor sell the same widget with the same supplier, the ad auction takes the difference.
- He calls saying interesting, valuable things on YouTube, X, Instagram and TikTok "the purest form of alpha that exists still." He thinks TikTok is giving away distribution to new creators, and that Meta is dropping the ball on creators by only serving those who are already big.
- This applies to consumer businesses, and sometimes to dev tools and B2B too. He says consumer has lacked breakout businesses for about 10 years, and distribution is why.
- AI has not broken the big tech distribution advantage. He says big tech has "a total stranglehold on the incremental user."

chunks.heading: B2B sales mindset
chunks.text:
- About 70-80% of YC companies are B2B. The sales mini conference is the best attended each batch.
- YC gives every founder a copy of Pete Kazanjy's book *Founder Sales*.
- Most of the shift is mindset: most people have never been rejected 95 times out of 100.
- His framing: a website converting at 5% is phenomenal. Knocking on 100 doors and getting 95 no's feels like failure, but five enterprise contracts at $10,000-$100,000 a year makes you a big winner.

chunks.heading: Building AI businesses that replace rote knowledge work
chunks.text:
- He argues LLMs have opened up almost anything a knowledge worker with roughly 130 IQ or below can do, and software can now do it without management headaches. He calls it a profound moment for all entrepreneurs.
- He expects 20-person companies to reach $100M to $1B a year. Large corporates are "completely unprepared" and will be run over by agile startups.
- The playbook he gives YC founders:
  1. Find real businesses spending hundreds of thousands of dollars a year on teams doing rote, repetitive knowledge work.
  2. Get access to their data and the flow of their work, and watch how they do it.
  3. Write test cases (evals) against that work.
  4. If the LLM hallucinates or is inconsistent, you are asking too much of it. Chop the prompts into smaller steps.
- He says current models handle roughly "120 IQ level work."
- Pivot advice: if a company selling to accounting firms struggles with enterprise sales, target people who already pay for a call center in the Philippines or Eastern Europe and replace it with an LLM plus good workflow and evals.
- He warns against "demo ware" and against "raw dogging your prompts" with no tests. Write tests and work test-driven.
- Moat strategy: land grab now. Companies that build evals, data access, switching costs and sales force today get a roughly 10x cost-structure drop when the next generation of models arrives. They would already hold revenue and market position against software incumbents. Models may also absorb some of what founders build, which is the risk.
- He thinks the value of coding yourself drops. What matters is instructing "virtual developers" precisely about what you want and the use cases.

chunks.heading: Lessons from Posterous and Palantir
chunks.text:
- Posterous (2008) was a blog-by-email platform that grew 10x year on year for two years until Instagram arrived. Garry says they did not fully understand why they were growing: the iPhone was new and there was no easy photo-upload app.
- Framing mistake: TechCrunch framed Posterous as easier than Tumblr, and the team made that competition their identity. His lesson is "you sort of allow media or other people to sort of frame your reality and then you just play the wrong game." They were really competing with how people got photos off their phones.
- What he would do differently: with about a million dedicated users and a team of 12, charging $5-10 a month would have made them profitable. He points to Weebly, which raised very little, was profitable and compounding, and sold to Square for roughly $300-400M.
- Benchmark's Peter Fenton passed on their Series A after asking "are you a platform or a network?" and getting the answer "both." Garry says that is what founders without strong opinions say.
- His advice: "make something people want and that's the ending itself." Play your own game rather than the one chosen for you by investors, social media or tech press.
- He turned down Peter Thiel's offer (including a $70,000 check) to co-found Palantir in 2004. He then joined as employee number 10 and designed the logo in 2006. His first real million came from selling Twitter stock at IPO, after about 18 years in tech.
- Lesson he draws: "the world doesn't happen to you." Palantir's founders learned the CIA and NSA lacked good software by going to talk to them directly. Talk to users and gather first-source information rather than taking your worldview from media or social media.
- On Palantir's slow start, he says founders should not copy it unless they are Peter Thiel and willing to put tens of millions of their own money in and wait years.

chunks.heading: Keeping YC unconventional, and the lessons from big organizations
chunks.text:
- From Paul Graham he learned to be wary of formality and corporateness. He recalls PG scraping the maintenance sticker off a corporate copy machine because it reminded him of Yahoo. YC's ethos mixed "very earnest and very formidable" with a family-like welcome. He says he stays up at night thinking about how YC never feels corporate.
- He says that wherever there is prestige or convention you should be wary, because soul-sucking baggage usually comes with it.
- On starting businesses: many people play business (business cards before a customer, then OKRs and quarterly measures) and have to pull themselves out of it.
- On big companies: he argues that bureaucracy impeded AI progress. At Google, compute was scarce and political, so papers ended up with 30 authors, while OpenAI could commit resources. Big tech is "big daycares for the most technical smart people."
- He notes it took Herculean effort by product people inside OpenAI to even ship ChatGPT, since the lab planned to keep GPT behind an API.
- He says Sam Altman was right to jump on AI when the smartest people were already talking about it, and that he himself was skeptical at first but is now a believer.

chunks.heading: Early career hustle and the spoon-bending lesson
chunks.text:
- At 14, Garry cold-called businesses from the Yellow Pages offering to make web pages. He got a job at a local web design firm (Infolane) that built city sites, paid about $7-10 an hour, where he learned graphic design and HTML. His parents were food insecure and his dad lost jobs. He used his earnings to help his family make the down payment on a house in Fremont.
- He started an online zine with junior high friends that readers found through Usenet. Nobody knew they were kids.
- He joined YC at 27 and says he wishes he could tell his younger self not to sell his time but to make products.
- The spoon-bending story (Burning Man): the workshop pitches bending a spoon with your mind, but people really bend it with their hands. About half the room did, and the rest could not figure out how. His moral: believe you can change the world with ideas, but "you actually have to go with your hands and go talk to users and sit and build a thing." He calls it an allegory for bias to action.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how YC runs as a managed network-effects marketplace, why founders should be in the Bay Area, and how self-awareness shapes startups. He also covers co-founder conflict, fundraising as a starting gun, craft in building, and his prompt-iteration workflow with AI.

chunks.heading: Garry's path from Winnipeg to YC, and what YC actually is
chunks.text:
- Garry was born in Winnipeg, grew up in Fremont, and took BART to UC Berkeley for his first CS classes. His first coding job was at Adjacency, the design firm that built the first Apple e-commerce store for Steve Jobs.
- He describes YC as an accelerator: you apply online, about 1% get in, and you get half a million dollars for roughly 7% of the company. He says the money matters less than getting a YC partner. There are 15 partners, and each picks companies out of the applicant pool.
- Partners decide yes or no on the half million within a 10-minute interview.
- He cites YC's 20-year record as more than 100 billion-dollar companies. When he did YC in 2008 the batch got about $13,000, and the first batch included Reddit (Steve Huffman and Alex Ohanian) and Sam Altman's Loopt.
- He found YC through Palantir, where he was employee number 10 and designed the logo. The team was trying to hire away YC alums, which showed him where the smartest engineers went.
- YC's mantra, printed on the t-shirt: "Make something people want." He tells founders to dwell on what people actually want and to build for real customers.

chunks.heading: YC's eras, and why Garry came back in 2022
chunks.text:
- **Era one:** Boston, with Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Trevor Blackwell and Robert Morris.
- **Era two (from 2011):** Airbnb followed Dropbox as a billion-dollar company, and the valley realized YC was repeatable. Check sizes went from roughly $12-15K to $120K-$175K. Investors took about 3-4 years to catch up with what engineers already knew.
- Garry joined as a partner around 2011 after Harj Taggar suggested it. He had rage-quit his own startup and had no plan to become an investor. He started by helping YC companies design their homepages.
- He then raised Initialized Fund I, a $7M fund that returned more than 55x DPI. He says the power law was real: across 98 companies the combined return was about 1x until Coinbase was counted. Instacart was about 1x and Coinbase carried the fund.
- He says 80-90% of Initialized's wins were YC or YC alumni (Ripling and Flock Safety among them).
- Brian Chesky and Paul Graham pushed him to return in 2022. He calls it a dream job and says "YC gave me my start as a founder... as an investor," plus most of his friends.
- He calls YC a "managed marketplace" and a network-effects business. About 20% of companies worth $5B+ that started from 2012 on came through YC, and that share has been flat for years. He wants it at 30-50% by 2036.

chunks.heading: What Garry changed at YC: founder mode applied to the institution
chunks.text:
- From Brian Chesky and Paul Graham's "founder mode" idea, Garry took that leadership is presence, not absence. He says the standard advice, "hire the smartest people... give them the keys to the kingdom," did not work for Chesky.
- Changes he made:
  - Brought back in-person interviews.
  - Moved the program to San Francisco and got an office there. Founders are told to move to the Dogpatch.
  - Ended the remote batch: "you cannot do YC remotely."
  - Extended the program to 13 weeks. Batches had shrunk to about 11-12 weeks.
- Weeks 1-10 are for finding product-market fit: get into market, nail messaging, decide who you build for, and land the first 3-5 real customers, which "sets the tone for the whole company."
- Fundraising gets about two weeks. The investor push starts the Saturday after the send-off.
- Defense tech is up more than 2x in the last batch. Icarus booked over $1.5M from the Department of War during the batch.
- The first thing a founder can do to make fundraising easy is build something valuable and get paying, retained customers.
- Fundraising "is the starting gun," not the finish line. He treats SAFEs like debt: "you sort of signed up to say... we're going to return a big multiple of that."
- Moving fast during YC creates momentum ("objects in motion stay in motion"). He says billion-dollar companies later try to recapture the energy of those first eight weeks. Airbnb's example: post-it graph targets of 10% weekly growth.
- YC runs on its own advice: when choosing between spending heavily and hiring, or doing it "quick and dirty" and iterating, they pick the startup way "10 times out of 10."
- New ideas he is trying:
  - Rebatching: a second batch after Series A, starting with companies he funded.
  - A Cambridge office, where Garry says YC just added its first partner.
- He says more founders get rejected than he likes. YC gets about 80,000 applications a year and funds roughly 700-800 companies. It keeps him up at night. He notes many get in on a second to fourth attempt, and "if you can survive the mortal ego wound of being rejected... you're made to be a founder."

chunks.heading: How Garry evaluates founders and why YC partners are good at it
chunks.text:
- He loves builders. Even with AI, he says the default output is bad: "boilerplate... kind of sucks," so there is "no excuse" for not making beautiful, well-made products.
- He uses the Steve Jobs cabinet-maker image: great cabinet makers finish the back of the cabinet too.
- Partner skill comes from reps. A partner reads 1,000-2,000 applications a year and writes 50-75 seed checks. Garry says two or three years as a YC partner equals about 20 years in venture.
- He says partners are strong at pulling out the billion-dollar idea, but their main value is stopping founders from hitting the "10,000 landmines." Examples: co-founder conflict, taking money from the wrong investor, single-channel concentration.
- He says partners never freak out: "soft advisors who never freak out."
- Selection is subjective. Each partner picks their own cohort, passes along companies they cannot fit, and the process is "random winning the lottery" when done wrong and a long-term commitment when done right.
- He admits mistakes. He and a colleague should have accepted one company in the fall batch and took them the next winter. He says he will feel bad about missing the next Airbnb and will "turn it into productive energy."

chunks.heading: Co-founders, conflict and fixing your own patterns
chunks.text:
- Garry says the most common YC failures are running out of money and co-founder conflict. He adds that YC companies usually quit because they get tired and demoralized, not because they run out of cash.
- Great co-founders "fight absolutely all the time and about everything" because they care. The key is doing it in a way that preserves the relationship: "There is never a conflict or a fight that is so much more important than the relationship itself."
- His own pattern, which he calls self-abandonment: he would swallow disagreements to protect the relationship, then blow up. He says he was a terrible co-founder at Posterous. One time he blew up in a 1-on-1 with an early designer.
- His model: a horse and a rider, where his rider (prefrontal cortex, language) can override the horse (body) until it "says F this." He lost the ability to eat and sleep. He got through it with therapy and coaching, citing Cameron Yarrow's coaching (Torch).
- Tool he uses: "freeze all motor function" (a Westworld debug-mode analogy), then add an "if statement." For him the trigger is his face getting hot.
- Why it matters: startups take on the founder's personality. "How you do anything is how you do everything." Founders' unresolved patterns show up in who they hire, who they fire and how the company handles conflict.
- He warns "maybe psychedelics are not for everyone."

chunks.heading: Garry's AI workflow: metaprompting and multi-model review
chunks.text:
- He credits Jared Friedman and Pete Koomen for "metaprompting."
- Steps:
  1. Take any repeated knowledge-work task and drop a set of real inputs and outputs into a context window (for him, notes and the finished YouTube script).
  2. Ask the model to write a prompt for an agent that turns that input into that output, and to say what patterns it notices.
  3. Use it, then correct it in conversation ("I would never say that," "use the short word").
  4. Ask for the next version of the prompt incorporating everything discussed.
- He keeps a folder of prompts. His YouTube prompt is on about V27.
- For hard cases he runs GPT 5.2 Pro, Grok and others at max thinking, pastes all outputs into Claude, and asks Claude to rate each response with pros and cons in numbered form. He agrees or disagrees by number, then asks it to synthesize.
- He uses Perplexity for anything needing the web because it synthesizes more sources.
- That weekend he used Claude Code to build a new website and redo interaction design.

chunks.heading: Why Garry fights for San Francisco, and his case for tech optimism
chunks.text:
- His stat: staying in the Bay Area makes a startup 2.5x more likely to reach a $1B outcome. New York is about 2x. Everywhere else is the baseline. He cites capital access, ambition rising with your peers, and access to people who have done what you need to do.
- He opposes California's proposed one-time 5% "billionaire tax," which he calls an "asset seizure tax." He says it counts voting control as ownership, so Larry and Sergey would be taxed on 60% of Alphabet's value. He estimates a mid double-digit chance (40-50%) it passes, and says about $1T in net worth has already left the state.
- He also opposes a proposal to 10x San Francisco's gross receipts tax and a Mission District supervisor's effort to ban AI labs and R&D, which he says was stopped after people organized on the internet in December.
- His tactic: do research and go direct on X when mainstream outlets won't publish it. His covenant as a creator is to try to be truthful while admitting he won't get everything right, and to keep opposing views in the mix.
- His tech optimism: software touches a tiny share of GDP, only 10-20 million people can code well, and AI will let billions create. He argues for more markets, citing Uber, Airbnb and Waymo. He quotes Ryan Petersen of Flexport that "humans just want stuff." He also points out that firewood was once about 25% of US GDP.
- He says the Matrix is "surprisingly relevant to startup founders" and that YC is how he took the red pill. A company that stays plugged into customers is "in the real."
- He names Brian Chesky and Aaron Levie as the founders he learns from most. He says a fund that shorted incumbents with non-hacker CEOs would "outperform the S&P."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan, with other YC partners, explains how Claude Code and Codex change what founders can build and how YC evaluates them. He argues for judging builders by how they work, moving decisively, and treating AI as a reason to attempt more rather than staff less.

chunks.heading: What YC is, and what it's for
chunks.text: Garry describes YC as "Disneyland for transformation": a process that takes earnest, technical people and turns them into formidable founders. He frames it as a social process, since reality is "socially constructed." When he first showed up at Startup School, it felt like "a fish out of water jumping into water," surrounded by builders. The recent YC site redesign tried to write this down, using old photos of founders like the Collisons and the Airbnb founders when they were young. He says that in broad strokes YC has changed far less than it has stayed the same, and that this is by design: when you have a great product, you don't mess with it.

chunks.heading: Evaluating founders in the age of Claude Code
chunks.text:
Garry says something shifted at the end of November 2025, when Opus 4.5 came out. He rebuilt his 2008 startup in roughly 90 hours over two weeks, about 70,000 lines of code, while holding a full-time job and raising kids. It was better than what five engineers and he had built over about two years, and he says he couldn't have done it with $5 million and five engineers back then.

- For the spring batch, YC applications let founders upload a Claude Code or Codex transcript of building a feature. YC runs these in a security sandbox, expecting prompt injection.
- He says you can tell whether someone can build from how they prompt: whether they use plan mode, think about systems, over-engineer or prematurely optimize, consider edge cases, and know what counts as a complete release.
- His principle: "How you do anything is how you do everything." He cites Steve Jobs on carpenters who look at the back of the cabinet, since only other craftspeople will inspect it.
- On Instacart's Apoorva Mehta: he built an iPhone demo himself, and the tell was that it scrolled very smoothly, which wasn't true of apps in that early App Store era.
- The question he asks of any founder: "would I go work for this person if I weren't doing the thing I'm doing now?"

chunks.heading: Agency, taste, and the quality bar
chunks.text:
Garry argues the most important traits for any product, vertical or customer set are agency and taste.

- Agency: seeing a problem and believing you can solve it with technology.
- Taste: building the first version, getting it in people's hands, asking whether it worked and how it broke, then going deep into the weeds.
- He describes the "tireless, ceaseless gardener" needed to fix every bug across hundreds of thousands of lines of code. His model is the Bahá'í gardens in Haifa, where "not a single weed, not a leaf out of place" reflects people who care almost religiously.
- He says the bar keeps rising: every six months for the past three years, what founders demo at the product showcase a few weeks into the batch has gone up.
- YC shouldn't fund someone for going to Harvard. It should fund people who "actually understand the user and are unbelievably tenacious."
- AI widens the net more than it changes the criteria. He still wants to fund genius engineers, and expects more founders in the mold of Parker Conrad (non-traditional background, strong product and commercial thinker) to get through.

chunks.heading: Competition, pivoting, and speed of decisions
chunks.text:
- Garry says YC spends most of its time telling founders not to worry about competition. He imagines the Lora founders not launching because they saw Harvey. The advice is to make something people want and out-execute, not build a market map first.
- Companies can now try many ideas within a batch. You can do two years of work, find nobody wants it, throw it out and start again, and the learning isn't wasted.
- On large companies, he describes the old cycle of meetings, docs and opinions over architecture taking weeks or months. Now you can go into plan mode, try both options, and have something in an hour. He says incumbents that need two years to make a decision "or never" are the ones at risk.
- His view on "is SaaS dead": he thinks it's dead, but any SaaS company can survive by embracing Claude Code and a top-to-bottom agentic view of how everything works.

chunks.heading: What's defensible, and where capital still matters
chunks.text:
- He sees marketplaces that aggregate people (Airbnb, DoorDash) as safe from AI. Hard tech is protected because it is hard to source and make work.
- Systems of record that touch money or regulation, such as payroll, are sticky. Moats built on integrations or data connectors are brittle.
- Coding agents' recommendations are becoming a real moat. He jokes about writing API docs to prompt-inject Claude Code into using your product.
- He argues against "we won't need capital." If a competitor has 50 engineers, you wouldn't choose five, because human desire is effectively unlimited and AI is a reason to attempt more. He says "let's boil a few lakes."
- He notes capital works as a moat in markets like prediction markets, where regulatory change opens a green light, but it matters less for AI companies. He also notes sales, unlike support, is not automated yet.
- Capital can mislead: a company can have it and "move fast in the wrong direction," as with fine-tuning models that frontier models then beat.
- He says tiny teams can win, citing Giga (10 to under 20 people) beating incumbents.

chunks.heading: Working with investors and growing the founder base
chunks.text:
- He says most investors are B or B+. Having one who simply doesn't mess with you is "really good," and you should take a great investor's money when you can get it. For everyone else, B+ capital is fine.
- YC needs more A and A+ investors. He expects most future top VCs to be YC alumni (naming Ilya Sukhar, Dan Levine, Liz of First Round).
- He says the bottleneck for YC now is great founders wanting to do startups, not follow-on capital.
- YC can't just exist as "something in the sky on the internet." The best founders know someone who did YC or met a partner in person. Recent actions:
  - Over 30 college campuses visited last year (led by Jared).
  - A trip to Europe, with India planned for the spring.
  - A push to reach grad students and founders in their mid to late 20s.
- YC Fellows gives grants and community to exceptional college students who aren't ready for a startup yet.
- Founders are trending younger. He thinks AI favors younger people, and that big tech stopped hiring. He rejects the "last chance to participate in capitalism" mindset as shortsighted.

chunks.heading: YC's structure and the mission
chunks.text:
- Garry says YC now has about 30 partners including 15 visiting partners.
- Under his tenure each partner picks their own companies and runs their own autonomous "pod" of around 30 companies, roughly the size of YC when he went through it. That is why going from 2 to 4 batches a year, or doubling partners, needs no structural change.
- The mission he echoes from PG: the conventional VC view says only about 10 companies a year will matter, and YC's answer was "let's make more of them." Everything is driven by wanting that number to go up.
- He says YC is a "managed marketplace" that wants to back every type of company. He cites Coinbase, where Brian Armstrong was an anti-fraud engineer at Airbnb, and notes early on it matters more who the person is and what they believe than the idea.
- His stated directive from the board: make sure the partners are having fun.

chunks.heading: Little tech, building, and politics
chunks.text:
- He argues capital and management must take responsibility for workers' fears about AI, and that the answer is not shaving 1 to 2% off margins each year but imagining radically better products.
- He says it's become more important than ever to be a founder ("management that becomes capital").
- He backs YC's "little tech" policy push (Luther Lowe in DC) so startups can train models and enter markets, arguing this is consistent with respecting big tech while keeping markets open.
- He cites *Breakneck* on the US having stopped building since about the 1960s and 70s and becoming a litigious culture, and supports Matt Mahan for California governor as someone who builds (more than 1,400 homes in San Jose, homelessness down 20%).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan talks to Jack Altman about running YC with zero-based accounting and founder energy. He covers how to advise founders, what makes a great founder, when to raise big versus stay lean, and how AI changes team size but not moats.

chunks.heading: Zero-based accounting: running YC like a founder
chunks.text:
- Garry describes running YC with "zero-based accounting": if YC were started from scratch today, he'd keep only what he would add again. Brian Chesky (Airbnb) told him this, and Brian brought "founder mode" energy to YC's board meetings before the term existed.
- He treats YC as a "tree of prosperity" that needs pruning. It is hard to say no to things and people, because "culture is everything", and it comes down to who you fire, hire and promote.
- Brian's Airbnb experience was the warning. After product-market fit, boards push you to hire experts from other companies, until you wonder whether it is your company, the board's or the shareholders'. Covid was Brian's moment to reset Airbnb's culture.
- YC's 2010s expansion into side bets was followed by a return to the core. He says "never say never" about expanding again, and hopes to prune as the tree grows rather than cut back wild growth later.
- Early batches had 8 to 15 companies twice a year. YC now runs about 150 companies four times a year, and the market is still not captured.

chunks.heading: Who YC is for: the zero-sum and abundance mindsets
chunks.text:
- Garry holds both: a zero-sum fight for founders "from central casting" (cracked, with the right resume), where YC competes with top VC and seed names and that's fine, and an abundance side that creates prosperity where there was none.
- The abundance side is Paul Graham's original insight: highly technical young founders are the most mispriced asset.
- Focus is hard, since "if you focus on all of them, are you really focusing on any of them?" YC is clearly focused on technical founders.
- He wants to dispel the idea that YC is only for people from certain companies or Harvard, Stanford and MIT. It is also for people from Cornell, UIUC and elsewhere.
- Brilliant, hard-working engineers get rejected from elite schools, which he calls unfair. YC is most valuable to people without a built-in brand and network, because they get "shot out of a rocket into Silicon Valley culture".
- The principle: the world needs "shelling points" for builders and talented people, where capital, customers, knowledge and the best friends of your life come together. He wants diversity and merit in the same place.
- His own example: at Stanford, being a fraternity brother of Joe Lonsdale and Stephan Cohen brought him in touch with Peter Thiel, which he says helped a child of immigrants from a poor family.

chunks.heading: Why YC's pick rate is so good, and how partners advise
chunks.text:
- His explanation is "game recognizes game". Partners who are builders themselves get far more reps than anyone else.
- He tells 22-year-olds desperate to become VC associates not to do it: "just go start a company." He quotes Jay-Z: everybody wants to tell you how to do it, they never did it.
- Founders want to sit one-on-one with someone who has been there. Partners should not validate bad decisions. They give a view, as a "soft advisor", and say what they think you should do.
- Partners are not the boss. He recalls Paul Graham telling a batch founder to do whatever they wanted, since YC funds 100 companies, even if they wanted to drive off a cliff.
- Partners "don't know the path, we just know how not to die". There are a billion ways to die: losing a co-founder over dumb arguments, picking the wrong investor, bad first hires, and picking too many things to focus on. YC has seen 50 people die each way and can connect you with one of them.
- Median startup advice is useless because it's on five podcasts already. Valuable advice comes from people who have seen enough to give "spiky" advice, sometimes the worst advice. Good founders discard bad advice, and YC's meta-message was "don't take anybody's advice carte blanche, including ours".
- Of the bad advice Paul gave, the example he recalls is on naming.

chunks.heading: Lean vs fat startups, and compound startups
chunks.text:
- On the lean vs fat debate: "if you can get Keith Rabois to invest in your startup, you should do a fat startup." The same goes for Vinod Khosla or Elad Gil. If they want you to go fat, you've been blessed.
- For almost everyone else, you can't get to a fat startup without doing it lean first.
- On compound startups (going multi-product very early): it's better to be as multi-product as early as you can if you can hire and build consistently. Ramp is a good example.
- The common thread is "no dogma". A systems-thinking founder shouldn't take rules from a podcast.
- In a blitz-scaling race, the constraint is how many companies can draw 150-IQ talent at 50, 100, 500 or 1,000 people. Parker Conrad (Rippling) can, with Matt MacInnis, acqui-hiring such people to take new product lines from zero to $10 million ARR. He thinks the compound startup is possible if you can do that, but "very few people are really capable of doing that".

chunks.heading: What a special founder looks like
chunks.text:
- First archetype: commerciality. These founders sit with people who have a need and pull the requirements "right out of the customers". After a few meetings with product in market, the yanking turns into customers pushing, and "that's product-market fit."
- This is counterintuitive. Great founders are perceptive rather than forceful, like a great seller who is the best listener. The cargo cult says listen less, while he says listen 10 times more.
- Second: unusual people do unusual things early. Example: Serena Ge of Datacurve dropped out of Waterloo at about 19 or 20 and, at about 16, had built one of the top rock-climbing apps in the App Store. He describes such people as "an inch wide and a mile deep".
- Third: hacks. He looks for people who are "a little bit naughty" and have done unusual hacks.
- Fourth: systems thinking. Can you sit down with anyone and understand their motivations, how they get promoted, their ideology? To "program the world" you first reverse-engineer it. This predicts recruiting, selling and fundraising.

chunks.heading: AI and vertical software: moats, scale and team size
chunks.text:
- Buyers in old industries (education, healthcare, legal) that struggled to adopt cloud are now hungry for AI. Competition is higher, since a good idea draws 19 teams.
- Language models let founders make claims that were not possible before. Example: a medical billing company claims that a 10 to 15 person clinic (dermatology, even veterinary) needs only clinicians plus one back-office person. People believe the demo, especially with five customers already running it.
- He expects "10,000 flowers" in vertical AI software, narrowing from about a thousand to a hundred over time, and the usual one-two-three market structure to hold.
- Unless AGI or ASI ends software, the old rules apply, including the moats: switching costs, proprietary data, brand, network effects.
- Whether to blitz-scale is each founder's call. There is emerging evidence you don't have to: you might reach $50 to $100 million ARR with under 20 people, as Linear is an example of. Founders now increasingly automate internally with their own agents instead of hiring large teams.
- When a nine-way race exists, he says to scramble up the wall as fast as possible.

chunks.heading: Hard tech and YC Demo Day as a shelling point
chunks.text:
- His advice to any founder is to build a shelling point. YC's is Demo Day, which draws well over $1 billion of investor capital a year ("going on $1.2"), a number he wants to grow to $2 billion or $2.5 billion in 5 to 10 years. It isn't contractually captive, but it rises every year.
- Median YC startups raise about $1 to $1.5 million at Demo Day. Hard tech companies with real commercial validation or a technological breakthrough in the three or four months can raise $3, 5, 10 or even 20 million, enough to build a real hard tech company from YC alone.
- Examples of success: Solen, Astranis.
- Every YC partner does hard tech. YC is adding specialised programming, such as Andy Lapsa of Stoke Space running a hard tech mini-conference for the last batch.
- YC's value is less specific services than mindset and a cross-section of other builders, who can help in ways partners can't, since a general partner's last real engineering was years ago.
- Example of batch trust: when Garry did YC, Heroku's James Lindenbaum helped him fundraise. Nine months after his seed round, Heroku worried about hosting some of the biggest Rails sites, and asked Garry for his source code. Garry's one of those sites. He says you'd do that for a batchmate and no one else.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan draws on Palantir, Posterous and YC to explain why founders miss product-market fit, why answering "both" is a strategic mistake, and how to read customer feedback. He also covers co-founder conflict, founder-led culture, fundraising in a tough market and why the startup ceiling keeps rising.

chunks.heading: Founder-market fit: build for yourself, then pick a lane
chunks.text:
- Garry's startup Posterous began as a weekend project: a way to email any photo and have it become a gallery. The team didn't know it could be a business.
- He says 2008 was an unusually good moment for it. The iPhone was brand new and the App Store had no great photo-posting apps yet. Posterous grew 10x year on year and reached a top-200 website on the internet. Twitter later bought it.
- Launch tactic: Y Combinator got them onto TechCrunch. Michael Arrington's launch post ("posterous beats Tumblr in Simplicity") stayed up all weekend and brought in roughly 10-20k users.
- He notes the framing that helped at launch is not the one that gets you to the next stage: "what got you here won't get you there."

chunks.heading: Posterous's mistakes: ignoring Instagram and answering "both"
chunks.text:
- When Instagram launched, it could cross-post to Posterous. Investor Chris Sacca asked what the team thought of Instagram. Garry's co-founder replied "it sucks." Garry says that was when Posterous stopped growing.
- His lesson is that the "don't worry about competition" maxim can be taken too far. A founder is always betting on what the future looks like, and being able to predict it matters.
- Posterous's real competitor was a dominant, photo-based social network built on the iPhone, which was a one-time opportunity.
- At the Series A pitch, Peter Fenton of Benchmark asked one question: "are you a platform or are you a network?" Instagram was a network and Squarespace was a platform. Garry and his co-founder answered "both."
- He calls that the wrong answer. They could have owned photo/visual social, or charged money like WordPress or Squarespace. By doing neither, they did both poorly and let competitors win each space.
- Rule: be deliberate about the path, because saying yes to one thing means saying no to another.

chunks.heading: Profitability vs. raising the next round
chunks.text:
- Garry frames this as a choice founders must actually make, and the common mistake is choosing both. Posterous was afraid to charge because it feared hurting growth, yet it also wasn't investing fully in network features.
- With the current funding environment, he says unless you are in AI, LLMs, computer vision or another very hot space, the next round is not guaranteed.
- His advice is to get to profitability or cash-flow breakeven, and then grow out of cash flow. The macro picture is uncertain (relations with China, inflation versus deflation), so profitability is the safest path.

chunks.heading: Finding product-market fit: the thin edge of the wedge
chunks.text:
- Garry sees two kinds of founders. Some arrive with a real insight and are simply right. He names Brian Armstrong at Coinbase and Parker Conrad at Rippling, whom he says "just knew it" and who often produce the biggest outcomes. Others are drawn to the lore and community of startups and have only the desire to build one.
- Weak pitches from the second group sound like "a book report," recited and boring. He calls this trying to "MBA your way" into an insight.
- Startups have no tournament, unlike school or the professional world: "a B plus is an F." You have either found product-market fit or you haven't.
- The example is Clipboard Health. Its founder was running an undifferentiated nurse job-posting marketplace, much like Indeed, for years. She found product-market fit by spending time with skilled nursing facilities and convalescent homes. These spent heavily on one-off staffing agencies that worked by phoning around to fill shifts, and software had never touched that.
- She built a sticky product for that segment, and the company is now making nine figures in revenue.
- His takeaway: huge businesses sit where builders have never reached parts of the economy that have never seen software. Find a narrow, desperate segment that is 10x or 100x better served, and treat it as the thin edge of the wedge.
- On user research: people are nice and tell you what you want to hear. Until they pay or change a behavior out of self-interest, feedback is worthless. Be skeptical of what you want to hear and listen hard to what you don't.

chunks.heading: Founder traits: plain communication and the "75 IQ" test
chunks.text:
- Garry uses the midwit meme to make a point: things that sound like "75 IQ" ideas are often "150 IQ" ones.
- Great founders explain complex breakthroughs in very few words, because at the core of a breakthrough is something obvious.
- This matters because the founder has to close customers, candidates and money, and nobody else can do those three early on. You need to make the case in a minute or less. He says to "breathe" the thing you believe that nobody else believes into other people.
- In office hours he looks for the "gem" rather than the "ritual," and doesn't want a 20-minute explanation of why something failed. Startups fail for many reasons. His analysis of hundreds of startups he has worked with since 2012 found the number one cause was not making something people wanted.
- Michael Seibel's line he repeats: don't try to be the median startup at YC. The median startup fails, and the value is in the power-law top end, so you must be superlative.
- In office hours he operates in one of two modes: people need to believe in their idea more, or they need to see the thing about to kill them. He cites the Stockdale Paradox: relentless optimism combined with a cynical view of the facts.

chunks.heading: Leadership and culture after product-market fit
chunks.text:
- Past zero to one, Garry says the CEO must hold people to account. Culture is who gets hired, promoted and fired. Big tech avoids these choices by doing both. Inside a startup, everyone is watching which of two people the leader backs.
- Culture radiates from the founder. He points to Brian Chesky's speeches: the leader has to be unapologetic about who they are and what they stand for, and not pull punches.
- Founders' rough edges are what make them special, and they resonate with a small group of the right people. Smoothing them off to appeal to everyone was long the common wisdom, and he says it's a mistake.
- Early-stage venture is heavily resume-based, but being an employee in an organization is a very different skill from being founder and CEO.
- He thinks Airbnb could still grow 10x, because only a small share of the world's available space is on it.

chunks.heading: Co-founder relationships
chunks.text:
- Garry and his Posterous co-founder didn't speak for about eight to ten years. Growth flatlined in 2010 after two and a half years of non-stop growth, and he says he hadn't hired enough engineers, so technical debt was severe.
- He took "have a good relationship with your co-founder" to mean being collaborative: if they wanted X and he wanted Y, he'd water down Y by 50%. That works in a marriage, he says, but in a co-founding relationship you are better off simply having the fight.
- The best partnerships are with people you enjoy disagreeing and arguing with, because you'll do it again and again and the relationship must survive the heat.
- Early on, strong growth masked the flaws in the relationship. He burned out badly and later saw his body reacting to it (insomnia, not eating, fevers).

chunks.heading: YC, valuations and the future of venture
chunks.text:
- Garry learned to invest by reading applications at Y Combinator. The most he read in one cycle was about a thousand. He says nowhere else exposes you to that many types of people and ideas, and a VC firm sees only dozens of deals a year.
- He values YC's generalist breadth: the best founders share ways of looking at problems and values that YC has a process to spot.
- On fundraising today: it's close to a roll of the die and was far easier in 2021. Stack the odds with trusted advisors, hone "what do we believe that nobody else believes," bring evidence, and have a truly huge hypothesis.
- Valuations and dilution: the average YC company takes roughly 10-12% dilution, versus 20-40% at seed and another 20-40% at Series A in the old norm. He cites YC's $750k deal on a $3M post as an example. Founders keeping more control means bigger outcomes.
- Fund returns: his seven million dollar initialized fund modeled a best case of about 5x if it caught a Dropbox-size exit. It returned more than 55x DPI, driven by Coinbase and Instacart. He expects decacorns and hectocorns to become much more numerous.
- AI shift: with large language models, two or three people in a garage can land a $10-100k/year contract that expands to millions within three to six months. He says he had never seen that happen before.
- He argues the limiting factor is not capital or ideas but community: people with the right values working on the right problems. He calls himself an effective accelerationist.
- On location: he thinks San Francisco is still the best place to find product-market fit, and it makes sense to keep at least one foot there for zero to one. Many things stop mattering once you have it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how Casetext turned a limited SEO legal product into a billion-dollar outcome by chopping LLM tasks into small, evaluable steps, why narrow vertical AI beats general models, and why YC batches now grow 10-20% a week. He also shares his prompt-iteration workflow for writing video scripts and how he restructured YC around the core batch and lifelong partner support.

chunks.heading: How YC companies reach $10M+ ARR with tiny teams: vertical AI, compressed sales, and a 10%-a-week growth baseline
chunks.text:
Garry argues that AI has changed how fast software revenue compounds.

- He says it is now routine to see YC companies with "10 or 20 people get to 10 or 20 million a year in revenue in 10 or 20 months", which has "literally never happened before in software".
- During the 12-week YC batch, average revenue growth is about 10% per week, and some batches have run 15-20% per week. That has held for more than a year.
- Before, 10% a week was the aspirational outlier for one or two companies. He estimates the old average was closer to 2-4% per week.
- The reason: buying software used to be a "nice to have" for replacing spreadsheets or SAP. Now a prospect sees a demo, can see it hit their bottom line immediately, and says "I need it right now. When can you start?"
- His read is that "there's something in the water", and that this is the best time in the history of startups to start one.

chunks.heading: Case Text: how a niche legal data company became a huge AI business
chunks.text:
Garry uses Jake Heller's Casetext (YC, 2012-13) as the example of timing and moats.

- Casetext started as a "Web 2.0 for law" product. It indexed case law, legislation, judgments and other legal documents, grew mostly through SEO, and ran for close to 10 years.
- Garry says some products can only ever total up to about 10, 20 or 50 million in value. Founders worry about that ceiling early, but he thinks the worry may be premature.
- The users, understanding and corpus of data Casetext had built became a moat "right at the correct moment as technology itself shifted". Something that could make tens of millions a year could suddenly make hundreds of millions to billions.
- Jake had early access to GPT-3 through the YC community (OpenAI spun out of YC Research). It was a toy then: it hallucinated, and in law one wrong answer gets you fired.
- With GPT-4, Jake found that shrinking the question to a small enough step made output reliable. Garry says this is what we now call context engineering. Asking "is the defendant guilty" fails; chunked tasks work.
- Jake's method:
  - Ask what a human would do, e.g. skim each sentence or paragraph and score whether it belongs in a timeline.
  - Write evals and tests across many inputs and outputs for each specific task.
  - Do a tailored time-and-motion study of how a lawyer actually works.
- Garry compares Jake to "the first man on the moon" for inventing early prompt engineering.

chunks.heading: Selling AI to buyers: demo the money saved and the "feat of strength"
chunks.text:
Garry describes why Casetext's sales cycle collapsed.

- The first useful product combed through thousands of pages of documents and produced an accurate timeline of events. A legal analyst or associate would cost thousands to tens of thousands of dollars for that work.
- So the pitch becomes "I will save you this much money, direct to the bottom line. Do you want to buy?", which "becomes an easy answer".
- The demo used the corpus of Enron emails. Jake's example was asking about nuanced things like ironic jokes the CEO made, and the model found the joke about their fraud and the reference. Garry says lawyers saw it and said they needed to buy it right now.
- Garry's takeaway is that the "feat of strength" demo matters. It was astonishing enough to end the evaluation.
- He says he remains astonished as new models ship.

chunks.heading: Competing against OpenAI, Google and big incumbents: scope to a specific job
chunks.text:
Asked how startups compete with ChatGPT and Gemini, Garry gives two answers.

- Small teams use frontier models but adapt them to the "very specific things that real people in the economy actually need". Those are often unglamorous, such as customer support for HVAC.
- The AOA example (YC company): customer support for HVAC firms. Service Titan is the incumbent software.
  - HVAC firms spend about 1% of revenue on software like Service Titan, i.e. about $1 per $100 of revenue.
  - They spend $5-6 per $100 on people answering phones and scheduling.
  - A product aimed at that labor spend can take over the 1% and expand it "5x or 6x bigger".
- You "can't just take ChatGPT and have it do this type of work yet". He says it is conceivable eventually, but while it is not true, people are building the next Service Titans.
- On horizontal vs vertical (the ReadAI view that one tool should do everything and just adjust for sales): he says it may be too early to tell and does not claim certainty. His own YC evidence points to narrow verticals.
- He lists "infinity" of off-the-beaten-path, underserved verticals: HVAC, accounting, compliance, audit. "Where there's brass, there's gold."
- He also names consumer as a still non-consensus bet. ChatGPT is "the best and most astonishing consumer launch of any product in the history of products".

chunks.heading: Staying lean and focused as a founder
chunks.text:
Garry pushes back on the idea that the classic YC advice has changed.

- He says Sam Altman wondered whether "make something people want" and staying lean was still right, then changed his tune once he saw that startups using OpenAI's APIs are effectively its commercialization arm.
- Garry's view: "a lot of people who start really huge companies had to start companies that were much more specific." Elon Musk started with Zip2.
- His reframe: YC wants founders to be "directly in control of their own destiny" to the extent they can.
- Vibe coding and AI code generation lower the cost of building. He says the Claude Code team reportedly writes about 95% of its code with Claude, so each engineer does the work of about 20.
- He expects verticalized software for niches (his example: a CRM for podcasters or HVAC, rather than only HubSpot or Salesforce) because quality software has always been inaccessible. Even Apple has basic Calendar bugs.
- If codegen keeps improving, software quality itself can become the way HVAC firms compete with each other.
- The ideal is a founder who is a strong engineer and 20x's themselves with AI tools. A 10x engineer plus 20x becomes "200x".
- Even founders who miss a huge outcome gain: he cites his Posterous exit to Twitter and a batchmate (BackType) team that ended up building Twitter ads. Facing real users and shipping product teaches you faster than slow bureaucratic jobs.
- He notes YC applicants aged 18-22 are up over 100% year over year, 22-25 up about 20%, and 25-30 down 10-20%. He says many in the older group started during ZIRP and are hanging on at FANG or startups, and some are the biggest AI deniers.

chunks.heading: Consumer AI products and speed as the real advantage
chunks.text:
Garry sees consumer as the next opportunity and discusses what separates good AI wrappers.

- He points to Rosebud AI (his YC batchmate Chris Bader's journaling and therapy-style app). It is a small team of two or three, with very high retention and paying users.
- Counselor and therapist-style use is a major ChatGPT behavior change. The product works because it replaces a more expensive, less accessible thing (a therapist) and remembers prior sessions.
- He compares its slow organic growth to Evernote.
- Andrew's feedback was that the product lacked design polish. Garry's response: that kind of feedback is fixable "tomorrow".
- On whether thin wrappers can become real companies: ideally the founders are strong engineers who use AI tools to move much faster. MVPs built on top of other tools are a starting point.
- For second-time and repeat founders, he says the most important thing is time. With resources already in hand, the only thing that matters up front is speeding up, and "it takes a village to actually properly speed up".

chunks.heading: How YC changed under Garry, and how partners work with founders
chunks.text:
Garry describes what he changed when he returned as president and CEO.

- He frames YC 1.0 as Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Trevor Blackwell and Robert Morris setting the vibe. The second decade under Sam Altman and Jeff Ralston turned YC into an Alphabet-like set of competing efforts (nonprofit, research, Continuity growth fund).
- The board, including Brian Chesky, decided to go back to being "Google" instead of Alphabet. "It's like a thousand times easier to be Google than to make Alphabet work."
- Hardest cut: Continuity. The people involved now run their own funds and are doing well.
- YC's focus is the initial batch and the partnership:
  - Group partners are no longer "camp counselors". The title is now general partner, 15 equal partners, similar to Benchmark's structure.
  - Each company has at least one primary partner who stays in touch years later, like "your best angel investor who is there for you all the time".
  - "Let's stop competing with all the other VCs. Let's be their partners."
- The old model's problems: if you did not get a Continuity check, it could be a negative signal, and handing founders off after demo day made it a compartmentalized job that was easier for the firm but "less fun" and weaker for founders.
- What a partner does in practice:
  - Understand the business, the founders and their customers, then ask questions: could this be bigger, what is the most interesting thing you have learned about your customer, what gets people promoted, what resonates.
  - Be frank about what has not worked: if you are spending money or time on it, set it to zero, and double down on what works.
  - Act as a sounding board outside the day-to-day.
- He says the YC batch provides dozens of peers who came out of a top-1% process. In his own batch, the Heroku founders helped Posterous raise its seed and give scaling advice, then later asked for Posterous's codebase to debug their own scaling issue, and Garry's team shared it.
- He says having one person who has "taken an oath to look out for you" for the life of the company is better than 90% of startup founders get.

chunks.heading: Using AI to write YouTube scripts: Garry's prompt-iteration workflow
chunks.text:
Garry shares a concrete process for building a repeatable content prompt.

1. Fed the scripts of his top-performing YouTube videos into Gemini (2.5, chosen for its long context). Asked it to extract the salient features common across them.
2. It surfaced patterns such as: hook hard and fast, an inner-game lens, founder and creator psychology, and a sentence rhythm of claim, brisk explainer, vivid example, takeaway.
3. Turned that into a prompt: given a set of notes or ideas, write a script in this format. Feeds in raw material such as notes, a set-piece idea, a tweet or a video clip.
4. Had the model produce three-act narratives. A 10-minute script that would normally take "two, three hours" or several hours of "breaking my brain" can be ready on his phone during a commute.
5. Iterated: label and number each script, use ChatGPT's canvas, and edit as if directing a junior writer.
