6. At the end of each session, asked: "given what we did in this session to improve the prompt, output the next version of the prompt." He has done this about 20-30 times.

- The prompt grew into a "grab bag of tricks" the AI and he co-discovered over 10-15 scripts, including a pop-culture cold open (a 15-45 second film or TV news clip that mirrors the thesis before the hook) and an authority pillar quoting Paul Graham, Alan Watts or Naval Ravikant.
- First versions were bad; the output improved with each pass.
- His rule: if you give no direction and just say "write me a script", it is bad. The creator has to inject their own voice or it is "slop". He treats the model as a co-writer.
- He plans to publish the prompt session publicly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan and the Light Cone hosts apply Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers (process power, cornered resources, switching costs, counter-positioning, brand, network economies, scale economies) to AI startups. Garry's core message is to find a painful problem and move fast first, since moats only matter once you have something worth defending.

chunks.heading: Find a painful problem first; moats come later
chunks.text:
- Garry's core advice is to find a specific person with a real, severe pain point and solve it. The advice is deliberately "anti-business school": "make something people want."
- He says you can go almost anywhere and find problems that software, and especially AI, isn't solving. They are so numerous and severe that solving one can mint a billion-dollar, $10 billion or even hundreds-of-billions market cap business, "lying in plain sight."
- He says moats show up along the way. You stumble into the seven powers as you work with customers, build the product and work out what data you need.
- The pain should be existential for the customer: "I am not going to get promoted this year. Maybe I will get fired", or "the business is going to go out of business." It should not be a "nice if I could do this."
- His closing advice is to focus mainly on speed, which he treats as a moat in its own right (it is not one of Hamilton Helmer's seven powers). Go zero to one first.
- Most of the powers below are problems of going from one to a billion, ten billion or a trillion. Using this framework to avoid a startup, or to pick between two ideas by forecasting five-year moats, is "the real stupid thing."

chunks.heading: Why moats matter at all
chunks.text:
- Garry notes the irony that "The 7 Powers" (Hamilton Helmer) is business school material, while YC's own maxims are simple and anti-business-school.
- He cites Peter Thiel's "competition is for losers." With infinite competition, margins go to zero and the business dies, so a moat is "relatively existential eventually."
- A moat is a defensive tool. You need something worth defending, and before that "it's just like a puddle in a field."

chunks.heading: Process power and cornered resources
chunks.text:
- **Process power:** Garry's best example is Plaid, which has to support thousands to tens of thousands of financial institutions, each with different sites and crawlers, plus a huge CI/CD structure.
  - Better engineering is "the most profound form of process power."
  - He speculates that Plaid's founder Zach would want the latest code-gen tools to add every new financial institution faster than anyone else.
- **Cornered resource, government:** He points to Scale AI and Palantir with the DOD.
  - Getting there takes hiring the right people, long stretches in DC and Langley, and building skiffs (special secure data centers).
  - The cornered resource can be "the diamond mine in your customer's heads", meaning mindshare inside government.
- **Cornered resource, startups:** Closer to what YC sees is the forward deployed engineer (FDE) model, where founders sit with customers who normally never get good software.
  - They map the real time-and-motion of the process. For example: a request arrives by email, gets enriched in a certain way, and sometimes a call center phones the person.
  - That becomes the startup's own prompts, evals and eventually data sets for tuning models. All of it is "incredibly valuable."
- **Models are not required early:** Context engineering gets you 80 to 90% of the way, which is "plenty" for the first two years of a startup.
  - Cursor did not begin with full-parameter fine-tunes. It "started just by making something people want."
  - He says don't use the frameworks to "count yourself out prematurely."

chunks.heading: Switching costs in the AI era
chunks.text:
- AI can lower switching costs and also create new ones.
- **Lowering them:** Garry says that if you can use code gen to extract data from old, ossified systems or from competitors, you can take a switching cost that protected an incumbent "potentially down to zero." Startups can use this as a lever.
- **Consumer memory:** He says memory is already a switching cost for him. His ChatGPT relationship has evolved over the last year and it now seems to know what he cares about. He thinks that will grow, and personalization for consumers is a huge piece of it.

chunks.heading: Counter-positioning against SaaS incumbents
chunks.text:
- **Per-seat pricing:** He sees per-seat pricing as a structural trap for incumbents. If their AI works, customers need fewer seats, so success cuts their own revenue. Startups price on work delivered or tasks completed instead.
- **Cultural lag:** The top thing he hears from late-stage founders is how hard it is to reset engineering culture to use AI tools and to do context and prompt engineering. Teams that can't become AI-native can't ship products that work.
  - His closing advice to the last YC batch was to spend a month at a late-stage company to see this.
- **Bigger wallet share (Avoca, HVAC):**
  - He thinks ServiceTitan gets about 1% of an HVAC company's gross transaction value.
  - Avoca sells customer support software and can capture 4 to 10% of their spend, because it takes over the customer-support work itself.
  - His conclusion: "we may well be all undervaluing how powerful and how big the vertical SaaS AI companies will actually be."
- **Labor displacement:** He argues customer support jobs have 50 to 80% annual attrition, so people are quitting anyway.
  - Per Avoca, former support staff now manage AI agents, handle the interesting edge cases and can adjust prompts. He calls this "way more interesting" than following a script.

chunks.heading: Brand and ChatGPT vs Google as counter-positioning
chunks.text:
- Garry calls Google losing the consumer AI lead to ChatGPT a perfect example of counter-positioning. Google had the greatest cash cow in history, so disrupting its own ad business was unattractive, even at the cost of slowing access to knowledge by a few years.
- He gives the ChatGPT origin story as a speed moat. It shipped in months with a very small team of a couple of engineers.
  - Getting there took Sam Altman, YC Research and Greg Brockman hiring Ilya Sutskever out of DeepMind.
  - Many of OpenAI's founding people came from DeepMind, which was in the right place but "didn't nurture exactly the thing that society really needed."

chunks.heading: Schlep work is what keeps the last 10% yours
chunks.text:
- On reliability, Garry notes that a hackathon version of an AI tool is faster than ever to build, but the work after it is different. It means getting it to run reliably across tens of thousands of KYC requests a day.
- That last stretch is "painstaking drudgery work" that many engineers don't want to do. He expects it to be hard for people at big labs inventing AGI to get excited about the final 5% of consistency on one vertical tool.
- Vertical knowledge matters here too, because you need it to know what the edge cases are.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Light Cone conversation with Kelvin French Owen on coding agents. Garry describes returning to building after years in manager mode, why test coverage unlocked his speed, and how agents raise the bar for shipping software that works for users.

chunks.heading: Coding agents: why Claude Code and Codex feel so fast, and how to use them well
chunks.text: Source: Y Combinator Light Cone, "We're All Addicted To Claude Code" (2026-02-25). Only Garry's views are kept.

chunks.heading: Garry on coming back to coding with Claude Code
chunks.text:
- Garry describes his past decade as "manager mode": he used to code like a marathon runner, then stopped.
- After roughly nine days on Claude Code he says it was an "incredible unlock", like a bionic knee that lets him run five times faster.
- He says he can do "five people's worth of work in like a single day", calling it "rocket boosters".
- Part of the thrill is nostalgia: he used to hand-write odd regexes to refactor and understand code. Now the agent does that work.
- He finds it "weird" that CLIs, 20-year-old technology, beat the IDEs that were supposed to be the future.
- He uses it on his own Rails project; it can reach his dev database directly, which the sandboxed approach could not do easily.
- Example: it debugged nested delayed jobs "five levels in", found the bug, and wrote a test so it "never happens again". His reaction: "This is insane."
- He admits he has even let it access his production database to debug a concurrency issue, adding "I'm not sure if I'm supposed to do this".

chunks.heading: Garry's view on tests, debugging and agent memory
chunks.text:
- For the first 2 to 3 days of his nine-day stretch he had few or no tests.
- Then he ran a "refactor day" to reach 100% test coverage, and "I just sped up like crazy."
- With strong coverage he rarely has to test manually, and "nothing breaks".
- He links this to prompt engineering at AI companies: test-driven development, where the test cases are your evals (he recalls the Jake Heller episode).
- Debugging story: the agent wrote a comma-delimited string where a priority job queue expected a JSON array, so no jobs ran.
  - He watched it spend about 30 minutes reading thousands of lines of Rails ActiveJob internals before finding the bug.
  - Ten years ago he would have searched for a Stack Overflow thread or a Rails blog post.
- He wonders whether agents need their own "Stack Overflow" for coding agents.
- He is intrigued by a model-generated wiki, "Grokipedia" style, as a way to share fixes across people.
- He warns about Clawbot-style personal agents: "do not give it access to emails", because it is unclear how safe it is and prompt injection is likely.

chunks.heading: Garry on a future of custom software and agent-first data
chunks.text:
- Garry imagines software 40 years from now as "entirely personal": instead of one shared codebase, each customer gets a fork they edit by chatting with an agent.
  - His example: every company that signs up for Segment gets its own copy on its own servers.
  - The vendor pushes new features and an agent merges them into each fork.
- He thinks data models and the system of record still need to be consistent and correct.
- He sees an opening for something "agentic first" that generates the data for many custom views while keeping one source of truth.
- He sees the maker schedule changing: code used to need a block of 4+ hours to fill your own context window with class names and functions. Now he can build in short pockets, even "in the meeting".
- Yet he describes his own YC job as largely manager schedule, which now no longer blocks building.

chunks.heading: Garry on distribution in an agent-driven world
chunks.text:
- Download-and-run CLI tools win on distribution because you do not need anyone's permission to start.
- Garry notes Netscape Navigator was free for non-commercial use, and the company later tracked IPs to find commercial users and sell licenses. He wonders whether that top-down capture could work again.
- Developers may increasingly let the agent pick their stack. Garry's example: if Claude Code says to use PostHog, they use PostHog.
- He notes Supabase has become the default LLM answer for "how do I set up a backend" because of strong open-source docs, similar to how Stack Overflow won search before.
- He sees auto-bug-fixers (Sentry, New Relic MCP) as a natural fit, since the context sits right in the CLI.

chunks.heading: Garry on how new engineers and founders learn
chunks.text:
- His 10-year-old used AI for a writing assignment and produced a phrase "not a turn of a phrase that a 10-year-old is capable of".
- He applies this to the 18 to 22 year olds YC works with: they have not done real management work, such as combing through hundreds of thousands of errors after product-market fit.
- He asks how the next generation learns architecture and operations. Can Claude Code teach it, or will people just "bump your head into it"?
- He argues the best young builders could develop "off the charts taste" because they ship and touch reality ten times as much as the previous generation.
- He relates to the ADHD-style founder with ten half-finished branches: Claude Code "gets you over the line" on everything, with a constant novelty factor that feels like a video game.

chunks.heading: Garry's practices and stance on tooling choices
chunks.text:
- He reads what the agent is doing and does not run in skip-permissions mode (his words: "Not I like to read").
- He tried Codex on his Rails project and found it clearly under-served for Rails, which he calls "a vestigial language" that he happened to go deep on 10 years ago.
- His ask to Codex: add syntactic sugar for the top ~15 runtimes, "probably 10 PRs at most".
- His point: there are "far fewer excuses for software that doesn't quite work for a user now than ever".
- On YC itself: "YC has progressed a little bit from a startup. We still act like one though, which is, I think, important."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how he went back to coding while running YC, using Claude Code, Conductor and Open Claw to ship at roughly 400x his old output. He covers boiling the ocean with tokens, thin harness plus fat markdown skills, high test coverage, and why people should own their personal AI.

chunks.heading: Why Garry went back to building, and what he rebuilt
chunks.text:
- Garry coded for the first time in about 13 years after a Light Cone episode and Claude Code. He says the experience "awakened my 25-year-old self."
- He started because he wanted to write about issues he cares about, like letting San Francisco middle schoolers take algebra. He built Garry's List (a 501c4, now a C3 and a PAC) so smart people with shared beliefs could organize. He says "bringing together people is so powerful."
- He rebuilt Posterous (blogs by email, his 2008 YC startup, sold to Twitter for about $20M) three times:
  - Original: about $4M, 6-7 people, about 1.5 years.
  - Posthaven: about $100K, 2 people, about 3 months.
  - 2026 version: about $200 (a Claude Code Max account) and about 5 days.
- The 2026 version is a full blog platform plus RAG and agentic retrieval. It crawls the internet recursively, does deep research on any topic, and extracts quotables.
- He claims he went from roughly 2/3 of his time coding in 2013 to about 400x the output, while running YC full-time.

chunks.heading: "Boil the ocean" and token maxing
chunks.text:
- Garry's Garry's List newsroom, modeled on what Jake Heller (Casetext) described, does the work of a human researcher for about $5-$10 of Opus calls.
- His rule for agentic design: think about what a human would do with the context. Which book would they pull, what would they search?
- Boil the ocean: don't settle for one source when you can fetch 20, cross-reference them, and feed all of it into the core prompt. He uses Perplexity's API for deep research, X's API, and Grok's API for research on X.
- He argues that "if there is incremental work that makes something more complete, more awesome... you should token max." You "zap the rocks harder" and pay more.
- He thinks every kind of knowledge work can be token maxed. People still supply the agency ("I'm the one who's sitting here caring about algebra").
- He compares token spend to San Francisco rent: it is expensive, but it is more expensive not to pay it. He gave $500 in tokens in a single day as an example of spend a builder should accept if the product is valuable.
- He ties this to the YC maxim: live in the future and build what's missing.

chunks.heading: How G Stack started
chunks.text:
- G Stack began as notes in Apple Notes: prompts he kept retyping into Claude Code. He did not plan it as a product. It went viral, with about 200,000 views on the first post.
- The first piece was the plan eng review. Before any work, Claude must make ASCII diagrams of data flows, state machines, dependency graphs, processing pipelines, decision trees, user flows, inputs and outputs, and error messages. Loading that context made the output more complete.
- Review sections cover architecture, code quality, and tests.
- Testing lesson: when he hand-coded he did the minimum. When vibe coding, the code worked for the 80% case but fell over once users touched it. He pushed to 100% test coverage and later concluded that 80-90% is the best practice.
- Office hours skill: simulates a YC conversation. How do you know people want this? Who is it for? What does it do? What is the impact? He still uses it for new products and features.
- CEO plan (first called the "mega plan"), built with meta prompting. It channels Brian Chesky's 10-star experience exercise: go from a 3-star hotel experience up through 6, 7, 8 stars and beyond. It also asks for the 10x check: what is more ambitious and delivers 10x more value for only 2x the effort.
- He describes himself as an "ADHD CEO" who loves potential, and says those two sentences unlock a lot.

chunks.heading: His daily workflow and the QA browser
chunks.text:
- He runs Conductor with many parallel agents. He says he dropped 13 PRs in 48 hours by queuing ideas, planning in plan mode with the CEO and eng skills, then approving.
- Bottleneck: about 15 features piled up waiting for him to test them by hand, even after unit, integration, and end-to-end tests passed.
- The Claude in Chrome MCP took 2-3 seconds per turn, too slow for QA. He told Claude to wrap Microsoft's Playwright instead. That became `browse`, a long-lived HTTP daemon with about 70 commands as a CLI.
- The QA skill is `browse` plus a prompt: look at what changed on this branch, and if there is UI or data mutation, test it in the browser. He says it blew his mind: "Mini AGI is already here."
- His plan order: office hours, CEO review, design review if there is UI, developer experience review if developers will use it, eng review, then Codex.

chunks.heading: Using Codex as a second opinion
chunks.text:
- A YC alum told him many people prefer Codex. His view: Claude Code is ideal for the ADHD CEO, but Claude models "are not the smartest." For crazier problems you need "the 200 IQ nearly non-verbal CEO."
- The `/codex` skill takes the plan (or the implemented repo), runs Codex from the command line with a prompt to find all problems and bugs, and reports back to Claude Code. He then works through the feedback. He later added `/claude` so Codex users can bring Claude in briefly.
- G Stack leans heavily on ask-user-question. He argues the human must supply understanding of what to build, and he doubts software will be made with the human fully out of the loop. "I never want to be entirely out of the loop."

chunks.heading: Thin harness, fat skills
chunks.text:
- The name came from Pete Koomen. Companies keep rebuilding the harness, which is the core loop that takes user input, calls the LLM, and runs tool calls. Garry says to use the best existing harness (such as Claude Code) and spend time on the markdown instead.
- Test for markdown: if you were an event planner writing a checklist for the next person to throw a wedding, what would you write in plain English? That goes in markdown. Real actions, like calling 20 venues, go through deterministic code (for example, a Twilio call).
- Common failure he sees: people put things that belong in markdown into code. Code is brittle and does not understand special cases or who you are. LLMs have latent space and can handle general cases.
- Skill for the engineer: decide how much lives in LLM land and how much in code land. Then unit test each piece, then test the integration. Untested code with real users is "10x worse" than human-written code.
- He says markdown is effectively code compiled differently, and he no longer uses Visual Studio.

chunks.heading: OpenClaw, G Brain, and personal AI
chunks.text:
- He compares OpenClaw to a Ferrari: exhilarating, but "you better be a mechanic." It can break down at the worst time and you fix it yourself. Setup took roughly 2-3 hours and $500-$1,000 in tokens and cloud for a technical person. He calls this the Homebrew Computer Club / Apple 1 moment.
- G Brain started when he realized his markdown context repo was only searched with grep, which wasted context. After Karpathy's post on LLM wikis, he used what he learned building Garry's List (vector embeddings, hybrid RRF, chunking) and asked an agent to extract that code. He chose Postgres with pgvector and built a full RAG system for his OpenClaw.
- His split now: about 50-60% of building time is in Claude Code, about half is through OpenClaw, and most of his time is on G Brain.
- Open source: he says "we're entering the golden age of open source." You can point an agent at your own repo and tell it to extract and reuse the proven parts.
- His big prediction: within about a year, everyone will have a personal AI. The choice is owning your data, integrations, and prompts, or living in a corporate-controlled feed. "Will you have control over your own tools or will your tools have control over you?" He says if you don't write your own prompts, you sit "below the API line" for a PM or developer who won't understand your needs.

chunks.heading: Lines of code, and why the 400x claim holds
chunks.text:
- He drew criticism for saying he coded at 100x his 2013 rate. After stripping to logical lines of code with a published tool, the figure rose to 400x.
- Agent output was trimmed slightly by the logical-line count. The surprise was that his own 2013 output dropped by about 70%.
- His point: humans can pad lines of code, but an agent isn't optimizing for the metric. It may build the wrong thing if you steer badly, but it isn't padding.
- Per industry literature, a professional engineer's tested, production-ready output is about 30-50 lines a day. He says his own was about 14, part-time.
- He admits he should have explained this earlier instead of trolling. He says the people attacking the metric are the ones with taste and technical skill who would benefit most from trying it: "All someone has to do is believe."
- Caveat he gave: the same model feels different across harnesses. His OpenClaw agent fails on moderately complex programming tasks that Claude Code handles, so he switches back to Claude Code for them.

chunks.heading: Time scarcity and mindset
chunks.text:
- Asked whether a full-time CEO job helped, he said his time is scarce, which forced him to automate everything. He called himself "in a crazy rush."
- He frames token maxing as borrowing machine time: "You could have infinite time by borrowing the time from the machines." He says he can be a time billionaire this way, serving YC and builders and the causes he cares about.
- Seeing Boris Cherny say his team writes no code showed him it was possible: "we have the same prompt. We have the same MacBook Pro."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan lists six skills that raise a founder's odds: engineering, product, design, sales and marketing, finance, and management and leadership. Go deep in one or two, stay broad in the rest so you can hire and work with experts, and fill the gaps with a team. Skills make startup risk more calculated, not deterministic.

chunks.heading: Skills are leverage, and leverage attracts people
chunks.text: Garry lists six skills a future founder can build before starting: engineering, product, design, sales and marketing, finance, and management and leadership. He says the more of them a founder has, the likelier the startup is to succeed. He stresses that none of them is required: "Starting a start-up isn't deterministic like that." Some people with few of these skills succeed, and some with all of them fail. The skills make the risk "a more calculated risk."

chunks.heading: Why breadth attracts cofounders and employees
chunks.text:
- People want to join a rocket ship taking off and avoid anything that will fail without them. Founders therefore "repel people when we need them the most" and attract them when they have other options.
- The more of the six skills a founder has, the more high-quality cofounders and employees they attract.
- His rule: be deep in one or two areas and "broad enough to be dangerous" in the rest. Breadth lets a founder tell who is actually good in each function and work with the best people in it.
- Early in a career, find which skills you are particularly good at and enjoy, but still learn the others. Strength in your own area makes you complementary to the rest of the team.

chunks.heading: Engineering: technology as the ultimate moat
chunks.text:
- Garry says technology "remains the key leverage in this world. It's the ultimate moat." His example is PageRank, which protects something worth billions because nobody can walk in and take it without building it first.
- A computer science degree isn't required but helps. Top CS schools remain the gold standard.
- For a non-technical founder looking for a technical cofounder, he advises learning enough to be dangerous. Most people searching for technical cofounders don't try to understand the craft. A founder who builds a good but not perfect first version stands out from that sea of non-technical applicants and gets the ball rolling.
- Ways to learn online: Codecademy, Insight Fellows (for scientists moving into data science and data engineering), and Career Karma, a YC startup that helps people find the right bootcamp or decide whether the bootcamp path fits.

chunks.heading: Product: a continuous process, learned by shipping
chunks.text:
- Product is knowing what to build and for whom. Garry cites Suhail Doshi: it is running the process "on a machine to continually find and refine product market fit. This isn't a one time thing."
- There is no obvious route to becoming a good product person except practicing. His top recommendation is side projects.
- The practice loop: build something, release it to users, and see whether they stick. Then talk to users about why they did or didn't take to it: did it solve their problem, and what were their hangups?

chunks.heading: Design: interaction design, visual design and taste
chunks.text:
- Design has two parts: interaction design (UX, how it works) and visual design (how it looks).
- Visual design can be cultivated like drawing or painting. Doing it yourself isn't required but gives faster iteration, and it helps most for consumer products.
- Taste matters more than execution. It means knowing whether a design fits the aesthetic and mood, speaks to the customer, and conveys the right level of quality. Garry says it is important particularly for consumer, "but these days, for all businesses."
- He calls interaction design "the meat of design." It is closest to product and moves from who it's for and what problem it solves to how. Questions it answers:
  - Where do the buttons go and what do they say?
  - What copy around the pages gets people through something complicated?
  - How is a complex multi-step process broken into manageable pieces?
  - How does the user know where they are and where they want to go?
- Recommended learning: Steve Krug's *Don't Make Me Think*, and his own two-hour Y Combinator Startup School talk on YouTube.

chunks.heading: Sales, marketing and brand
chunks.text:
- Garry quotes Ryan Peterson of Flexport: "Sales is the most underrated profession."
- He cites cofounder Alexis Ohanian: everybody is a brand, and a brand's ability to capture attention has never mattered more.
- Brand is important because "every business today is a meme," and it has never been easier for a startup to reach exactly the people who have the problem.
- Being able to sell and get in front of people is "super key."
- Engineering, product, sales and marketing are the key to getting product market fit.

chunks.heading: Finance: essential once you go from zero to one
chunks.text:
- Finance isn't very important at the outset, but financial literacy becomes "absolutely essential" after zero to one.
- He cites Matt MacInnis of Rippling: finance helps you figure out how to grow repeatedly and how well you're doing. "Every business in the world is either growing or dying," and without metrics you can't tell which.
- Finance and budgeting make sense of decisions such as:
  - Should you hire that executive and let them build a team?
  - Should you invest in that new office?
  - When do you get paid back, and does it make economic sense?

chunks.heading: Management and leadership
chunks.text:
- Leadership is getting people to do things, sometimes without authority, first "by example." Garry rejects the idea that leadership is being stern. He quotes Harvard professor Barbara Kellerman: "Followers are more important to leaders than leaders are to followers."
- Leading from empathy builds a more connected team that can weather more storms and make better decisions together.
- Beyond empathy, leaders must hold people accountable. That means crucial, hard conversations about what went wrong, as constructive as possible, while making clear that the bad thing can't continue.
- How to practice: in school, take leadership roles that run programs and coordinate people (a sport, a club). At work, take on projects that require coordination with many people and drive toward a numerical outcome, such as increasing sales by X percent or creating a set amount of value.
- Recommended book: *How to Win Friends and Influence People*. Despite the cheesy title, he says it applies skills needed across the whole gamut, so reading it improves leadership and the other skills too.

chunks.heading: Teams cover what one person cannot
chunks.text:
- Getting good at even one or two of these skills takes a lifetime or two. One person can realistically be great at only one or two.
- A startup that matters needs a team that is great at all of them. Putting lifetimes of experience in one room is the process of building a startup team.
- Founders are "the speck of dust that forms the crystalline structure that actually solves a real problem," which is why teams are crucial.
- Having all the right skills is still no guarantee of finding the right idea or building the right team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A conversation with Gobble founder Ooshma Garg, where Garry (a board member) frames what to do when a flailing competitor's IPO kills your fundraising: test whether you're already profitable. Covers proprietary IP for retention, cohort retention as the key health metric, and why founders should try profitability before selling or shutting down.

chunks.heading: Default alive: Garry's lesson from Gobble's pivot to profit
chunks.text:
Garry (a Gobble board member) describes how Ooshma Garg took Gobble from burning over $1M a month to earning nearly that much in profit, with a global pandemic going on, after a failed Series C.

- Gobble's overfunded competitor Blue Apron had a badly underperforming IPO. Garry says it damaged the whole meal kit market.
- Gobble could not close a Series C. Garry lists the four options Ooshma faced: shut down, recap, sell (asset sale, customer list sale or acquihire), or turn the company around and operate profitably.
- Garry notes that most founders end up with one of the first three. Ooshma chose the fourth, profitability, after reading her retention cohorts and cutting marketing spend.
- Garry says the result was that "we basically like raised a series C of millions of dollars in free cash ourselves" without diluting the company.
- His takeaway: "you can go profitable, or at least you can try", and "it's a very important tool for the tool belt".

chunks.heading: Markets are voting machines early and weighing machines later
chunks.text:
Garry argues that early-stage startups live and die by popularity, and later by fundamentals.

- "The game is a popularity contest early. It's basically a voting machine early, and then later, it becomes a weighing machine."
- The weighing questions he names are: what kind of business have you built, what are the metrics, and does it throw off money?
- With Gobble, the market "voted against" the meal kit category, even though insiders could see from the competitive numbers that Blue Apron was not executing as well as it could.
- Capital raising is "somewhat divorced" from having the best product or service.
- Because the Series C partners could not bring the rest of the firms over the hump in an out-of-favor category, being able to generate your own cash gives a company leverage that a sale or recap does not.

chunks.heading: Cohort retention is the best health check, and it takes time to read
chunks.text:
Garry calls cohort retention "one of the most important tools for every founder" because it shows the health of the business as a brand and a going concern.

- Plot customers who bought in month zero. The curve starts at 100% and drops each month.
- The best, enduring brands have an asymptote that "stretches into infinity".
- He ties this to valuation: the price of equity is the discounted future cash flows of the business, so knowing your retention cohorts tells you whether the company is actually valuable.
- Founders often cannot tell early. It can take six months, nine months or years to see what kind of business you have ("10-year overnight success", 2011 to 2020).
- Ooshma modeled scenarios before cutting marketing: if marketing stopped, would 20%, 40%, 50% or 60% of users remain in six months, and what would they do in each case? A vast majority stayed, which she called the most exciting validation in 10 years.

chunks.heading: Digital ad spend: marginal customers get worse, and "turn off marketing" is often a lie
chunks.text:
Garry explains the demand generation dynamics behind Gobble's turnaround.

- Digital marketing (Facebook and Google ads, direct mail, email marketing and other tools) has depth. The first customers are well targeted, sticky, high LTV and cheap to acquire. As you chase more marginal customers, they get worse, especially with a huge amount of capital funneled in.
- If you need to show 3x or 5x growth a year, "you could probably do it by burning a mountain of cash."
- Founders have a growth knob: grow faster and burn more, or grow slower and more sustainably. Even 50% a year growth with real cash generation can be a great business.
- Ooshma's warning, which Garry endorses in discussion: "one of the biggest lies that startups tell themselves and their boards is that they can turn off marketing and be profitable." Near-cancerous marketing growth can obscure cohorts and long-term retention while you just refill a bucket.
- The test: if you turned the marketing knob off, are you already profitable underneath the extra spend? Be honest about it, especially in an environment like a pandemic.

chunks.heading: Garry's Posterous regret: never trying to charge
chunks.text:
Garry uses his own startup, Posterous, as the counterexample.

- Posterous had tens of millions of uniques a month and close to a million regular posters.
- If even a small percentage had paid $5 a month, he says the company would have been "wildly profitable" on a base of five or 10 engineers.
- Nearly all the market value created came from the initial seed round. Seed investors, common shareholders, co-founders and the team did fine, but he doesn't think the Series A or B investors made much money.
- He attributes this to not being cash efficient and never charging money, and calls it "one of the biggest regrets I have as a founder."
- Lesson: you can try going profitable, and most founders never even try.

chunks.heading: Why Gobble's product is defensible: proprietary food IP
chunks.text:
Garry backs the product thesis that made Gobble's retention work.

- Typical meal kits gave you a tomato or an onion plus an instruction card, which Garry calls the "onion in a box" model, and took about an hour to make.
- Gobble's approach is better, faster and cheaper: proprietary sauces and recipes that cut prep time by 30 to 50 minutes. Garry says customers will happily pay an extra dollar or $2 a meal for that.
- Ooshma's version: "the secret sauce is the sauce". Gobble has 2,000 proprietary SKUs and sauces, and you can't recreate a Gobble recipe at the grocery store. Convenience makes it sticky and proprietary flavor makes it stickier.
- Garry's framing is that this contrasts with competitors using commodity ingredients, where deal hunters switch between boxes weekly and the cost of maintaining the customer base is far higher.
- Shipping boxes via USPS, FedEx or UPS also helped contribution margin per box, since multiple nights of food go in one box instead of one delivery per night.

chunks.heading: Finding other founders for real talk
chunks.text:
In closing, Garry reinforces Ooshma's advice for her 22-year-old self.

- The hardest startup problems are the unknown unknowns, so have closed-door conversations with founders a step or two ahead of you or in your industry.
- Startup culture pushes a "killing it" posture at conferences and VC dinners.
- Garry's advice: find the tribe of people you can be real with. "If you don't find that, then this whole thing becomes 10 times harder."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using Ignaz Semmelweis, who cut maternal deaths with handwashing but died in an asylum, Garry lays out five lessons for founders pushing new ideas against resistance. The core point: a breakthrough is only half the work; communicating it, persistently and professionally, is the other half.

chunks.heading: Garry's framing: the Semmelweis reflex and the cost of changing the world
chunks.text:
- Garry opens with Ignaz Semmelweis, the first doctor to find that handwashing saved mothers' lives, as a warning about what happens to people who make something new.
- He names the "Semmelweis reflex": people reject anything that challenges them out of hand. His position is that anyone building something that "will push forward humanity and break the existing status quo will face incredible pressure."
- "Great change comes at a great cost... it doesn't come for free." Breakthroughs mishandled "have the potential to break us."
- His answer is that true change takes perseverance, fundamental focus, and then communicating the breakthrough.
- He lists five mistakes Semmelweis made so founders can avoid them (and the asylum). Garry made the video in about 3 hours, aiming for one video a week to help future founders and makers reach the next stage.

chunks.heading: The Semmelweis case: a breakthrough that was not adopted
chunks.text:
- Semmelweis was born in 1818 in the Kingdom of Hungary and worked at a Viennese hospital where maternal mortality ran as high as 18%. Women begged not to be admitted.
- At 29 he required handwashing with chlorinated lime between autopsy work and patient examinations. The death rate went from 18.3% in April 1847 to 2.2% in June and to zero in August of that year.
- The theory was almost completely rejected. Doctors believed in miasma theory (bad air), and many felt that being gentlemen meant their hands could not be unclean. Many also misread him as only saying the fever was contagious, missing the point that organic dead tissue transmitted disease.
- He died in an asylum at 47 (1865), two weeks after being subdued by guards when he tried to escape, from a wound on his hand. Germ theory took about 20 more years to be widely accepted.

chunks.heading: Lesson 1: Speak for yourself
chunks.text:
- Semmelweis never published on his own or directly addressed the confusion in the journals. His students wrote the lectures and papers for him.
- Garry's rule: "Don't expect others to speak for you." Data cannot speak for itself; "without you, the data is mute."
- In the 1800s you had letters and journals. Today things move overnight.
- Tactic: practice writing and social media now, and get in the habit of communicating with strangers on the internet. At critical moments later in your career, that skill will matter.

chunks.heading: Lesson 2: Persevere and don't ragequit
chunks.text:
- Semmelweis's boss, Chief Resident Johann Klein, did not want to keep him on for political reasons. He fought a little, then quit one day and never came back.
- Garry admits this has happened to him in his own career. Things get heated, plans go wrong, promises are not honored.
- His guidance: take a breath, think about the people around you and what you actually want from the situation. He has "yet to meet a person who has ever told me they wish they were more rash when making a hard decision, like where to work."
- You still have to decide, but "feel the emotions, but be sure it's the rational part of you doing it."

chunks.heading: Lesson 3: Speak truth when you know you're right
chunks.text:
- At 29, unestablished, Semmelweis was not taken seriously by heads of maternity hospitals and professors. They were also structurally wrong: no scientific understanding, and a prevailing belief in miasma.
- Garry's lesson: "the establishment is often absolutely wrong." Continuing to say what you know to be right is "an act of courage."
- The condition: you must have the data and the conviction to back it up. "Just because people say things are so does not make it so."

chunks.heading: Lesson 4: When they go low, we go high
chunks.text:
- By 1861 Semmelweis was writing letters full of bitterness and desperation, and contemporaries concluded he was losing his grip on reality.
- Garry's rule: no matter how wrong your haters are, don't stoop to their level. Quoting Michelle Obama: "When they go low, we go high."
- How you address disagreement matters. The road is long and hard, but if you resort to the bad or worse arguments of your adversary, "nobody wins, especially not you."

chunks.heading: Lesson 5: The breakthrough is only half the work
chunks.text:
- Garry contrasts Semmelweis with Louis Pasteur, who overcame the establishment with data and engaged the debate at the right level so he could change minds.
- His bottom line: "The breakthrough is only half of the work. The other half is spreading it to the rest of the world."
- Innovations must be spread and communicated effectively to have any impact on the world.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues that pointing at a good idea isn't enough; founders must stress-test who they build for, whether it's feasible, and what unfair advantage they hold. He uses Standard Cognition and Posterous to show that a technology or insight no one else has can be the moat that justifies a startup existing.

chunks.heading: Why you, why now: stress-testing a startup idea
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues that pointing at a good idea is not enough. In his words, "You can't just point at the moon, you've got to build the goddamn spaceship." Before committing to an idea, a founder has to show an advantage that other people don't have. He sums that up as two questions: why me, and why now.

chunks.heading: The hard questions Garry asks before building
chunks.text:
He splits the exercise into two steps: define the problem, then define how you'll solve it.

**Define the problem:**
- Who am I building for?
- Who is my audience?
- What problem do they have?

**Define the solution:**
- Is my solution possible and feasible?
- How much will it cost?
- What technology exists today, and how much of it can I use? Is it open source or licensable?
- Is there published research describing a new method?
- What are the alternatives? How do people solve this today?
- Who else has tried this, and what went wrong with their solution?

**Then the advantage:**
- Why now?
- What do I have that nobody else has?
- Is it technology, or something that stops others from just copying me?

chunks.heading: The kinds of moat Garry looks for
chunks.text:
- **Pure technology.** He calls it "often actually the best moat of all."
- **Customer relationships.** Landing an early lighthouse customer who unlocks a whole industry. Example: Envoy, the visitor sign-in and check-in product, started by selling Airbnb as one of its first 10 clients.
- **A better go-to-market.**
- **Content or some other relationship.**
- **Something you do that nobody else does.** He asks founders to name it explicitly.

A moat that holds up is what makes the company protectable.

chunks.heading: What weak answers mean, and what to do with them
chunks.text:
Honest answers sometimes expose too many "no"s. Garry's examples of weak spots:
- The audience is too small.
- The problem isn't felt severely enough for anyone to fix it.
- It can't be built with today's technology.
- It can be built, but too expensively for buyers to pay.
- Obvious alternatives are just as good or cheaper, or the current way of solving it is "basically fine."
- You have no advantage over others trying to build it.

He calls this "the moment of maximum disillusionment," when people start thinking they shouldn't work on the idea. His reframe: the questions also show exactly what you need to work on as a founder. The weak answers become your to-do list.

chunks.heading: Technology as the moat for technical founders
chunks.text:
For a technologist, using technology as the moat is "the bread and butter." Garry says great engineers can find a way to be much better, cheaper or faster than all the alternatives.

His example is Standard Cognition, which has a pure technology moat:
- It put into practice a new method that had never been commercialized.
- As a result it has something "even Amazon cannot duplicate."
- It can offer cashierless checkout at possibly 1/10 to 1/100 the cost of the state of the art.

chunks.heading: Posterous (2008): a simple technical insight as the moat
chunks.text:
Garry's own startup, Posterous, was a dead-simple blogging-by-email platform. Users emailed one address, post@posterous.com, and it published.

- On day one it did something people thought wasn't possible. The common belief was that this couldn't be done securely, which is why other services used addresses like "secretpassword123@flickr.com."
- The solution was not machine learning. "Frankly, it was IF statements." If Posterous had received email from you before, it asked you to confirm it. Once confirmed, that sender's path was treated as safe. This anti-spoofing approach came from his co-founder, Sachin Agarwal.
- Because competitors couldn't work out what Posterous had, nobody copied them right away. They became a top 200 site without "fending off a thousand other copycats."
- The anti-spoofing limitation was enough of a moat to reach their first hundreds of thousands of users.

His lesson: "Without that moat, without that reason to be, without that thing that other people did not have, we didn't have a good reason to exist."

chunks.heading: The takeaway
chunks.text: Garry says there isn't just one way to get a moat, but it's prudent to ask: "Why me? What do I have that nobody else has?" His closing rule: "if that answers nothing, you've got to keep working."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan argues founders fail by not trying enough distinct hypotheses, so they should explicitly timebox each product-market hypothesis (a set of people plus a problem) and move on. He breaks failure into acquisition problems and not-a-real-problem, and lists levers for retention and pilot expansion.

chunks.heading: Why founders get stuck: too few tries
chunks.text:
Garry's core idea is that a founder has a finite number of tries, and timeboxing each try lets you make more of them. He says founders mostly fail because they don't try enough things, and they don't try enough things because they keep repeating the same thing and won't drop a hypothesis that time has proven false.

- He defines a product-market hypothesis as two parts: a set of **people** you can reach, and a **problem** to solve for those specific people. One hypothesis is one possible try.
- He quotes Alcoholics Anonymous: "Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again, and expecting different results."
- He pushes back on the hustle idea of never giving up, quoting W. C. Fields: "If at first you don't succeed, try, try again. Then quit. It's no use being a damn fool about it."
- He says new insights are the hardest thing to come by. Ideas multiply execution, and good ideas are rare. A bad idea is a zero that cancels perfect execution.
- He sees very talented founders get stuck here. They have great engineering, product and marketing, yet it can't be sold, the numbers don't go up and there's no growth.

chunks.heading: The two failure cases, in order
chunks.text:
Garry names two common failure cases and says the order matters:

- **A:** It's a real problem, but you can't get people to know about it and use it.
- **B:** It's not a real problem.

This ordering implies a specific system for startup need-finding. Test acquisition first, because failing to reach people looks the same as having no demand until you've tried enough channels.

chunks.heading: Stage one: getting users with many channel experiments
chunks.text:
In office hours with very early-stage startups, most of the focus is on how to get the product in front of people. Garry cites Ben Horowitz: "there are no silver bullets, only lead ones."

- Channels to try:
  - content marketing
  - SEM
  - SEO
  - events
  - webinars
  - partnerships
  - street teams
  - Craigslist
  - stealing users from other platforms
- Other obvious ones he lists: enterprise sales, cold emails, searching for warm introductions, LinkedIn spelunking, and selling through existing platforms.
- His advice is to "get creative."
- The most common failure is getting stuck on one or two tactics and doing more of what doesn't work.
- What success looks like:
  1. Try one thing and it works.
  2. Double down and it works again.
  3. Keep going until you establish a new normal, a steady state much bigger than where you started.
  4. That is scalable growth, and it is product-market fit.

chunks.heading: Stage two: keeping users (retention and the pile of pilots)
chunks.text:
Once you have an initial go-to-market, Garry says the real struggle begins: keeping the users.

- He has funded companies with incredible early traction followed by massive churn, and that still doesn't work.
- Another failure mode is pilots that don't expand. He calls this the **pile of pilots** problem, a well-known issue in digital health and biotech. You can get a pile of pilots that never expand.
- The consequence he gives: "you have a seed company that cannot raise at Series A."
- What's required is expansion and net retention. If you can't get them, he says this isn't something people want.

chunks.heading: What to do when users don't stick
chunks.text:
Garry lists four moves, each of which counts as a whole new try:

1. **Improve the product.** Go directly to the people using it and ask, "Why aren't you using it?" Solve those problems and you get another shot.
2. **Change who you're solving the problem for.** Go back to the product-market hypothesis and change the people.
3. **Change the price point.**
4. **Pick a different problem to solve.** A different set of people has different needs, which you may be able to fill with better software.

chunks.heading: How to timebox a hypothesis
chunks.text:
Garry's tool is to explicitly set how much time you'll spend on any given hypothesis, and then quit when it's up.

- You need enough time to know either way, and he describes the risk on both sides:
  - **Too short:** you may give up on something that could have worked.
  - **Too long:** you waste time you'll never get back, and burn critical runway in ways that hurt you fundamentally.
- When you timebox, you set aside a specific amount of time for this market and problem, then move on to the next lead bullet.
- His promise: if you're a great team doing the right things and you timebox, keep trying new things and keep "firing new lead bullets," "you can and will find product market fit."
- If it's not something people want, you have to do something else.
- Timeboxing is a way to be very conscious of how long you spend on any given problem.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry and Andrew Lee lay out the three kinds of acquisition (strategic, revenue, talent), when to consider selling, and how to run an M&A process. Key lessons: companies are bought not sold, build a BATNA, go through the product owner instead of corp dev, and never treat M&A like a VC fundraise.

chunks.heading: Selling a startup: the three types of acquirer
chunks.text:
Garry and his partner Andrew Lee split acquisitions into three types, ordered from highest to lowest purchase price. Garry's own exit: Posterous sold to Twitter for $20M.

- **Strategic threat:** the company threatens an incumbent's business. Example: YouTube bought by Google for about a billion dollars, with Viacom also bidding because it saw YouTube as a real threat.
- **Revenue generating:** the buyer expects to earn more than it pays. Example: Guitar Hero bought by Activision for about $100 million, because the CEO knew marketing spend would return more than the price.
- **Team and talent:** the buyer wants the tech or people. Example: Salesforce buying Quip for Brett's tech and talent.
- Garry's framing: "companies are bought, they are not sold." A bigger company has something to protect, such as a moat or a new business line, and goes out to buy.
- Most of the companies they back are meant to be strategic threats, so they either get bought or IPO and "crush their competition."

chunks.heading: Why Garry actually sold Posterous (and why founders really sell)
chunks.text:
- Garry is blunt that most founders sell because the company is in trouble: "We were out of money... You made something good and then you're not growing. You can't raise more money. The company's going to die."
- The conundrum: buyers approach when you are growing and don't need anyone, which is the best time to sell.
- Posterous grew very fast for two years. Growth stopped when Instagram launched. Early iOS photo apps were primitive, so email was the easiest way to get photos off a phone, and Posterous grew on that new behavior.
- Garry's read on the flatline: "that's how we knew that we weren't reaching, we weren't continuing to scale product market fit."
- The exit: employees and investors made money and the team learned the craft, though Garry says he wanted to build for a billion people and didn't get there.
- Without another network to grow off, there was no virality.

chunks.heading: When to consider M&A: stage and risk
chunks.text:
- Garry's plan A is always to build toward product-market fit, because the upside of a great company is "so obvious and so tantalizing."
- Pre-Series A, without product-market fit, there is nothing to sell except the team. That is acqui-hire territory, and he notes founders could just take jobs at big tech companies instead. Focus on product and market.
- Start thinking about M&A when managing risk. Every time you need to raise and you are not default alive, "the future of your company is not in your hands." He links Paul Graham's essay on default alive vs. default dead.
- Selling is trading growth for safety. At each stage you have built a team, product, customers, recurring revenue, sometimes negative churn. Any of these is valuable to someone else.
- His test: if you think you will run out of gas before the next gas station, or the station may be closed to you, consider M&A.
- Take care of employees, investors and yourselves: "It's okay to sell your business along the way, actually."
- Andrew adds that it is a personal decision that hurts, and founders feel like frauds or lose confidence.

chunks.heading: Four questions to ask before deciding (from Atul Gawande's "Being Mortal")
chunks.text:
Initialized uses these end-of-life-care questions with founders:

1. **What is your understanding of the situation and its impact?** Runway, market landscape and similar factors.
2. **What are your hopes and fears?** You may still want your vision, and teaming up with someone else may be how you get there.
3. **What tradeoffs will you make, and not make?** Salary, the work itself, the people around you, location.
4. **What is the course of action?** The most important one; it turns the answers into a plan.

chunks.heading: Level-setting before you go to market
chunks.text:
- Know your metrics: ARR, runway, burn, and debt. Debt "turns out to actually be a really big issue."
- Talk through where the co-founders and leadership stand.
- Watch for brilliant jerks. Garry agrees "that happens," and Andrew says it can kill companies and sometimes holds up a deal.
- Take the employee temperature, especially if you are aiming for a talent and tech acquisition.

chunks.heading: How to run a sale
chunks.text:
- **Start with strategic partnerships**, especially in enterprise. It is hard to sell to a larger company that can't tell you apart from a competitor. Make them a customer or partner to build trust.
- **Go through product, not corp dev.** Find whoever runs the line-item budget or the relevant team. That person is your champion against decision-makers who don't want to buy.
- **Extend runway** by pulling forward sales and cutting burn. If you have to lay people off: "cut quickly, cut deeply."
- **Interview leadership first.** Talent acquirers will want to interview your employees. Do that only once real offers are on the table, because it is disruptive and scary to non-founders, who aren't built for this risk.
- **Check references and build a BATNA.** Ask the buyer about their previous acquisitions and speak to those founders or CEOs. In parallel, keep alternatives alive: a fundraise, higher revenue and lower costs, and competing offers from other acquirers.

chunks.heading: The #1 deal killer: treating M&A like a VC fundraise
chunks.text:
- Garry says M&A deals most often die because founders run them like another fundraising process.
- Corp dev and VCs have different motivations, a principal-agent problem. What gets a junior VC promoted differs from what gets a corp dev person promoted.
- Corp dev wants to get the deal done but not at any price. Their incentive is not overpaying.
- VCs often have groupthink: more bidders makes them more rabid to win, especially with a 100x on the other end. That dynamic doesn't exist in corp dev.
- Without a BATNA, corp dev can be "extremely unscrupulous." Garry: "Deals fall through. Always maintain some sort of BATNA." Their entire job is to bring the price down.
- Andrew adds that corp dev often gets a bonus for coming in under their approved amount. Small deals go smoothly because they are all upside, and very large deals also close because they are existential strategic threats.

chunks.heading: Andrew's JamLegend sale and how they chose a buyer
chunks.text:
- JamLegend was wedded to music games. It grew virally (C-Net Webware 100, Alexa 100) then flatlined.
- Zynga was doing "fast follows," copying rising games within a month or two and hiring talent. Production costs were rising, so staying independent meant raising a significant round.
- There was no offer on the table at first. The choice was whether to talk to people who had asked to acquire them.
- They met several companies, got multiple offers, and chose Zynga because it fit what they cared about: a place for everyone on the team and a return for investors. The Zynga IPO was expected in a year or two.
- Garry's close: as long as you build something valuable, even if it doesn't go to plan, there is a way forward that lets you take care of everyone around you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan's 2014 advice to YC applicants covers who should apply, how to pick a problem, team composition, writing clearly, getting feedback and not waiting for permission. The core lessons apply to any early startup: solve a real problem or do it right, pair a builder with a hustler, and write in plain English.

chunks.heading: Pre-A is the right window, and YC multiplies progress
chunks.text:
Garry says the most common question he gets is whether a team is too early or too late for YC. His answer is that YC can help any company before its Series A.

- Teams range from fresh college grads with an early prototype to companies that already raised a seed round and have revenue and employees.
- He cites Crowdtilt and Thalmic Labs as some of the best-performing YC companies, and both came in having already raised seed rounds. They did so well during YC that they raised competitive Series A and later rounds right out of demo day.
- His framing: "It turns out to be a multiplier on success."
- For first-time money seekers, he says this is not a summer program or an internship. You are committing to build a serious business and telling investors you will return their money plus a healthy return. "It's not a grant."
- His reason for doing startups: to create massive value and reward yourself and the people who help create it.

chunks.heading: Hair on fire problem, or do it right
chunks.text:
Garry argues technology creates no value by itself. It only matters as a way to solve people's problems. Great hackers get caught up in the technology and forget this.

He repeats Paul Buchheit's two categories of successful startup ideas:
- They solve a "hair on fire" problem that has never been solved before.
- Or they solve a problem that already has solutions, but do it so much better that they are "done right."

How to pitch each:
- **Hair on fire:** state how bad the problem is. How do you know it exists, who has it, and how specifically have you solved it? A new problem is an uphill battle just to let people know you exist, so show you can get people to notice you.
- **Crowded space:** be very clear about how your solution is unique. "It's not OK to do exactly the same thing." Explain what you have figured out that nobody else has.

His rule of thumb: "If you're new, focus on explaining what you are. If you're not new, focus on explaining how you're different. If you're neither of these types, you're doing it wrong."

chunks.heading: Founding team: builder and hustler
chunks.text:
Garry used to say a startup needed three roles (designer, engineer, hustler). He changed his mind after seeing evidence to the contrary, and now says the ideal team needs two: **builder** and **hustler**. Designer and engineer collapse into "builder." Some enterprise software companies don't need much design, but all tech startups need tech cofounders.

- He has seen teams of hustlers fail because they could not create any product on their own.
- He has seen teams of pure builders (amazing designer/engineers) fail because they could not get the product into users' hands.
- The roles don't have to map one person to one role. What matters is that the team is capable of both.
- If you lack a skill, find your most talented and trusted friends who have it and get them to join you.
- Be realistic about what you and your teammates are good at.
- On cofounders: "You are getting married to your cofounders." You are on a life raft in the ocean together and must work well together to survive.
- Starting without a strong team is "going to war without guns, ammo, training, or all of the above."

chunks.heading: Write clearly and concisely
chunks.text:
Garry says that over five years this became more obvious as examples piled up: the best startups are incredibly good at writing and communicating in as few words as possible.

- Paul Graham's lesson: if a founder can't express an idea clearly to others, the likeliest explanation is that the idea isn't clear to them either.
- He points applicants to PG's essays as the standard to aim for. Everything should be crisp, articulate and to the point.

His writing process:
- Write down every idea copiously and brainstorm to get it all out.
- Then edit. Group similar concepts next to each other.
- Edit mercilessly until no word can be removed without losing significant meaning.

The common pitfall is trying to sound professional. He says to use the plain English you would use to explain things to normal people with no special background. Sounding corporate or like a press release is "among the worst ways to communicate in the history of language." Writing should communicate, not get in the way.

His rule of thumb: does it sound like something you would say to a friend? If not, rewrite it.

chunks.heading: Get feedback from as many people as possible
chunks.text:
Garry advises getting as many trustworthy, intelligent eyes as possible on a written application. He says this holds for any application, because more reviewers help you flesh out concepts, spot weak links and strengthen your case.

- Ask your mentors.
- Email founders of YC companies, or founders of any company, for feedback.
- His reasoning: "We're here to help -- someone helped us."

chunks.heading: Keep building whether or not you get in
chunks.text: Garry's closing advice is to keep working on the startup no matter what the outcome is. He says you don't need anyone to give you a "permission slip" to create your own startup.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains why good startup ideas are rare and arise from technology, regulation, or macroeconomic shifts, so copycats are inevitable. Ideas only multiply execution; the response is to share loudly, own the problem space, and ship faster than copycats, who can only copy an older version of you.

chunks.heading: Why ideas get stolen, and why it matters less than founders fear
chunks.text:
Garry says it does happen: good ideas are rare enough that it is often easier to look at what already works and copy it. His mock example is the "brain rape" scene from Silicon Valley (VCs pumping a founder for details), which he calls extreme and not what to expect in the Valley. The real reasons are structural, not malicious.

- Ideas that actually work are "very, very rare."
- They appear when one of three things changes: technology, regulation, or a macroeconomic force.
- When that change hits, many people see the opening at once, so fast followers will often find the same idea independently.

chunks.heading: The three forces that make an idea possible
chunks.text:
Garry's checklist for why a startup can work now:

- **Technology:** The first iPhone needed battery tech, display tech, miniaturization, and software efficient enough to use far less memory. "Almost a perfect storm." Platforms stack: before Instagram could happen, you needed the iPhone.
- **Technology example from his portfolio:** Standard Cognition does cashierless checkout like Amazon Go but with no shelf sensors, cameras only. He says that can cut deployment cost by 10 to 100 times.
- **Regulation:** Telemedicine took the FDA putting out a letter saying a doctor in the loop, driven by software through a smartphone or browser, is "okay to do now." When regulation shifts, a wave of activity follows because something you could not do suddenly becomes allowed.
- **Macroeconomic forces:** Remote work is the example. San Francisco housing pushed cost of living so high that retaining software engineers became nearly impossible. These forces are bigger than any one person or company but enable whole new markets.

chunks.heading: Answer "why now" before anything else
chunks.text: Garry says answering the "why now" question is fundamental for anyone starting something new. If you can name which of the three forces unlocked your idea, you understand why the opening exists, and why others will see it too.

chunks.heading: The idea is only a multiplier on execution
chunks.text:
- Because workable startups are bounded by these specific forces, fast followers are inevitable.
- His conclusion: "the idea is only a multiplier on execution." Ideas are out there and everyone can pursue them.
- What distinguishes you at the end of the day is execution. He frames it as three questions: What is your product like? Is it actually what people need? Do people choose you over all possible alternatives?
- A great idea alone is not enough. To take advantage of it you have to "jam it down their throats," which means a lot of manual work and pure execution.

chunks.heading: Don't clam up: lean in when you have competition
chunks.text:
Garry calls this one of the most counterintuitive facts about bringing ideas to life in startup land.

- Many founders facing copycats or heavy competition freeze, get scared, and stop sharing the idea. He says that is "almost the exact opposite of what you need to do."
- With lots of competition, lean in harder. Become so deeply associated with the problem space, and the best solution for it, that you win.
- That association is how you crowd out competitors. "If you clam up, you're doing exactly the opposite of what you need to do to beat your competition."

chunks.heading: How to beat copycats: outrun them
chunks.text:
- Execute faster, go to market faster, and innovate ahead of everyone else.
- Then even people trying to copy you can only copy the version of you from six or nine months ago.
- His summary: "You can beat the copycats, but you've got to outrun them."
- He closes with Jeff Bezos on competition: the number one thing behind Amazon's success "by far" is obsessive focus on the customer rather than obsession over the competitor. Bezos says he can tell when other founders talk about customers but are really focused on competitors.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan uses the New Yorker's Spotify profile to show the anatomy of making something people want: a precisely defined broken problem, a measurable product bar (200 ms), proprietary tech that only needs to buy a 6-month head start, and a painful schlep that becomes the moat.

chunks.heading: Garry's starting point: a precise problem statement
chunks.text:
- Garry says the Spotify story shows what YC tries to help founders create: "something people want."
- He notes that "all of the great era-defining startups seem to start" with a simple problem statement: what was broken?
- For Spotify, the problem was piracy. Daniel Ek's framing (quoted by Garry): Napster was a "great consumer product, not a great business model," and "It's not like people want to be pirates. They just want a great experience."
- Garry's takeaway: Ek knew exactly what was broken, which is why he could sketch a better product than the thing people were stealing.

chunks.heading: Turn the product vision into one measurable standard
chunks.text:
- Spotify's product vision was that streaming should feel like the music is already on your hard drive. Ek's question was "What would it feel like?"
- He turned that feeling into a hard number: music starts in 200 milliseconds or less, about half an average blink, so people perceive no delay.
- Ek told his lead engineer Ludvig Strigeus: "I don't accept anything that isn't below two hundred milliseconds."
- Garry's point: because they knew how to measure success, the target was unambiguous. If streaming acts like local storage, you win.
- Pattern he draws out: pick the specific dimension on which your product must be better than the incumbent behavior (here, piracy), and make it testable.

chunks.heading: Hard technology that gets you off the ground
chunks.text:
- Strigeus first said "It can't be done. The Internet isn't built like that." Ek replied, "You have to figure it out."
- The solution was a faster streaming protocol plus a custom peer-to-peer network. They had a working prototype in four months.
- Garry splits the question in two:
  - Can it be done? Until those early prototypes, it hadn't been.
  - Can it be cloned? "As with almost anything software related, yes."
- He argues novel tech is "not an infinite defense, but it was enough of one for Spotify to get off the ground."
- The advantage doesn't need to last forever. It only needs to last long enough that competitors are copying your innovation from 6 months ago. Fast following can take that long, which keeps unoriginal competitors at bay while you "blaze ahead."

chunks.heading: The schlep is the moat
chunks.text:
- Ek assumed he could "pick up a global license" like buying from a corner store, and planned to launch in the U.S. and Europe together. In reality he had to negotiate with every copyright holder, a "herculean task."
- The labels initially weren't interested: Ek was an outsider, a Swedish techie, and the pitch was to co-opt the people who had been pirating their music.
- Ek's quote: "If anyone had told me going into this that it would be three years of crashing my head against the wall, I wouldn't have done it."
- Garry's lesson: if founders knew how much work these things would be, often they wouldn't do them (he links Paul Graham's essay "Schlep"). But those who do build "protectable long term enterprise value."
- Implication: the grind that deters others, like licensing, is itself the durable defense.

chunks.heading: Caveat: hindsight and building anyway
chunks.text:
- Garry stresses the analysis is done with 20/20 hindsight. In the moment, Ek, his cofounders and investors had no idea they'd be right.
- They figured they might be, so they built it.
- The framework in sum: name what is broken, define a measurable better experience, build the hard tech to hit it, and push through the schlep others avoid.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan analyzes how Hideo Kojima made Death Stranding to extract four habits of great creators: a real mission, making your own decisions instead of following surveys, knowing what to outsource versus do yourself (while collaborating well), and showmanship. He applies these lessons to founders and indie makers.

chunks.heading: Mission-first: build the product around a purpose
chunks.text:
- Garry says an auteur "clearly has a mission". Hideo Kojima's mission for Death Stranding is to be "nothing less than an actual cure for loneliness".
- Garry's reading: video gamers are "notoriously lonely people". Kojima aims at shut-ins such as Japan's Hikikomori, who sometimes interact with no one but delivery people.
- The game's design carries the mission. The player is Sam Porter Bridges, a porter who brings disconnected post-apocalyptic cities online by delivering food and medicine. Garry compares this to a DoorDash delivery person.
- Kojima's stated aim: players should feel there are others like them, and "use in the real world" what they learn in the game. Garry notes a player may spend 50 hours on it and come out "changed".
- Garry's takeaway: think about what effect you want to have in the world, then "orient your whole project around it".
- Norman Reedus, quoted by Garry: "It's not a kill 'em all game. It's a bring people together game."

chunks.heading: Make your own decisions instead of outsourcing them to surveys
chunks.text:
- Garry argues that once you have a direction, it is tempting to survey and pick the most popular, safe choice. An auteur does not do that.
- Example: Death Stranding art director Yoji Shinkawi says the focus is not on getting as much attention as possible. The team develops characters that are interesting and cool to them, rather than basing them on market research.
- Garry's claim: "When things get big, they get safe." Outsourcing decisions to a survey or quantitative thinking feels safer.
- He says an independent approach, whether an indie software maker or an indie game developer, often yields much better creative output.
- For something truly creative, he says you "just can't do it that way".

chunks.heading: Take action: know what to do yourself, what to delegate, what to outsource
chunks.text:
- Garry says you must delegate, but not everything. You have to hold on to some of the important stuff.
- Example: Kojima edited the launch trailer himself. He first builds the structure of what the trailer should convey (story, world, gameplay and "most importantly, what the message is"), then chooses a song.
- Standard practice is to outsource launch trailers to a film company. The source quotes a figure of 200 million, which Garry's editor note reads as yen (about $1.8 million USD), probably a translation slip.
- Kojima says he is likely the only game creator who edits his own trailer.
- Garry's takeaway: great founders and great auteurs know what they can outsource, what they can give to their team, and have an intuitive sense of the few things they must do themselves. "It's not everything, it's just a few things."

chunks.heading: Great auteurs collaborate: say "yes, and"
chunks.text:
- Garry warns against misreading auteurship as control-freak behavior: "Great auteurs are incredible at collaboration."
- Reedus contrasts directors who "short circuit" when you add to their scene with Kojima, who says "yes, and then let's add this" and keeps building on others' contributions. "His mind is always going forward."
- Garry's rule for every creative project: you need to listen, say yes, and incorporate other people's ideas. Only then can you collaboratively create something greater than you could individually.

chunks.heading: Showmanship sets the tone and expectations
chunks.text:
- Garry calls the right level of showmanship "really underrated".
- Example: the entrance to Kojima's studio is theatrical. Conan O'Brien's visit reaction was "Oh my God." Everyone enters the studio this way, not just celebrities.
- Why it matters, per Garry:
  - It sets the tone for newcomers, prospective hires and partners.
  - It sets expectations so the team and everyone around you treat the work as something that could be great and special.
  - It shows up in the office, the brand and the design.
- His line: "It takes a little bit of showmanship to do something no one else has ever done."

chunks.heading: Garry's four habits of auteurs (summary)
chunks.text:
- **Mission:** have one, and orient the whole project around the effect you want to have.
- **Make your own decisions:** don't rely on surveys or on what will be popular.
- **Take action:** know what you should do, what your team should do, and what to outsource.
- **Showmanship:** don't be afraid to be a showman when doing something nobody has done before.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan explains how big-corporate culture (busywork without results, cover-your-ass politics, buzzword-following) trains people in habits that fail in startups. The fix is relentless focus on concrete results, building product and talking to customers, and a founder culture reinforced by the people around you.

chunks.heading: Why big-company experience misleads founders
chunks.text: Garry argues that corporate culture is learned, and that its habits cause experienced founders and corporate-trained hires to fail at startups. Founder culture is learned too.

chunks.heading: Corporate work can look productive without producing results
chunks.text:
- Garry says big-company employees can "just do things that look like work that aren't," and nobody can tell.
- Customers are easy to get (sometimes trivial) with a large installed base, a sales force or a huge brand name.
