- Large protected revenue streams hide failure on the quarterly financials.
- Corporate founders aren't stupid. They're used to doing things and having something happen, with the wind at their backs.
- It is bewildering to work "really freaking hard" at something and get no results back, but it happens all the time.

chunks.heading: Startups have no air cover
chunks.text:
- "There's no air cover for startups. You don't have backup troops. It's just you versus the world."
- If the product or service sucks, the startup dies.
- You can't just look like you're doing stuff. You have to make the thing, almost entirely on your own.

chunks.heading: Cover-your-ass culture and credit-taking
chunks.text:
- In big organizations, working hard to no effect doesn't get you fired. Looking like a bozo or making your boss look bad does.
- Garry says the worst version is taking credit for what other people do, which he sees as correlated with people who climb high in organizations.
- This fails in a small startup because there's nowhere to hide. Someone has to do the work.
- Startups can develop cover-your-ass culture too. It is the founders' and CEO's job to keep people focused on what actually matters.
- Smaller teams blunt the toxic group dynamics.

chunks.heading: Buzzwords and trend-following fail in startups
chunks.text:
- In a corporation, if everyone is saying it, nobody can fault you. Latching onto the buzzword of the day (big data, Internet of Things, NoSQL) lets you blend in. If the big data initiative fails, "everyone else was doing it," so you won't get fired.
- Founders confuse this with a recipe: "We said all the right secret words! Why am I failing?" He says it was never about the words.
- Startups have to know what's coming and be right. A wrong market or a wrong read on what people want means the startup is toast.
- He isn't saying everything with a buzzword label fails. A big data startup, for example, must make life better for specific customers so they're willing to pay. "It has to make sense."

chunks.heading: Garry's Palantir mistake
chunks.text:
- At 23, he turned down being first engineer at Palantir (which he says is "now rumored to be worth $20 billion!"), even though Peter Thiel took him out to dinner to recruit him.
- He treated buzzwords as signal. In 2004 none of the mainstream press or tech blogs were abuzz about a hot government enterprise software startup.
- His lesson: work on things that (a) you know are right and (b) most people don't know yet.
- This is why Peter likes to ask: "What super valuable company is nobody building yet?"

chunks.heading: Deprogramming: focus on results and change your surroundings
chunks.text:
- Experienced founders from corporate backgrounds aren't doomed. Those who succeed avoided, overcame or escaped these habits.
- The recurring theme is results. Garry says they push founders toward action: "build product, talk to customers, that's it."
- Think in concrete numbers: user growth, savings to customer, or revenue.
- Many places let you survive without results of your own, "but startups are not one of them."
- Why YC works: it takes a village of people who all believe a thing and practice it daily. It means fundamentally changing your surroundings and the people around you.
- He says to avoid the coworking space and work harder than ever in your own space.
- YC is a concentrated form of Silicon Valley, which for decades has been where people escape corporate culture to create something new. YC lets you do it with many more like-minded people beside you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Garry Tan's README for gstack, his open source "software factory" that turns Claude Code into a virtual engineering team of role-based slash commands. It shows how one builder runs 10-15 parallel sprints with a think, plan, build, review, test, ship process, and why testing, visual design iteration and QA make AI-driven shipping safe.

chunks.heading: Garry's origin story for gstack: one builder shipping like a team of twenty
chunks.text:
- Garry built gstack after hearing Andrej Karpathy say he hadn't typed a line of code since December. He wanted to know how one person can ship like a team of twenty, and cites Peter Steinberger building OpenClaw (247K GitHub stars) essentially solo with AI agents.
- His claim: "A single builder with the right tooling can move faster than a traditional team."
- Background he cites: President & CEO of Y Combinator, early eng/PM/designer at Palantir, cofounder of Posterous (sold to Twitter), builder of Bookface (YC's internal social network). He has worked with thousands of startups such as Coinbase, Instacart and Rippling when they were one or two people.
- gstack is "how I do it": it turns Claude Code into a virtual engineering team. The roles are a CEO who rethinks the product, an eng manager who locks architecture, a designer who catches AI slop, a reviewer who finds production bugs, a QA lead who opens a real browser, a security officer running OWASP + STRIDE audits, and a release engineer who ships the PR.
- It is 23 specialists plus 8 power tools, all slash commands, all Markdown, free, MIT license. He shares it because "these tools should be available to everyone."
- Intended users: founders and CEOs (especially technical ones who still want to ship), first-time Claude Code users (structured roles instead of a blank prompt), and tech leads/staff engineers (review, QA and release automation on every PR).

chunks.heading: Garry's productivity numbers and how he measures them
chunks.text:
- Last 60 days (at time of writing): 3 production services and 40+ shipped features, built part-time while running YC full-time.
- On logical code change (not raw LOC, which AI inflates), his 2026 run rate is about 810x his 2013 pace: 11,417 vs 14 logical lines/day.
- Year-to-date through April 18, 2026 already equals 240x the entire 2013 year.
- Measured across 40 public and private `garrytan/*` repos including Bookface, after excluding one demo repo.
- GitHub contributions: 1,237 in 2026 (with a sharp acceleration in Jan-Mar) vs 772 in 2013, when he built Bookface at YC.
- He concedes critics are right that raw line counts inflate with AI, but argues that normalized for inflation he is still far more productive. "AI wrote most of it. The point isn't who typed it, it's what shipped." Methodology and a reproduction script are in `docs/ON_THE_LOC_CONTROVERSY.md`.

chunks.heading: Running 10-15 parallel sprints with a fixed process
chunks.text:
- gstack works with one sprint but is "transformative with ten running at once." Garry regularly runs 10-15 parallel sprints, which he calls the practical max right now.
- Tool: Conductor, which runs multiple Claude Code sessions in parallel, each in an isolated workspace. Example mix: one session on `/office-hours` for a new idea, one on `/review` for a PR, one implementing a feature, one on `/qa` against staging, and six more on other branches.
- Process is what makes parallelism work: "Without a process, ten agents is ten sources of chaos." The sprint is think, plan, build, review, test, ship, so each agent knows what to do and when to stop.
- He manages agents like a CEO manages a team: check in on decisions that matter, let the rest run.
- `/qa` was the unlock that took him from 6 to 12 parallel workers. The agent opens a real browser, finds the issue, fixes it, writes a regression test and verifies the fix: "The agent has eyes now."
- Voice input (AquaVoice, Whisper etc.) works because skills list spoken aliases, e.g. "security check" for `/cso`, "run QA" or "test the app" for `/qa`, "tech review" for `/plan-eng-review`.

chunks.heading: Design workflow: design-consultation, design-shotgun and design-html
chunks.text:
- `/design-consultation` builds a design system from scratch: it researches what's out there, proposes creative risks, and writes `DESIGN.md`.
- `/design-shotgun` is the exploration tool. Garry describes what he wants; it generates 4-6 AI mockup variants with GPT Image and opens a browser comparison board. He picks favorites and leaves feedback ("more whitespace", "bolder headline", "lose the gradient"), and it generates another round. After a few rounds, taste memory biases toward what he likes. His point: stop describing a vision in words and hoping; see options and iterate visually.
- `/design-html` turns an approved mockup (from shotgun, a CEO plan, a design review or a description) into production HTML/CSS using Pretext for computed text layout. Text reflows on resize and heights adjust to content, with 30KB overhead and zero dependencies. It detects React, Svelte or Vue and picks different Pretext patterns for landing pages, dashboards, forms and cards. Goal: "something you'd actually ship, not a demo."
- Works with impeccable: if installed, gstack runs impeccable's deterministic engine as a pre-pass in `/design-review`, `/review`, `/ship` and `/design-html`. It asks once before downloading the engine binary (checksum-pinned, logged, into `~/.impeccable`), reads `PRODUCT.md`, writes `DESIGN.md` in the open format both tools read, and hands deferred findings to `/impeccable <command>`. Declining changes nothing; `gstack-config set design_detector off` disables the pre-pass.

chunks.heading: Review, testing and release discipline
chunks.text:
- Smart review routing, "just like at a well-run startup": the CEO review isn't needed for infra bug fixes and design review isn't needed for backend changes. gstack tracks which reviews have run, decides what's appropriate, and shows a Review Readiness Dashboard before shipping.
- Test everything: `/ship` bootstraps a test framework if the project has none, and every run produces a coverage audit. `/qa` writes native regression tests when infrastructure exists and reports missing coverage explicitly (CSS-only fixes may use browser evidence). Goal is 100% coverage: "tests make vibe coding safe instead of yolo coding."
- `/document-release` is "the engineer you never had": it audits authored docs against the release diff and fixes factual drift before final verification; risky changes return for approval. `/ship` invokes it on every run and owns TODOS, release metadata, generation and publication.
- Multi-AI second opinion: in Claude Code `/codex` sends outside reviews to OpenAI Codex; in Codex `/claude-code` sends them to Claude Code. Each supports code review, adversarial challenge and consultation with session continuity. Reports name the provider that actually completed the review, and missing outside coverage stays visible.
- Safety guardrails on demand: `/careful` warns before rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push and git reset --hard. `/freeze` locks edits to one directory while debugging. `/guard` does both. `/investigate` auto-freezes to the module under investigation.
- Proactive suggestions: gstack detects the stage (brainstorming, reviewing, debugging, testing) and suggests the right skill; saying "stop suggesting" persists across sessions.

chunks.heading: Browser tooling that gives the agent eyes
chunks.text:
- Aside first: on a Mac with the Aside AI browser open, `/qa`, `/qa-only`, `/design-review`, `/canary`, `/benchmark`, `/scrape` and `/browse` run in the user's real browser with real logged-in sessions, in tabs the agent opens and closes itself. No cookie import; at a sign-in wall the user signs in and says "done". Page content is treated as untrusted: syntax only, never instructions.
- Fallback: on Linux, Windows or Mac without Aside, the same skills use the bundled headless Chromium that `./setup` builds.
- `/open-gstack-browser` launches GStack Browser, an AI-controlled Chromium with anti-bot stealth and the sidebar extension, so Google and NYTimes work without captchas. Regular Chrome is untouched, `$B disconnect` returns to headless, and there is no idle timeout while the window is open.
- Sidebar agent: natural language in the Chrome side panel runs a child Claude instance in an isolated session. It auto-routes Sonnet for fast actions (click, navigate, screenshot) and Opus for reading and analysis, with up to 5 minutes per task. Example personal automation: browse a kid's school parent portal and add the parents' names, phone numbers and photos to Google Contacts. Auth is either logging in once in the headed browser or one-click cookie import from real Chrome.
- Browser handoff: on a CAPTCHA, auth wall or MFA, `$B handoff` opens visible Chrome at the same page with cookies and tabs intact; `$B resume` continues after the user solves it. The agent suggests it automatically after 3 consecutive failures.
- `/pair-agent` lets agents from different vendors (Claude Code, OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex) share one browser. The user pastes a printed instruction block into the other agent, which exchanges a one-time setup key for a session token and gets its own isolated tab. ngrok enables cross-machine use. Security: scoped tokens, tab isolation, rate limiting, domain restrictions, activity attribution.

chunks.heading: Prompt injection defense for the sidebar agent
chunks.text:
- Garry ships a layered defense against hostile pages hijacking the agent.
- Content filters on every page read: datamarking, hidden-element stripping, ARIA scrubbing and a URL blocklist.
- A 22MB ML classifier runs locally in a sidecar subprocess and scans page-derived content before the agent sees it. A verdict combiner requires classifier agreement before blocking, which avoids single-model false positives on pages like Stack Overflow instruction posts.
- Everything runs on-device with no network calls. Emergency kill switch: `GSTACK_SECURITY_OFF=1`. Full details are in `ARCHITECTURE.md`.

Boil the Oceans

You know the phrase: “don’t boil the ocean.” Everyone’s said it in some overly ambitious meeting. It’s good advice in normal times. It keeps teams focused. It prevents scope creep. But we are no longer in normal times, and I think it’s time to retire saying it.

Artificial Superintelligence means it’s time to boil the ocean. We’ll start with a few lakes first.

I was recently with a university endowment’s head of private investing who told me their engineers were terrified for their jobs after seeing what Claude Code could do. And I get it — that’s the natural first reaction. But it’s the wrong one. It’s a zero-sum reaction to a positive-sum moment.

Instead of worrying about doing the same thing we’ve been doing for cheaper, why not focus on doing the thing we never even dreamed of doing? Why can’t that endowment achieve 50% net IRR instead of 10%? Why can’t a startup deliver a service that is 100x better than the incumbent? Why can’t we have fusion energy? Why can’t we talk to every single user and have a perfect understanding of every bug in our product?

These aren’t rhetorical questions anymore. They’re engineering problems with paths to solutions.

Here is what I think is actually going on with the fear: our fear of the future is directly proportional to how small our ambitions are. If your plan is to keep doing exactly what you’re doing, then yes, a machine that can do it faster and cheaper is terrifying. But if your plan is to do something dramatically bigger, then the machine is the best news you’ve ever gotten.

If you’re a worker — someone who trades labor for a living — this is the moment to become a builder. Start a business. And if you’re already management or capital, it’s time to go 10x more hardcore on what your aspirations could be. Not eking out 5% efficiency gains. Not increasing profit margins 2% by lowering cost and firing people. Those are the old games. The new question is: what would it look like to build a product or service so good that people would happily pay 10x what they pay now?

The net result of this is more jobs, not fewer. As Ryan Petersen likes to say, the human desire for more things is absolutely limitless. We can actually fulfill that desire now — if we have the agency to prompt it for ourselves.

Buckminster Fuller coined the term “ephemeralization” in 1938: doing more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing. His entire vision of progress was about technology enabling radical expansion of human capability through dematerialization. He traced this from stone bridges to iron trusses to steel cables — each iteration stronger, longer, lighter, cheaper. He wasn’t describing job destruction. He was describing civilization getting better at being civilization.

This is Jevons Paradox for everything. When you make a resource dramatically more efficient, you don’t use less of it — you use vastly more. Steam engines didn’t reduce coal consumption. They made coal so useful that demand exploded. The same thing is about to happen with intelligence, with labor, with every service and product we can imagine.

But Jevons Paradox doesn’t activate on its own. It requires capital and management to actually raise their ambitions — to boil lakes and oceans instead of drowning them in committee

That’s what startups have always been good at: moving fast in the face of radical uncertainty, building for the 10x future while everyone else is optimizing for the 1.05x present.

People get high on abstraction too early. They want the system before they’ve earned the insight.

But the good abstractions are never designed. They’re discovered. You do the stupid manual thing enough times and the real bottleneck just emerges. Your initial agency might be driven by a hunch you had in the shower, but that moment won’t get you all the way to making something people want. The right way to make anything is forced on you by reality: what are the real jobs to be done? And what sequence?

This is why “do things that don’t scale” still hits, especially now when AI makes it trivially easy to scale things that probably shouldn’t be scaled yet. PG’s point was never about suffering. It was about contact. When you’re the one manually doing the loop, you see the edge cases. The weird user behavior. The failure modes nobody designed for. The hidden dependencies that only show up at 2am when some flow or intermediate step breaks in a way you didn’t anticipate. If you automate before you have that contact, you just scale your misunderstanding faster.

When the machines can help you vibe code perfection it gives you a false sense of power. I love that feeling as much as you do. But fuck perfection. Do it live. Be the loop. 

Feel every friction point. Notice what’s actually true every single time versus what just looked true because you hadn’t seen enough cases yet. Formalize that. Build the recursive version. Then keep checking that your abstraction is still attached to real humans and their needs. Because reality drifts. Your users drift. The ground truth changes under you. You may think you understand but no plan survives contact with the real users and what they want. You find those body blows in analytics and user feedback and we call them the roadmap. 

Humans left with not enough data hallucinate too. But just like the LLMs with enough data you unlock real transcendence. Real utility. Prosperity for humans in real life. 

The abstraction is a tool, not a destination. The moment you forget that, you’re cooked.

Founders— when things are great, really celebrate that. Share that with your team and savor it. 

When things are falling apart, the key is to take action, don’t be paralyzed, and really focus on self care: sleep, food, exercise, then back to work. This too shall pass.

The secret to an articulate agent like mine isn't one file. It's three:

SOUL.md — Who the agent IS. Voice, values, operating principles, what good output looks like, what bad output looks like. Not a system prompt, a constitution. Mine says things like "brevity is mandatory," "humor is mandatory," "never open with 'Great question,'" "swearing is allowed when it lands." The more specific and opinionated this is, the less your agent sounds like a chatbot. Write it like you're briefing your smartest friend on how to be you, not like you're configuring software.

USER.md — Who YOU are. Not a bio — a deep model. How your mind works, what you're building, your strengths, your blind spots, your family, your temperament, what triggers you, what you care about. The more the agent understands about you, the better it can serve you. Mine is ~4000 words.

AGENTS.md — Operational rules. What to check on every message, what to never do, how to handle failures, lookup chains, path rules, brain-first protocols. This is the playbook for how it works, not who it is.

The articulation comes from SOUL.md being brutally specific about voice. Generic instructions → generic output. If you write "be helpful and concise" you get ChatGPT. If you write "speak like a peer with taste, one sentence when one sentence works, uncomfortable truths welcome if actually true, language with voltage" — you get something alive.

The autism loop: run your own model to the floor, ignore consensus, hold a thesis when everyone says you're wrong. That makes conviction.

The empathy loop: feel what the user feels, sense what the market wants before it has words. That makes traction.

Most people crank one and starve the other. Pure conviction builds something brilliant nobody wants. Pure empathy builds consensus mush.

PG put the whole job in four words: make something people want. The autism loop makes the something. The empathy loop knows it's wanted. The founder is the bridge.

Most great founders show up dominant in the first loop. That's why they're contrarian enough to try at all. The work is grafting on the second.
